title: Decide whether Eon agent workspaces need isolated execution targets
description:
## Why

Eon may eventually gain meaningful security and portability value if an agent workspace can run behind an attachable execution target instead of sharing the human host account and filesystem by default. The source discussion combines that useful boundary with agent dashboards, transparent container navigation, microVM lifecycle, and virtualized GPU work; only the execution-target decision is distinct from existing Eon workspace planning.

## Evidence

- Source discussion: https://github.com/luccahuguet/yazelix/discussions/685.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Product boundary` assigns product policy and launch to Eon, persistent sessions, attachment, and transport to Orbit, and native presentation to Venus.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Sequencing` requires Orbit and Venus proof before Eon composition.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Ownership rules` permits Eon boundary adaptation while forbidding duplicate child behavior.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` section `Activation boundary` requires later slices to earn scope through dogfood.
- `eon-pxn` owns local Eon workspace topology and explicitly leaves remote machines outside its first slice.
- Apple Containerization runs Linux containers in separate lightweight VMs on supported macOS hosts: https://github.com/apple/containerization.
- microvm.nix provides NixOS microVMs across multiple Linux hypervisors and vfkit on macOS: https://github.com/microvm-nix/microvm.nix.

## Decision Contract

After the local Eon workspace slice is proven, decide whether one demonstrated agent-security or remote-workflow need justifies an execution-target contract. Compare doing nothing, a restricted host user reached through ordinary SSH, an existing remote SSH host, rootless OCI execution, and one platform-native microVM provider. Start from an explicit threat model and user workflow rather than assuming that containers are always insufficient.

If a target contract is justified, Eon owns target selection and product lifecycle policy, Orbit owns the smallest attachment or transport mechanism, Venus displays target identity and state, and the selected external provider owns VM or container mechanics. A valid decision may be to keep workspaces host-local.

## Scope

In scope:
- Name protected assets, trusted and untrusted actors, credential boundaries, repository access, network policy, persistence, and recovery expectations.
- Evaluate one concrete Linux path using exact primary-source revisions. EON-C7 excludes macOS/X11/Xwayland host implementation and proof; provider portability is background evidence, not Eon support scope.
- Define the smallest user-visible target identity, attach, failure, shutdown, and cleanup behavior only if evidence requires it.
- Determine whether existing SSH and provider CLIs satisfy the behavior without an Eon provider framework.
- Route any missing transport mechanism to a separately approved Orbit contract before Eon consumes it.

Out of scope:
- Agent dashboards or panels already covered by workspace and Venus planning.
- VM, container, SSH, filesystem, networking, credential-broker, or sandbox implementation.
- Literal filesystem traversal across hosts, transparent path equivalence, multi-tenant hosting, multiplayer, web/mobile, or automatic repository synchronization.
- Virtio-GPU, GUI applications inside guests, DRM Native Context, GPU sharing, or desktop virtualization.
- Claims that a restricted user, rootless container, or microVM is secure without a stated threat model and platform proof.
- Nova compatibility or changes to the first local Eon workspace contract.

## Implementation Notes

1. Begin only after `eon-pxn` proves useful local multi-session workspace behavior and dogfood records a concrete isolation or remote-target need.
2. Inspect exact revisions of microvm.nix, the selected Linux OCI or microVM candidate, and Ptyxis only for terminal-target UX; retain Apple Containerization as historical comparison rather than a required macOS investigation; distinguish OCI image/runtime compatibility from VM lifecycle and terminal attachment.
3. Compare no feature, restricted user plus SSH, remote SSH, rootless OCI, and one microVM shape on ownership, security boundary, startup cost, filesystem and credential exposure, recovery, Linux fit, dependencies, and removal cost.
4. Prefer direct invocation of an existing provider and an ordinary Orbit endpoint over a generic provider abstraction.
5. Record one recommendation, meaningful rejections, the evidence that would reverse it, and the cheapest isolated proof. Do not implement during this decision bead.

## Verification

- `br show eon-pxn --json` must confirm the local workspace prerequisite and its deferred remote scope.
- `rg -n "Orbit|Venus|Eon|transport|launch" docs/ARCHITECTURE.md docs/CONTRACTS.md` must identify current owners before proposing a contract.
- Every security and platform claim must cite an exact primary-source revision and the exercised platform; compilation or documentation alone is narrower evidence.
- The final Bead state must contain the threat model, ownership map, comparison, recommendation, dependency and tool impact, residual risk, and explicit user decision.
- No runtime, contract index, documentation, dependency, package, CI, or ambient user configuration changes during the decision.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if no dogfooded user need exceeds ordinary host-local or SSH behavior.
- Stop if the proposal requires a generic provider framework before one concrete provider proves value.
- Stop and request a product decision before adding an Orbit transport, security guarantee, credential owner, or supported remote-platform promise.
- Stop if isolation cannot protect the named assets without exposing equal authority through shared credentials, writable mounts, or host control.

## Maintenance Notes

Priority P4 and deferred pending local AgentRun dogfood and explicit user selection; `eon-pxn` is the related horizon, not a requirement to complete every unrelated epic feature. Decision effort M, implementation risk HIGH, confidence HIGH in the ownership boundary and LOW that microVM support will be justified before dogfood. Rejected as separate Beads: hideable agent panel because existing workspace and Venus planning owns it; transparent container-as-directory UX because it misstates the boundary; GPU virtualization because no Eon contract needs it.

## Docker VMM and Sandboxes evidence — 2026-08-12

- Docker announced the rebuilt first-party Docker VMM in public beta for Docker Desktop 4.86 on Mac and Windows: https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-vmm-public-beta/. The VMM is an internal virtualization layer beneath Docker Desktop; the same engine also powers Docker Sandboxes. Docker states that Linux support is planned for GA, but that roadmap is not current Linux proof.
- Current Docker VMM documentation records beta status, a 4 GB VM-memory minimum, manual host-directory sharing, absent Rosetta support, and known virtiofs/database limitations: https://docs.docker.com/desktop/features/vmm/. Eon must not target VMM internals or treat beta claims as a product contract.
- Docker Sandboxes supplies the relevant product boundary: a standalone `sbx` CLI creates per-agent microVMs with private Docker daemons, filesystems, and networks; Docker Desktop is not required: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/ and https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/get-started/. Current documented hosts are Apple-silicon macOS 14+, x86_64 Windows 11, and Ubuntu 24.04+ on x86_64 or aarch64 with KVM. NixOS support is unproved.
- Sandbox SSH integration is GA in `sbx` 0.37.0 or later. A named sandbox is addressable as `<name>.sbx` through an `sbx`-owned ProxyCommand, which is the narrowest plausible Orbit attachment path: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/integrations/.
- The default direct workspace mount is read-write and therefore does not protect the repository from the agent. Clone mode keeps the source mount read-only and moves work to a private clone. Shared agent skills are also mounted read-write by default unless disabled, and local MCP servers execute outside the VM boundary: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/security/.
- Sandboxes persist their VM, packages, Docker state, and agent state until explicit removal, and trade one VM plus one private daemon per sandbox for the stronger boundary: https://docs.docker.com/ai/sandboxes/architecture/.

## Current recommendation

Docker Sandboxes is the leading concrete microVM candidate only when dogfood demonstrates an autonomous-agent need for host isolation plus full Docker capabilities. Preserve the existing comparison against no feature, restricted-user SSH, remote SSH, and rootless OCI. Prefer direct use of the supported `sbx` CLI and its ordinary SSH facade; do not add a Docker SDK, Docker VMM API, Docker Desktop requirement, Eon-owned sandbox dashboard, mirrored provider state, or generic execution-provider framework. If protecting the working tree is part of the threat model, reject direct-mount mode and evaluate clone mode. Keep this decision deferred and P4 until one real workflow supplies the protected assets and failure cost.
design:
## Ghosthub-derived comparison constraints

Use Ghosthub 0.7.0 revision 072cc83559bd590ed5d759af05ec0a1868dbf359 only when remote SSH remains a credible candidate. Inspect its architecture, terminal-session contract, and threat model as comparison evidence; AGPL source is inspection-only and no Ghosthub, tmux, Herdr, or kwt compatibility is implied. These are decision gates, not adopted Eon behavior.

- Keep target inventory, liveness, and failures target-scoped. Cached rows may support navigation but never authorize attach, restore, mutation, or a live-state claim. One unreachable target must not make other targets unavailable or merge their inventories into one authority.
- Require a fresh owner-authored probe and exact target plus Session identity before attach, restoration, or mutation. A same-named replacement is a different target unless the selected provider proves a stronger stable identity.
- Keep detach, transport reconnect, target stop, and target deletion distinct. Reconnect must be bounded, serialized per target, cancelable, and non-destructive.
- Delegate host-key verification, authentication, effective route configuration, and encryption to system OpenSSH. Never weaken configured policy; invalidate cached connection authority when the endpoint, route, effective SSH configuration, known-hosts identity, or credentials change.
- Prefer no Eon-installed helper. If one is unavoidable, require an exact version for the detected OS and architecture, verify its digest after transfer, install it in a private per-user namespace, never replace a system binary, and define upgrade, rollback, partial-failure, and removal behavior.
- Keep credentials and interactive responses out of process arguments, environment, logs, durable Eon state, and provider-neutral schemas. Name the narrower unavoidable exposure and owner for each candidate.

Reject treating process names, cached output, or successful prior attachment as current authority; automatic enrollment of unknown hosts; retry that can create or mutate a target after the original one-shot authorization; and a generic remote-provider framework before one concrete target proves value.

## Docker comparison constraints

- Candidate interface: exact supported `sbx` CLI release plus its documented SSH facade. Docker VMM is provider-owned implementation evidence, never an Eon contract or dependency.
- Ownership: Eon may own target selection and lifecycle policy; Docker owns microVM, container daemon, mount, network, credential, persistence, and cleanup mechanisms; Orbit owns Session, PTY, and attachment; Venus may display opaque target identity and owner-authored state.
- Before selection, verify the exact `sbx` release, license and redistribution terms, CLI stability and machine-readable output, login and offline behavior, telemetry, behavior on the selected Linux/KVM host, stable target identity, SSH setup side effects, stop/restart/remove semantics, disk reclamation, clone/direct mount guarantees, shared-skill defaults, network and credential boundaries, and removal cost.
- Cheapest proof if activated: use a disposable repository and one named clone-mode sandbox; attach through the documented SSH path; prove exact target plus Orbit Session identity, stop/restart distinction, explicit removal, working-tree boundary, network/credential expectations, and cleanup. Do not install ambient SSH configuration or change host policy without explicit user authorization.
- Reject Docker Sandboxes if the demonstrated workflow needs only ordinary host execution or SSH, if behavior on the selected Linux host cannot be proved, if login or lifecycle requirements violate the chosen local-first contract, or if shared mounts, credentials, skills, MCP tools, or host control expose authority equivalent to the host execution being replaced.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The final comparison applies the Ghosthub-derived gates to no feature, restricted user plus SSH, an existing remote SSH host, rootless OCI, and one platform-native microVM candidate without assuming that Eon must support remote targets.
2. For every surviving candidate, the decision names the authoritative target and Session identity, distinguishes cached discovery from fresh liveness, defines same-name replacement behavior, and states what authorizes attach, restore, and mutation.
3. Failure and recovery policy is target-scoped and falsifiable: one unreachable target does not block other targets; reconnect is bounded, serialized, cancelable, and cannot stop, delete, create, or mutate work without a separate exact authorization.
4. Any SSH shape preserves system OpenSSH host-key, authentication, route, and encryption policy and invalidates cached authority after a relevant effective-configuration or identity change.
5. The decision either selects no helper or records exact helper ownership, OS and architecture selection, post-transfer digest verification, private installation path, upgrade, rollback, partial-failure, and removal behavior without replacing a system binary.
6. Credential and secret handling covers arguments, environment, logs, persistence, UI, helper transfer, and interactive authentication, and the threat model states any residual user-account or configured-host trust.
7. The user explicitly chooses keep workspaces host-local, defer, or authorize one separately scoped target contract. Closure creates no runtime, protocol, helper, dependency, supported host, security promise, or provider framework.
notes:
Durability reconciliation — 2026-08-12: eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf owns the product decision across presentation loss, Eon supervisor loss, reboot, and machine loss. eon-az9 remains only the remote or isolated execution-target decision. Activate it if the user selects remote compute as the stronger host-loss tier; local same-boot adoption, reboot reconstruction, or encrypted metadata sync do not require an execution-target framework. Ordinary SSH access to a still-running host also does not prove continuity after that host is lost. No dependency is added because the durability decision may choose a wholly local outcome.

Docker reconciliation — 2026-08-12: after reviewing the Docker VMM public-beta announcement and current Docker Sandboxes documentation, the user authorized the planning update. The evidence strengthens Docker Sandboxes as the first concrete candidate but selects no provider and changes no EON contract, dependency, implementation, status, priority, or prerequisite. Keep P4 and deferred until local AgentRun dogfood demonstrates a threat-model need. Docker VMM itself remains below the intended integration boundary.

Unpeel remote-control comparison — 2026-08-15:
- Exact primary source: Unpeel 0.2.0 revision 9580a83f009fe19775116cacb46e74570958ca56 and docs/plans/host-controller-transports.md.
- Comparison constraints: keep Host identity, advertised capabilities, liveness, output cursor, and connection generation explicit across direct, SSH, and relay transports. Resume reads from a committed cursor; do not automatically replay an effect after transport loss leaves its outcome ambiguous. A transport carries the same semantic contract and never invents product verbs.
- Boundary: controlling an existing remote Host is transport and presentation continuity, not proof that the execution target survives loss of that Host. It contributes to laptop-loss continuity only when the work already runs on a separately authoritative remote target.
- Rejected inheritance: an Eon-operated relay, account, pairing protocol, mobile controller, Unpeel compatibility, inferred capabilities, automatic ambiguous retries, or a generic transport/provider framework.
- Planning disposition: comparison evidence only. Keep this decision P4 and deferred until local AgentRun dogfood demonstrates a remote or isolation need; select no target, transport, helper, dependency, or security promise.

Planning-only batch authorized by the user on 2026-08-15; no issue was claimed.

2026-09-08 scope reconciliation: accepted local topology is already implemented. Activation still needs a concrete local AgentRun isolation/remote-workflow case and an explicit user decision; it does not require closure of every eon-pxn horizon. Current EON-C7 limits any selected host proof to separately approved Linux scope. Historical provider support matrices remain dated evidence to recheck, not current platform promises.

title: Remove Venus's macOS unsafe code for the CPU and RAM chips
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-27, to eon-overseer: "but create a bead to remove unsafe later". He gave it when he approved option (a) for eon-mac-launch-kz4p.3.

kz4p.3 relaxes Venus's lib root from `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to `#![deny(unsafe_code)]`. It adds one macOS-only `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` module in `venus/src/system.rs`: five Mach/sysctl calls for the CPU and RAM chips, each with a SAFETY note, using `libc =0.2.189` as a macOS-only dependency. The bin root keeps `forbid`.

## Goal

Venus's lib root returns to `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, with the macOS chips still working.

## Options (choose under the reference gate; recommend one)

- A maintained crate that wraps these calls in a safe API, for example `sysinfo`, which already uses the same RAM formula. That moves the unsafe code to an owner that maintains it, at the cost of a dependency (AP-DEPENDENCY-001: weigh transitive weight against owning five calls).
- Move the readings out of Venus. Eon Runtime, or another owner that already allows unsafe code, reads them and sends the values. That changes which component owns the reading and maybe a protocol, so it is a contract question for Lucca.
- A safe Rust binding that appears upstream later (watch `libc`, `mach2`).

## Prerequisites

eon-mac-launch-kz4p.3 landed. Native proof of the chips (kz4p.12), so the replacement can be compared against known-good readings.

## Acceptance

- `venus/src/lib.rs` is `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` again, and no `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` remains in Venus.
- The macOS chips read the same values as kz4p.3's approved definitions (VEN-C28, EON-C30), checked natively.
- Linux is unchanged.

## Scope boundary

No change to what the chips show, and no new widget.

title: Bind stop confirmation to the observed supervisor
description:
## Contract routing

Harden EON-C11 without changing its command surface. The consumer is one local user or automation invoking `eon stop GENERATION [--json]`; the trigger is a stop attempt whose validated control-socket owner is replaced before mutation; the result is that Eon stops only the supervisor instance it validated or fails explicitly while preserving the replacement and every Session. Normal same-owner human and JSON stop behavior remains unchanged.

This correction adds no EONW field, command, compatibility window, persisted runtime identity, child contract, or distribution promise.

## Why

Human stop confirmation currently describes supervisor A, waits for input, then opens a fresh path and accepts a same-generation response from supervisor B. Session labels restart at `session-1`, so the displayed generation and Session names do not bind the destructive action to A.

The exact audit reproduction stopped A, started B under the same generation while the old prompt waited, then answered `y`; the old confirmation terminated B and exited successfully.

Impact: HIGH. Effort: S/M. Implementation risk: MEDIUM. Confidence: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:840-879`: `stop_generation` inspects and displays one `GenerationRecord`, then waits without retaining the observed control-socket identity.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:881-905`: stop opens a new connection and accepts a `Stopped` response when only the generation string matches.
- `crates/eon/src/main.rs:315-357` and `:1439-1471`: presentation already captures and revalidates `SocketIdentity`, proving the repository has the needed owner mechanism.
- `eon-audit-eon-runtime-lifecycle-wqz` comment 271 records the exact 1b8836e reproduction, hashes, reference gate, and cleanup.
- EON-C11 in `docs/CONTRACTS.md` requires confirmed stop to name affected live Sessions and failure to preserve Sessions.

## Prerequisite and reference gate

- No implementation prerequisite. Fix this correctness defect before `eon-5rp` moves another owner out of `main.rs`; that refactor must preserve the corrected lifecycle behavior.
- Rebaseline the cited symbols after any intervening revision.
- Reuse the audit reference gate: Eon HEAD `1b8836e616222f29c57ac697916872010db14685`; Orbit source `64db581445bafca1a08a6530f8e44f9c1edbc169` with ORBS v2 proof `9d6d2bb37f20ab4ad9e186c7bc715eabef43e757`; Ghosthub lifecycle comparison `072cc83559bd590ed5d759af05ec0a1868dbf359`.
- Preserve fresh backend authority and exact destructive-target revalidation. Reject PID, process-name, pathname-only, or cached Session-name authority.
- No dependency or crate feature is expected. Stop for the crate gate and user approval before changing any manifest.

## Scope

In scope:
- `stop_generation` and the smallest existing runtime probe/connection helpers needed to retain and revalidate one `SocketIdentity`.
- One real-process regression in `crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs`.
- EON-C11 current-state proof metadata, `CHANGELOG.md`, and README LOC only as required after the accepted fix.

Out of scope:
- EONW schema or protocol changes, a supervisor nonce, PID files, process-tree inspection, persisted registries, daemonization, legacy stop support, compatibility windows, or child-repository changes.
- Changing confirmation policy, generation selection, Session naming, JSON structure beyond an existing bounded failure shape, attach behavior, or ordinary successful stop semantics.
- Refactoring unrelated runtime or managed-environment code.

## Implementation notes

1. Write the real-process regression first: pause a human stop after it displays A, stop A through its owner, start same-generation B, answer `y`, and require a bounded nonzero owner-changed failure while B and its child remain live.
2. Bind inspection and mutation to one validated socket identity. After confirmation, revalidate and send on the verified connection so replacement between check and use fails closed.
3. Route human and JSON stop through the same owner-bound helper where that removes duplicate policy; do not add a new protocol identity when the local socket identity is sufficient.
4. Preserve the current response-before-termination ordering and exact supervisor-owned cleanup.

## Acceptance

- The replacement regression fails on the audited implementation and passes after the fix.
- A prompt produced from supervisor A can never terminate same-generation supervisor B after path replacement.
- The failure is bounded, nonzero, and names that the validated supervisor changed; B, Venus state, and every B Session remain live.
- Human cancellation still changes nothing.
- Same-owner human and JSON stop still return the authoritative stopped Session list and terminate only that supervisor children.
- Existing presentation, attach, legacy, concurrent-launch, child-exit, workspace, and generation tests retain their observable results.
- No new product contract, EONW value, dependency, component identity, or public configuration surface is introduced.

## Verification

- `cargo test --locked -p eon --test workspace_control stop_confirmation_refuses_a_replacement_supervisor` should exit 0 and prove B remains live.
- `cargo test --locked -p eon --test workspace_control concurrent_launches_converge_and_generation_stop_is_owner_routed` should exit 0.
- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `cargo check --locked --workspace`
- `cargo test --locked --workspace`
- `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v1.json`
- `nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --no-update-lock-file path:.#default`
- `nix flake check --no-build --no-update-lock-file path:.`
- `git diff --check`
- After the proof-bearing commit, refresh the active `eon` profile without stopping running supervisors; verify the profile resolves the new artifact and report restart required for already-running generations.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the current stop owner or EON-C11 contract has drifted materially.
- Stop if a correct fix requires a new protocol field, persisted instance identity, dependency, cross-repository change, or destructive process inference.
- Stop if the regression cannot distinguish A from B without relying on timing alone.
- Stop if the same verification failure repeats twice after a reasonable correction.

## Maintenance notes

The first sufficient fix reuses Eon existing socket identity and owner-bound connection pattern. Reject a general lifecycle token framework, manager daemon, or broad stop redesign. The final `eon-audit-eon-runtime-lifecycle-wqz` pass must rerun this regression after `eon-5rp`.

title: Add a toggleable bottom shortcut hints bar
description:
## Contract

A full-Eon user can see a compact native shortcut-hints row at the bottom of the window and toggle it with physical Alt+Shift+B, like Nova. Start visible in a fresh window; retain that window's choice across tab switches, popup open/close and resize. Showing reserves one compact row; hiding returns its space to terminal content. The toggle also appears in the existing Alt+/ Shortcuts viewer so it remains discoverable when the row is hidden.

Show concise key/action pairs for real Eon workspace actions and enabled tool shortcuts, derived from the same descriptors and current popup catalog used by dispatch and the full viewer. Group shared modifiers once, following current native focus. Spread compact groups across the bar with outer groups at 12 logical-pixel side insets and equal inter-group gaps of at least 24 pixels at default typography; center a lone group. Keep 12-pixel within-group gaps. Give only each modifier header a rounded background, with 6-pixel inner side padding included in measured fitting. Keep the group bodies plain. Align the main region and footer sides using the existing pane inset (4 logical pixels at default typography). Use one continuous outer frame with the main region corner radius (12 logical pixels), a straight single-pixel separator at the join and the same bottom inset as the hidden-footer main frame (6 logical pixels at default typography). Reserve the bottom gap in addition to the compact hints row height, with a minimum row height equal to the existing corner radius; preserve hidden-footer rendering, input and pane-frame visibility. All spacing participates in whole-hint fitting. Use the inactive-tab background for the bar and the shared restrained outline, and coral red (#FF6B6B) modifier headers without braces separated from mint keys with gray labels. Omit F6, Project, Copy, Paste and Open link from compact hints while retaining their bindings and full-help entries. Compact group headers use C/A/S aliases and hyphens without braces, such as A-S; the tab range is shown as 1..9; concise labels include keys and hints. One move hint groups horizontal H/L and vertical K/J keys while full help and accessible labels retain the complete chords and distinct tab/pane actions. Creation labels retain their explicit tab, pane, or window target. Omit the header ? only when the visible bar fits every applicable hint, retaining it while keyboard-focused; retain Alt+/ and the full viewer. No minor mode exists yet; future real modes replace contents from their actual binding projection without a mode framework in this slice. Prioritize useful core actions and the hints/full-Shortcuts escape hatch; fit whole hints to the available width, dropping lower-priority entries rather than clipping a key into a misleading chord. Preserve keyboard focus, selected tab/pane, live processes and input. Normal terminal resizing is expected; a presentation toggle must not create/restart terminals or send its key bytes to them.

## Evidence and reference gate

Inspected 2026-10-11:
- Nova `38a5e29eb078e939d9729dfdbbdf3362292c20b9`: `docs/runtime-notes.md:224-259` describes Alt+Shift+B, visible-by-default startup, reclaiming the row and whole-hint fitting with workspace/action priorities. `defaults/zellij/layout.kdl:6-111` defines a one-row compact grouped-modifier display; `defaults/config.toml:41` supplies Nova's startup preference. Nova packages zjhints upstream `709d56292217920a5b7e2702302cd66b60ed6477` with `prototypes/zellij-distribution/zjhints-group-modifiers.patch` (`flake.nix:680-719`). These are comparison evidence, not an Eon dependency or copied implementation.
- Venus HEAD `14f6e7e32ff5dccf1f5f9b0b9c79faa2e11be18b` (current accepted runtime pin `58f2eaa8057627bdbf73262fdb10a1dc8b681ffc`): `src/application.rs:728` FIXED_SHORTCUTS and `shortcut_groups_for` already share native bindings with dispatch and project current popup entries; `workspace_scene:1639` and `initial_window_size:4539` feed native geometry/grid admission. `src/scene.rs:395,732` owns workspace/terminal rectangles. `src/render.rs`, `src/accessibility.rs` and `src/input.rs:402` own drawing, AccessKit and captured shortcut press/release sequences. VEN-C20/EON-C20 own the existing read-only full viewer.
- Eon Runtime `e30cf43b7ccc752d33edd4626aabbc4fd1cec579`, `crates/eon-runtime/src/managed_environment.rs:547`: popup collision validation reserves fixed workspace keys but currently does not reserve Alt+Shift+B. Reserve the chosen toggle there before delivery; do not silently steal an existing configured popup chord.
- Eon edge HEAD `d3b280870e046246f91c3c82f235c3ef9c6e90e5` has pre-existing working-tree changes. EON-C20/EON-C21 and each owner's reference routing remain the accepted baseline.

Before code, recheck exact sources, relevant native layout/input references and accepted child pins. Adopt Nova's compactness, toggle/reclaimed space and binding truth. Reject its Zellij modes, hint panes, plugin metadata and session-controller persistence: Eon has native window presentation and an existing canonical shortcut owner.

## Ownership, prerequisites and scope

Eon owns the chosen product outcome/default and exact composition. Venus owns one window-local visibility state, hint projection, responsive geometry, rendering, input precedence and accessibility. Eon Runtime keeps popup catalog validation/collision enforcement. Orbit owns terminal resizing and state; use its existing path. Existing EONW popup facts should suffice; no speculative schema or new dependency is planned.

The native viewer and Eon Bar prerequisites are accepted (`eon-deliver-native-shortcut-viewer-rif`, `eon-deliver-native-eon-bar-w4d`). This is independent of the version badge and Claude/Grok quota work; add no artificial blocking edge. Follow one active frontier, accept required owner changes, then pin accepted revisions in Eon and record the product contract before delivery.

Scope is one native, read-only bottom hints row, its toggle, the existing shortcut viewer entry, collision protection and affected geometry/grid/IME/hit/accessibility paths. Update affected documentation, changelog and LOC when implemented. Reuse current shaping and renderer; require no registry, second shortcut catalog, command polling or dependency.

No child-application key discovery, Zellij input modes, interactive hint buttons, new command palette, custom rebinding/settings UI, cross-window/session synchronization, durable visibility preference or platform expansion. Persistence beyond the current window is unspecified and requires a separate product choice.

## Acceptance and cheapest falsifiers

1. One isolated installed native x86_64 Linux Wayland workflow shows a readable single-row bar; Alt+Shift+B hides/restores it exactly once per press, captures repeats/releases, returns/reclaims the expected viewport space and retains the choice across tabs and popups. Full Shortcuts lists the toggle even when hints are hidden. The normal modal viewer's input-isolation contract remains intact.
2. Displayed hints agree with actual fixed dispatch and enabled/remapped tool entries; Project and F6 remain in full help; removed entries disappear and no child-application shortcuts are invented. A configured Alt+Shift+B popup collision fails clearly before workspace mutation. Use focused red/green checks for that boundary and shortcut capture, reusing existing harnesses rather than literal mirror tests.
3. Ordinary/narrow/tiny windows and scale changes fit whole hints, keep the top bar usable and preserve valid grid admission, terminal/popup geometry, IME placement, hit regions and accessible text. Repeated toggles preserve selected identities, focus, running processes and subsequent terminal input; normal resize is the only terminal effect.
4. Prove affected owner builds and the applicable Rust/Nix boundaries, then exact accepted manifest/lock composition. Refresh the active eon profile without restarting live supervisors and verify the installed behavior. Validate the approved Nix-free alpha artifact if its packaging changes. Record exact revisions, environment, commands/observations and proof phase; a mock or screenshot alone is insufficient.

Stop and resolve scope if sources have materially drifted or this needs a second shortcut/visibility owner, generic widget framework, new protocol contract or broader persistence. Existing live user work and desktop focus must remain intact.

title: Find refactor candidates: long files and tangled modules
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-28: "create a bead to check long files or files that we should refactor in general,
so we can find candidates". Several files have grown large enough to slow review and agent work
(context cost, merge collisions between parallel slices). Line counts at 7888609, tracked sources:

    8514 venus/src/application.rs
    7048 venus/src/render.rs
    6685 venus/src/scene.rs
    6638 eon/crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs
    5930 runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/workspace.rs
    3982 runtime/crates/eon-workspace-protocol/src/v23.rs
    3846 venus/src/accessibility.rs
    3478 runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/supervisor.rs
    2815 runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/sessions.rs
    2771 venus/src/render/chrome.rs
    2202 runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/managed_environment.rs
    2186 orbit/tests/lifecycle.rs

(orbit/proof/{view,lease,step}.bend are 60-74k lines; check whether they are generated before
treating them as candidates.)

## Contract

None. An audit that produces candidates; it changes no code and no contract.

## Change

Survey the workspace (Rust, Nix, Bend, shell, mac-proof tooling) and rank refactor candidates.
Length is one signal, not the criterion. Also look for: modules with more than one owner of a
behaviour or data structure (AGENTS.md "one owner"), duplicated logic across crates, long
functions, test files that mix unrelated suites, files most often touched by parallel slices
(`git log --name-only` churn and co-change), and dead code. For each candidate record: file and
size, the problem in one line, the proposed split or simplification, the owner boundary it keeps,
risk (wire/protocol, lifecycle, proof checks it would touch), and rough cost.

## Acceptance

- A ranked candidate list in a comment on this bead, with the evidence above for each.
- One child bead per candidate Lucca picks (each small, per the small-beads rule), not before.
- Generated or proof-owned files are identified and excluded, with the reason.

## Scope

Read-only investigation; delegate the reading to subagents. No refactors in this bead. Not on the
macOS launch path (eon-mac-launch-kz4p); do not schedule it ahead of that work.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Approval, relayed by eon-overseer (2026-10-29): Lucca, 2026-10-28: "create a bead to check long files or files that we should refactor in general, so we can find candidates"; Lucca, 2026-10-29: "we need to do more eon stuff / can we fire more agents?", choosing this bead. Roles (Lucca, 2026-10-28, relayed): Opus plans and gates, Codex does the reading; read-only, no child beads until Lucca picks.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Lucca, 2026-10-29, agreeing with the recommendation: pick candidates 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 (relayed by eon-overseer). Picking the Venus items approves their test modules (venus/AGENTS.md).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Ranked refactor candidates at 0b6ef93 (survey: Codex gpt-6.1-sol xhigh, read-only; gate: Opus spot-checked the top items against the code). Full Codex report, with raw tables: /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/claude-refactor-audit-work/report-survey.md.

## Main finding

Most of the size in the largest files is inline `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`. Six files hold about 22,900 test lines, and they are also the highest-churn implementation files in the last 300 commits (2026-10-21..29). The cheapest large win is to move those tests out as pure moves, with no product code changed. Production-code splits come second and are smaller.

Gate corrections to the survey:
- Contract path links. Splitting a test file whose path a contract cites means editing contract text, which needs your approval plus a Codex pass. Path links: `orbit/tests/lifecycle.rs` 36x in orbit/docs/CONTRACTS.md (plus BEHAVIOR, DEVELOPMENT, LIFECYCLE); `runtime/.../workspace.rs` 4x, `workspace_control.rs` 2x and `accessibility.rs` 2x in docs/CONTRACTS.md. `venus/src/render.rs`, `application.rs` and `scene.rs` have none. Docs cite tests by bare function name, and a move keeps those names.
- Dropped the survey's note that source moves "affect assembly identity" (eon/crates/eon/build.rs). Every commit changes that digest, so a move costs nothing extra there.
- venus/AGENTS.md says "A new Venus module is product scope." A new test module counts, so picking a Venus item below is your approval for its new modules.
- Each item is a code change, so it goes through the Codex-on-every-change loop. Cost: S = under a session, M = one session, L = several.

## Candidates (pick by number)

1. **Split `venus/src/render.rs` tests.** 7,105 lines; 4,056 are tests (from :3050, 30 tests); 36 commits; co-changes with chrome.rs 26x. Problem: padding, outlines, clipping, opacity, GPU-failure and shaping suites all share one module next to the renderer. Split: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests;` -> `render/tests/{mod(support),padding,outlines,text_clip,device,shaping}.rs`, moving the existing helpers (`padding_scene`, `painted_rects`, `clipping_test_fonts`) into the support module. Owner kept: Venus renderer, unchanged. Risk: none (pure move, no contract path links); keep GPU/native gates. Cost: M. **Recommend: yes, first.** Best ratio of benefit to risk.

2. **Split `venus/src/application.rs` tests.** 8,514 lines; 3,210 are tests (from :5305, 44 tests); 42 commits. Problem: a 1,129-line native probe test (:5812) and the unrelated retry, selection, workspace, shortcut and zoom suites make every event-loop change load ~3k extra lines. Split: `application/tests/{mod,native,retry,selection,workspace,shortcuts}.rs`, beside the existing `application/{geometry,scroll,shortcuts}.rs`. Owner kept: Venus native event handling. Risk: none from the move; keep the ignored/isolated-display attributes and the documented test filters. Cost: M. **Recommend: yes.**

3. **Split `venus/src/scene.rs` tests.** 6,685 lines; 2,830 are tests (from :3856, 23 tests); 43 commits, the highest churn of any implementation file; co-changes with chrome.rs 32x and accessibility.rs 31x. Split: `scene/tests/{mod,workspace,sidebar,bar,links,terminal}.rs`. Owner kept: Venus scene composition. Risk: none; keep the geometry and hit-target assertions. Cost: M. **Recommend: yes.** Leave the 644-line `WorkspaceScene::from_snapshot_with_zoom` (:2103) for later; splitting it needs its own read.

4. **Split `eon/crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs`.** 6,638 lines, 49 tests; 38 commits; co-changes with supervisor.rs 24x, sessions.rs 20x, cli.rs 19x. Problem: configuration/help, startup, directory picker, targeting, eonbase, recovery and generations suites, with ~700 lines of inline process/mock/managed-Orbit scaffolding (:39-133, :609-735). Split: one test target, with `workspace_control/{support,configuration,picker,workspace,recovery,generations}.rs`, reusing `tests/process/mod.rs`. Trap: the managed-Orbit helper re-execs the test binary as `--exact managed_orbit_helper` (:679, :722). Keep that test at the crate root, or change the filter to its new module path. Owner kept: Eon composed-product proof. Risk: test discovery and subprocess cleanup; 2 path links in docs/CONTRACTS.md and 1 in docs/DEVELOPMENT.md need updating (contract text edit). Cost: M. **Recommend: yes.** It is the file most often touched alongside runtime slices.

5. **Move Runtime's CLI output projection into `workspace/output.rs`.** In `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/workspace.rs` (5,930 lines; 17 commits), :2163-2600 holds `human`, `json`, `list_*`, `failure_*`, attention and shortcut formatting, and `json_escape`. `json_escape` is also used by cli.rs, generation.rs and windows.rs, so it does not belong inside workspace state. Split: a pure move into a private `workspace/output.rs` (or a crate-level `output.rs` for `json_escape`) plus its tests (:3703). Owner kept: Runtime owns both state and its CLI projection; output only reads snapshots. Risk: none; keep the exact CLI bytes. Cost: S. **Recommend: yes. Cheap, and it makes item 6 smaller.**

6. **Split Runtime `workspace.rs` tests.** 3,328 test lines (from :2603, 37 tests): replay/targeting, set capacity, topology, popups/pickers, directory changes, output. Split: `workspace/tests/{mod,set,topology,popups,replay}.rs`, sharing `catalog`, `prepared`, `two_workspace_set`. Owner kept: Runtime workspace state. Risk: none to logic; 4 path links in docs/CONTRACTS.md (contract text edit). Cost: M. **Recommend: yes, after 5 (same file).**

7. **Split `venus/src/accessibility.rs` tests.** 3,846 lines; 2,873 are tests (from :974, 23 tests); 33 commits; co-changes with scene.rs 31x. Split: `accessibility/tests/{mod,bar,terminal,workspace,dialogs}.rs`. Owner kept: Venus accessibility projection. Risk: none to logic; 2 path links in docs/CONTRACTS.md. Cost: M. **Recommend: yes, lower priority than 1-4.**

8. **Extract the supervisor's presentation process.** `runtime/.../supervisor.rs`, 3,478 lines; 37 commits. `venus_command` (:389) and `PresentationProcess` with its `Drop` (:482-657) sit between config/runtime-dir helpers and the 297-line `supervise` loop (:745) and the 330-line `dispatch_control_request` (:1744). Split: `supervisor/presentation.rs` with those items and their command tests. Owner kept: Runtime owns the presentation lifecycle; `SupervisorState` stays put. Risk: lifecycle-adjacent (spawn, control-channel close, wait, cleanup must move together); no wire change. Cost: M. **Recommend: yes, but after 1-6. It is the top production split and needs a careful review.**

9. **Isolate managed-Orbit acquisition in `runtime/.../sessions.rs`.** 2,815 lines; 32 commits; co-changes with supervisor.rs 22x. Record reading (:222), identity/peer validation (:312, :451) and `acquire_management` (:466) are separable from launch/recovery orchestration (:637). Split: `sessions/management.rs`. Owner kept: Runtime manages Orbit through the management protocol. Risk: **security and lifecycle boundary** (no-follow opens, peer credentials, process-start checks, deadlines). Cost: M. **Recommend: later.** The value is real, but take it only when someone is already working in sessions.rs.

10. **Move the managed-shell checks out of `flake.nix`.** 1,113 lines; 17 commits. `managedCommandPathCheck` and `fakeMise` (:888-1086) interrupt the composition graph. Split: `nix/managed-command-checks.nix`, following the existing `orbitChecks` import (:341). Owner kept: Nix composition. Risk: none, if check names stay identical (verify with `nix flake show` before and after). Cost: S. **Recommend: yes, as a quick win.**

11. **Move link handling out of `impl Application`.** `impl Application` is 2,956 lines (:732). The hyperlink block (:2853-3105: `link_scene` through `handle_link_button`, ~250 lines) is cohesive. Split: `application/links.rs`, the same pattern as `scroll.rs` and `shortcuts.rs`. Owner kept: Venus local link focus. Risk: none (pure move). Cost: S. **Recommend: optional; pair it with item 2 if that slice has room.** (Gate addition: the survey proposed no production split of application.rs.)

## Considered and not recommended now

- 12. `runtime/crates/eon-workspace-protocol/src/v23.rs` tests (1,611 lines): only 1 commit in the window, so it causes little collision. Skip. (Correction: v23.rs is the live, hand-edited EONW codec, not frozen history; EON-C28 retention starts at 1.0.)
- 13. `orbit/tests/lifecycle.rs` (2,186): 2 commits, and 36 contract path links. A split means a large ORB-C text edit for little gain. Skip.
- 14. `eon/tools/mac-proof/src/scenario.rs` (2,009): defer behind eon-mac-launch-kz4p, as the bead's scope says.
- 15. `orbit/tools/step-proof.rs` repeats the boundary.schema fact list (:50) and enum table (:244) instead of reusing tools/boundary.rs's parser (:74). This is a real duplicate owner of structure, but a schema change without a table update should fail the proof check rather than drift silently, the fix touches proof generation, and the generator changed only 3 times. Cost: L. Skip unless the schema starts changing often.
- Dead code: none found that can be deleted with confidence. The only suppression is `venus/src/application.rs:651` `expect(dead_code)` on macOS for `application_id`, a recorded native-host gap.
- Duplication checked and left alone: Venus selected/background transport retry already shares `apply_retryable_loss`; Runtime attention rollup vs the EONW check is author vs trust-boundary validation; the nine-line decoder `finish` helpers are too small to share.

## Excluded (generated or proof-owned)

- `orbit/proof/view.bend` (75,638), `lease.bend` (69,076), `step.bend` (61,840): generated by `orbit/tools/step-proof.rs` (header line 15; writer :1228). They are 61.5% of all source lines.
- `orbit/src/boundary.rs` (752), `orbit/src/boundary.bend` (1,212): generated from `boundary.schema` by `orbit/tools/boundary.rs` (:823-824).
- `orbit/LAWS.bend` (1,812), `orbit/PROOF.bend` (980): hand-written but proof-owned; you own the laws (orbit/AGENTS.md).
- `Cargo.lock`, `installer/`, `launcher/`, `relink/` `Cargo.lock`, `flake.lock`: lock data.
- `AGENTS.md`, `orbit|venus|runtime/AGENTS.md`, `docs/AGENT-PROTOCOLS.md`: rendered from Starcompass.
- `.beads/`: br-owned.

## Recommendation

Take 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 first. They are pure moves with no contract text, and they cut the Venus files that most often collide between parallel slices (scene/chrome/application/render). They touch different files, so they can run as parallel beads. Then take 4 and 6 (each edits contract path links), then 8. Leave 9 and 11-15 unless work already passes through them.

title: Add a GitHub bug report form before the public beta post
description:
## Why

Lucca plans a public-beta post to bring in users who run Eon and file bugs (Lucca, 2026-10-23: "1 public beta is good / 2 i will decide when to post / 3 file the bead"). The repository has no issue templates: `.github/` holds only `FUNDING.yml` and `workflows`, and the README's "Report a problem" link opens the issue list with no form. A bare issue rarely says which Eon build, compositor or steps hit the bug, so each report costs a round trip before anyone can act on it.

## Scope

In scope:
- `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml`: a GitHub issue form that asks for the Eon version (the `eon versions` output, which names every component), the install route (Nix profile, flake input or other), the distribution and compositor, the steps to reproduce, the expected and actual results, and optional logs or a screenshot. Mark the version, compositor and steps fields required.
- `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml`: keep blank issues enabled, so the README's Apple Silicon tester link and other free-form reports still work.
- Point the README's "Report a problem" link at the bug form (`issues/new?template=bug_report.yml`).

Out of scope:
- The announcement itself (Lucca writes and posts it).
- A feature-request form, label automation and CI.
- Any diagnostics command in `eon`.

## Acceptance

- On github.com, New issue offers the bug form with every field above. Check the rendered form; a test submission is not needed.
- The form's version instruction matches the real CLI.

## Verification

Planning and docs route: the diff, plus one observation of the form on github.com after the push to edge. No runtime profile refresh.
close_reason: Bug report form live on edge (6ee477a); GitHub validates and renders it.

title: Serve the tagged install from the binary cache
description:
## Decision
Lucca, 2026-10-15: make the README's tagged install command fetch cached binaries instead of
building from source.

## Contract
- Consumer: a first-time user running the README install command for the current release tag with
the optional `eon-yazelix` cache configured.
- Result: Nix substitutes the tag's `default` and `eonterm` outputs from the cache instead of
compiling them.
- Important failures: a cache miss still builds from pinned sources; nothing implies the cache is
required.

## Evidence (edge 5ae4e0f)
- `.github/workflows/cachix.yml` publishes only on `push` to `edge` or `workflow_dispatch`.
`docs/DISTRIBUTION.md` ("Optional binary cache") says tags have no guaranteed coverage.
- README installs `github:Yazelix/eon/linux-alpha-2026-10-14` (commit `e48fc29`), which predates the
first cache publish recorded at `068efcb`, so it is probably not cached.

## Approach
1. Cheapest check first: evaluate the tag's two output paths and query the cache with
`nix path-info --store https://eon-yazelix.cachix.org`. If they are present, record that and stop.
2. Otherwise run the existing workflow by `workflow_dispatch` on the tag ref (no code change), or
choose between adding a tag-push trigger and tagging only cached revisions. Record the choice;
update the release procedure and the DISTRIBUTION cache text to match.

## Prerequisites
Publishing to the cache and changing hosted CI are outward-facing: get Lucca's explicit request for
the dispatch or the trigger change (AP-CI-001: bound triggers and cost).

## Acceptance
The cache query shows both tag outputs present; a fresh substitution of the tag install fetches them
rather than building. Docs state the actual coverage policy.

## Stop boundary
No new release channel, signing or cache owner change.
close_reason: Tag outputs and full closure already substitutable from eon-yazelix and cache.nixos.org; verified by narinfo queries and an empty-store dry run.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Resolved by the first check; no publish, CI or docs change needed (2026-10-15, x86_64 Linux, Nix on Lucca's host, edge f916b56). title: Restore docs/CONTRACTS.md as the canonical current-state index
description:
## Contract
Consumer: a reader checking Eon's current product contracts.
Trigger: looking up or changing an EON-C contract.
Result: docs/CONTRACTS.md gives one concise current-state entry per existing contract, with its behavior, owner, boundary, status, proof or open proof, and limits.
Important failures: a lost current guarantee or proof, duplicate authority, or a status promoted by documentation alone.

## Baseline
At Eon 4ff62dbd1b4645ee8f2bd927d233388230f06a10 (2026-09-24), the index is 2,047 lines with 22 EON-C headings, EON-C19 before C1, and standalone qualification and integration histories. Its Rules assign historical execution evidence to Beads and Git. Closed eon-contract-index-current-state-iuh covered an earlier C1-C10 version.

Revalidated on 2026-10-04 at clean Eon cda9662c2cfac092d98a998b3a54c9b0fb4f2b7a: the current index is 2,092 lines with 23 EON-C headings, including EON-C23 independent windows. The historical baseline remains discovery evidence; condense the current C1-C23 guarantees and proof identities, including existing ownership and support limits.

## Prerequisites and reference gate
Read the full index and Rules, owning Beads/Git evidence for sections being condensed, the component manifest, and incoming documentation links. Use the matching docs/REFERENCES.md route if a substantive contract question arises. Reconcile current claims against their owner and record the evidence for any correction.

## Scope
Documentation only: docs/CONTRACTS.md, necessary link fixes, and README LOC. Preserve stable IDs, contract meaning, current proof identities and checks, platform scope, and durable gaps. Leave execution history in existing Beads and Git. No runtime, child-repository, manifest, new-contract, proof-promotion, or archival work.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. EON-C1 through EON-C23 each appear once, in numerical order, with the fields required by the index Rules. Planned contracts retain open proof; proved slices retain the exact accepted revision, component and platform context, check or observation, and artifact needed to support their claim.
2. Keep only contract-relevant current claims and their necessary proof under the owning EON-C entry. Historical execution detail remains traceable through an owning Bead or Git revision; no standalone history acts as current authority.
3. Accepted behavior, ownership, status, pins, and support scope retain their meaning. Resolve any conflicting current claim from accepted evidence or mark its gap explicitly; do not silently drop it or claim new proof.
4. The index is shorter, with before/after line counts recorded; changed links and contract IDs resolve, and README LOC is accurate.

title: Choose Orbit-owned generation shutdown semantics
description:
## Contract Routing

This is a planning-only cross-repository lifecycle decision. It changes no EON or ORB product contract, implementation, protocol, dependency, package, or compatibility promise by itself.

Consumer: a local Eon or EonTerm user invoking the accepted whole-generation stop action.

Trigger: the running Eon supervisor accepts an EON-C10/EON-C11 Stop request for its current generation.

Result: the user selects one bounded shutdown ownership contract and update order in which Eon owns orchestration and stop policy while Orbit remains the sole PTY, process, terminal-state, and Session authority.

Important failures: an accepted stop must not strand an Orbit-owned PTY child, wait forever, duplicate process-group discovery in Eon, silently weaken the result, or introduce an unapproved administrative protocol.

Impact: HIGH. Decision effort: S-M. Implementation risk: HIGH. Confidence: HIGH.

## Why

The current supervisor reports Stopped and then SIGKILLs each Orbit process. SIGKILL prevents Orbit's authoritative PTY cleanup from running, so the accepted whole-generation stop can return success while the PTY child survives reparented to PID 1. The repair crosses an ownership boundary and may require an indexed Orbit shutdown guarantee, so implementation must wait for an explicit contract decision.

## Evidence

- Eon `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1933-1945`: an accepted Stop response names the Sessions and returns the shutdown flag.
- Eon `crates/eon/src/main.rs:1606-1623`: the supervisor sends the response, then stops Venus and every Orbit child.
- Eon `crates/eon/src/main.rs:2139-2143`: `stop` uses `Child::kill` and `wait`; on Unix this bypasses Orbit cleanup.
- Eon `docs/CONTRACTS.md:169-174`: Eon terminates its own children, while Orbit retains process, PTY, terminal-state, and Session authority.
- Orbit `src/platform.rs:112-134`: child/foreground process-group cleanup runs from `Pty::stop_and_reap` and `Drop`.
- Orbit `src/platform.rs:246-254` and `src/main.rs:367-405`: Orbit already handles shutdown signals through its own owner loop.
- Closed audit `orb-audit-orbit-integration-ur9` at Orbit `7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16`: two exact Linux reproductions used Eon `3ee61a1b985fb1f44fc6ee0967c0c331b589a4b2`, Orbit `7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16`, and a HUP/TERM-ignoring PTY child. `eon stop` returned success, but the second child (PID 1262661, Orbit PID 1262660) survived under PID 1 until manually killed.
- This is distinct from Orbit platform-audit finding 3: that finding concerns a separate background process group missed after Orbit cleanup starts; this finding prevents all Orbit cleanup from starting.

## Reference Classification

Required before deciding:

- Current Eon and Orbit `AGENTS.md`, this complete Bead, the closed integration audit, EON-C10/EON-C11 and ORB-C1 contract rows, and exact current stop/signal/cleanup code and tests.
- Orbit `docs/REFERENCES.md` process-lifecycle route, including exact prior zmx, shpool/abduco, and Process Triage identities already recorded by the platform audit, but only for shutdown ownership, escalation, verification, and reaping.
- Exact known consumers: Eon workspace, EonTerm, and trackerless Eonova composition.
- Orbit decision `orb-decide-whole-pty-session-shutdown-dqi` must first choose whether authoritative explicit shutdown owns every PTY-session job-control group. This decision then defines Eon's orchestration against that exact Orbit disposition.

Comparison only:

- Existing Eon graceful child-observation/startup patterns and Orbit signal-driven shutdown tests.
- A private administrative shutdown request only if the existing process-control seam cannot provide deterministic bounded cleanup.

Rejected scope:

- Eon scanning or signaling PTY process groups, copying Orbit cleanup, a general process manager, remote shutdown, persistence, a new runtime dependency, indefinite compatibility, or unrelated platform-audit findings.

## Decision Method

1. Reproduce the exact failure at the recorded revisions and trace response delivery, supervisor cleanup, Orbit signal handling, PTY cleanup, and child reaping.
2. Compare the minimum complete shapes:
   - Eon requests Orbit's existing graceful signal-driven shutdown, waits a bounded interval, verifies process exit, then applies an explicit last-resort policy.
   - Orbit adds a narrowly versioned private administrative shutdown boundary, followed by Eon adoption.
   - Status quo SIGKILL and Eon-owned process-group cleanup as rejected baselines.
3. For each credible shape, record EON-C10/EON-C11 and ORB contract effects, completion/failure semantics, timeout and escalation owner, stale/corrupt Orbit behavior, Linux and macOS feasibility, owned LOC, tests, rollout order, and removal cost.
4. Recommend the first sufficient owner-correct shape. Prefer the existing process-control seam if it can be proved without adding a protocol.
5. Stop for the user's explicit contract and ownership choice.
6. If a correction is selected, create one Orbit owner implementation Bead first, one Eon consumer Bead second, and one composed acceptance step. Before closing this decision, replace the Eon integration audit's dependency on this decision with dependencies on the chosen implementation/acceptance work.

Portability disposition: neutral lifecycle policy with platform signaling isolated in each repository's existing process seam; this decision makes no macOS runtime claim.

## Scope

In scope:

- Shutdown ownership, request/acknowledgement semantics, bounded wait/escalation, failure reporting, exact known consumers, and owner-first update order.
- Whether the behavior hardens an existing contract or requires explicit user approval for a new/changed indexed contract.
- The smallest falsifying composed process test.

Out of scope:

- Editing source, tests, manifests, docs, contracts, or packages.
- Fixing Orbit platform-audit finding 3, changing ORBS/EONW, stopping live user generations, or creating implementation Beads before the decision.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The exact orphan reproduction is retained and distinguished from Orbit's separate background-group cleanup finding.
2. One owner is named for shutdown policy, PTY cleanup, timeout, escalation, verification, and the user-visible Stop result.
3. At least the existing-signal and private-administrative-boundary shapes are evaluated, with status quo and duplicate Eon cleanup rejected explicitly.
4. The selected recommendation states exact EON/ORB contract effects, known consumers, update order, old-version behavior, first check, effort, risk, and reversal condition.
5. No new protocol, dependency, compatibility promise, or implementation is implied without explicit user approval.
6. The decision consumes the exact disposition of `orb-decide-whole-pty-session-shutdown-dqi` and does not widen or contradict Orbit's chosen process-cleanup boundary.
7. The Eon integration audit remains blocked on this decision or its selected implementation successors.
8. Only Beads planning state changes.

## Verification

- Re-run the isolated composed stop reproduction without editing repository files.
- `rg -n 'Action::Stop|Stopped|fn stop|install_shutdown_signals|stop_and_reap' crates/eon/src docs` in Eon and the equivalent exact owner search in Orbit should enumerate all relevant owners.
- `git diff --check` should pass in both unchanged repositories.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only planning state.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if source or contract ownership has materially changed since the audited revisions.
- Stop before selecting or creating an implementation without the user's explicit contract/ownership decision.
- Stop if the selected shape requires a new cross-repository protocol, dependency, compatibility window, or broader process policy not compared here.
- Stop if another active issue begins owning the same lifecycle boundary.

## Maintenance Notes

The lazy root-cause shape is cooperative shutdown through the existing owners, not copied PTY cleanup. A last-resort SIGKILL may remain as bounded failure policy only if the selected contract defines its result honestly and the composed check proves that no accepted success strands the initial PTY child.
notes:
Historical decision — accepted 2026-08-14: option A selected cooperative direct SIGTERM to each exact Orbit Child, one bounded outer wait, Stopped only for successful exits, and Failure for nonzero/observation/timeout/SIGKILL. Orbit retained descendant containment and cleanup. Historical successors were orb-prove-no-survivor-session-shutdown-btg, ven-adopt-orbs-v4-without-interaction-expansion-zdc, eon-await-orbit-owned-shutdown-eu3, and eon-prove-installed-no-survivor-stop-3sx.

Current disposition — superseded 2026-08-20: accepted Orbit ORB-C13 source 86aa130629c09dce61d0f232150298656fa5cef4 replaces direct SIGTERM with validated management Stop. ORB-C12 cleanup ownership and the no-survivor outcome remain. Current implementation routes through eon-consume-orbit-same-boot-management-2y7, acceptance through eon-accept-eon-orbit-same-boot-recovery-iwc, and Eonova rollout through eon-prove-installed-no-survivor-stop-3sx. The direct-signal choice is historical evidence only.
close_reason: User approved cooperative signal plus verified Orbit exit; owner, compatibility, Eon consumer, and installed acceptance successors are recorded and the integration audit is rewired.

comments.text:
Decision evidence and recommendation — awaiting explicit user choice

Current and reproduced evidence
- Decision subject: Eon edge/origin edge 054f6f97703a6d28ccfa4bdd4ecbfed507b76fb5, AGENTS object e4c4463d471e903f636138749b75eb940b4b20d4; only the pre-existing shared .beads/issues.jsonl is dirty. Orbit read-only subject b1153b6f06dd398c1f924f3285c50316f1d2fdcb, AGENTS object 095e3a9ea7e87d36f4ebabec1818ae42a4a4fce2; only its shared .beads/issues.jsonl is dirty. No source, contract, manifest, test, package, or dependency file changed.
- Current ownership is materially unchanged. Eon crates/eon/src/main.rs returns LifecycleResponse::Stopped before cleanup, then stop uses Child::kill plus wait for Venus and every Orbit child. On Unix that is immediate SIGKILL. Orbit src/main.rs installs INT/TERM/HUP handlers and returns through its owner loop; Pty::stop_and_reap and Drop in src/platform.rs own HUP/KILL of the known PTY groups and child reaping. SIGKILL from Eon bypasses that owner entirely.
- Exact isolated rerun used audited Eon 3ee61a1b985fb1f44fc6ee0967c0c331b589a4b2 from /nix/store/wdbc6acg22lp9xn1nl52l8d3v9bp3d4s-eon-0.1.0 and Orbit 7d34399b15496513f7f91b94acd32e8d04389e16 built by Cargo, with EON_VENUS=/bin/false and a private temporary runtime. Before Stop: Eon PID 2771181/PGID 2771178/SID 2771178; Orbit PID 2771185/PPID 2771181/PGID 2771178/SID 2771178; HUP/TERM-ignoring shell PID 2771186/PPID 2771185/PGID 2771186/SID 2771186. `eon stop ... --json` exited 0 and returned Stopped for session-1; Eon exited 0; shell 2771186 survived as PPID 1. The harness killed only exact PGID 2771186 and verified cleanup. This reproduces the integration-audit finding and remains distinct from the accepted Orbit decision background-group case, which survives even when Orbit cleanup runs.
- Required Orbit decision orb-decide-whole-pty-session-shutdown-dqi is closed with the user-approved full-stop policy: explicit Session stop forbids survivors; kernel per-Session containment owns Linux membership, Orbit owns graceful cleanup, bounded escalation, empty verification, and result truth; Eon only orchestrates. No Orbit implementation bead or proof exists yet.

Compared shapes
A. Existing process-control seam: Eon sends SIGTERM to every exact child Orbit process, waits under one bounded generation deadline, observes each exit status, and reports Stopped only after every Orbit reports successful owner cleanup. Orbit owns its shorter internal grace/escalation/empty-verification deadline and exits nonzero on failure. Eon owns the outer orchestration deadline and may SIGKILL only an unresponsive Orbit process as last resort, then must return Failure rather than Stopped. This adds no protocol or dependency and is recommended.
B. Private Orbit administrative shutdown boundary: a request plus acknowledgement could make intent explicit, but correct completion is already represented by cooperative signal plus process exit. A new admin socket or ORBS message would add versioning, permissions, request/ack framing, one-client interaction, compatibility, tests, and another failure surface without improving ownership. Reject unless an exact Orbit proof shows signal plus exit cannot distinguish bounded cleanup success.
C. Current SIGKILL: rejected because it bypasses all Orbit cleanup and reproduces a false successful stop with a live orphan.
D. Eon process-group, SID, PID, process-name, or /proc cleanup: rejected because it duplicates Orbit process authority, races identity and forks, cannot safely prove completeness, and contradicts the accepted Orbit decision.

Recommended contract and owners
- Harden existing EON-C10/EON-C11; add no Eon contract ID. Stopped changes from acceptance-before-cleanup to a completed result: every named Session Orbit exited success after its authoritative shutdown. Existing Failure carries bounded stage/session detail for any nonzero exit, timeout, observation error, or forced Orbit kill. The wire vocabulary need not change.
- Eon owns Stop validation, generation-wide parallel signal initiation, the outer deadline, exact child-status collection, Venus teardown after Orbit completion, supervisor/runtime cleanup, and the final Stopped or Failure result. Orbit owns PTY/session identity, descendant containment, graceful signals, internal deadline, escalation, reaping, empty verification, and its exit status. The Linux kernel owns containment membership. Venus and EonTerm only consume the Eon result.
- On any Orbit failure, Eon never removes the generation as clean or reports Stopped. It responds Failure and exits non-success after bounded cleanup of only its own child processes. Potential remaining Orbit-owned work is an explicit failed shutdown, not false success.
- Known consumers are Eon workspace Stop, EonTerm Stop, and the private Eonova composition through EonTerm. No compatibility alias, fallback, or Eonova policy is needed. Immutable old supervisors retain historical unverified semantics; the new guarantee applies only to generations composed from the accepted Orbit shutdown proof.

Integration/update order
- Current Eon pins Orbit 6de95296d252c119d4fdba2d9b03cec1a09355ae and canonical ORBS v3. Current Orbit edge b1153b6 contains ORBS v4. A shutdown proof committed on current linear Orbit edge therefore cannot be consumed by current Eon plus Venus as a pin-only update.
- Owner-first order must be: (1) a separate Orbit implementation bead adds the approved explicit-shutdown contract and proves no-survivor Linux containment on current Orbit; (2) a separately approved minimal Venus ORBS v4 consumer proof, or another explicit release strategy, provides a compatible exact Venus/Orbit pair without a hidden fork or backport; (3) one Eon consumer bead hardens EON-C10/EON-C11, selects that exact pair, and proves cooperative shutdown; (4) one composed Eon/EonTerm/Eonova acceptance step verifies installed behavior. The large deferred kinetic-scroll feature must not be pulled in merely to unlock shutdown.
- Old Orbit or Venus compatibility, a maintenance branch, backport, adapter, and protocol window are not implied. Any alternate release strategy requires a separate user choice.

First checks, effort, risk, and reversal
- Orbit owner check: real initial, foreground, and HUP/TERM-ignoring distinct background groups inside per-Session containment plus an unrelated sibling outside; accepted shutdown succeeds only after containment is empty and the sibling remains.
- Eon TDD/composed check: use the exact proved Orbit; Stop must not return Stopped before Orbit exit and all contained PIDs are gone. A deterministic fake Orbit that exits nonzero and one that ignores TERM must produce bounded Failure; the latter may be killed only as failed last-resort cleanup. Send all Session signals before waiting so N Sessions do not multiply the deadline.
- Eon consumer effort M, composed/revision rollout M, risk HIGH because result timing, partial multi-Session failure, immutable generations, and the ORBS v4 integration frontier meet here. Orbit containment remains separately H/HIGH.
- Reconsider the administrative boundary only if signal delivery plus exit status cannot prove request identity or cleanup result. Reconsider permitted survivors only through a new explicit reversal of the already accepted Orbit lifecycle policy.

Recommendation: choose A, cooperative signal plus verified process exit, sequenced behind the owner proof and a compatible exact ORBS v4 pair. This comment selects nothing and creates no successor Bead; the current decision remains in progress pending explicit user approval.

Eon may SIGKILL only an unresponsive Orbit process as last-resort cleanup and must never convert that path into Stopped.

Accepted ownership: Orbit and its platform seam exclusively own PTY/session descendant identity, Linux containment, graceful cleanup, internal deadline, escalation, reaping, empty verification, and exit-status truth. Eon owns Stop validation, generation-wide coordination, outer deadline, exact direct-child observation, failure aggregation, later Venus teardown, Eon-owned runtime cleanup, and the final EON-C10/EON-C11 result. The kernel owns containment membership. Venus, EonTerm, and Eonova consume results only.

Contract disposition: harden EON-C10 and EON-C11; add no Eon contract ID and no administrative protocol. Stopped becomes verified completion for new exact-proof generations rather than acceptance before cleanup. Old immutable supervisors retain historical unverified behavior and receive no adapter or backport promise.

Authorized sequencing: the user permits advancing exact component revisions when useful. The selected owner-first path is Orbit explicit-shutdown contract/implementation proof; a minimal compatible Venus ORBS v4 consumer proof or separately approved release strategy; Eon cooperative consumer proof against that exact pair; then composed installed Eon/EonTerm/Eonova acceptance. Do not pull in kinetic scrolling, create a hidden maintenance fork, or widen child behavior.

The decision is accepted but remains in progress until a separate planning-only run creates the owner, consumer, and composed-acceptance successors and replaces eon-audit-eon-integration-62p dependency on this decision with the real successor gates. No source, contract index, manifest, test, package, dependency, or other Bead changed in this decision-acceptance run.
