title: Place Eon Bar items from an ordered Venus launch input
description:
## Why

The parent epic's `[bar] widgets` setting needs Venus to place bar items in a given order and to
leave out the ones that are off. Today the order is fixed in Venus: quota chips, then CPU, RAM,
clock, then the version label at the edge (VEN-C25/C27/C28, commit `0d27a46`). The version label
is the only one with a switch: absence of `--eon-version`.

## Evidence

- `venus/src/scene.rs` `WorkspaceScene::from_snapshot_with_metadata`: the label array
  `[version, cpu, ram, clock]` fits in that priority order, then the code reorders it to
  `[cpu, ram, clock, version]` for placement. Quota chips are measured and compacted
  separately (`measure_quotas`, the `compact` loop).
- `venus/src/accessibility.rs`: AccessKit children follow the same fixed order (CPU, RAM, CLOCK,
  VERSION after the quota nodes).
- `venus/src/application.rs`: startup inputs such as `--eon-version` and `--pane-frames` are
  parsed before window creation. `venus/docs/LAUNCH.md` documents them.
- `venus/src/application.rs` wake loop: `READING_INTERVAL` drives `CpuTimes::read` and
  `RamUse::read` every 2 s while a workspace snapshot exists.

## Scope

In scope:
- One Venus workspace-only launch input naming the shown bar items in order, for example
  `--bar-items codex_quota,claude_quota,cpu,ram,clock,version`. The exact flag name and syntax
  are part of the contract wording for Lucca to approve.
- Its absence keeps today's default order, so standalone runs and existing launches don't change.
- Placement in the given order (quota chips may sit anywhere in it); items left out get no chip,
  hit target, hover or AccessKit node. Turning CPU or RAM off also skips its `/proc` read.
- A fixed hiding priority under width pressure, independent of order: clock, RAM, CPU, version,
  then quota compaction (current VEN-C28 rule).
- Contract changes: VEN-C25, VEN-C27 and VEN-C28 (placement follows the input), plus
  `venus/docs/LAUNCH.md`, and `venus/CHANGELOG.md`.

Out of scope:
- Eon or Runtime configuration (child 2), quota polling (child 3), EONW changes.
- New widgets, per-widget options, configurable hiding priority.
- Changing how quota chips compact.

## Acceptance

- With the input absent, the bar is pixel-identical in layout to `0d27a46`.
- With an input, items appear in that order, and absent items have no chip, hit target or
  AccessKit node. Hiding under width pressure still follows the fixed priority.
- Missing, duplicate, unknown or empty-element input fails before window creation, like the other
  startup inputs. Whether `--bar-items ''` (all off) is allowed is part of the wording: recommend
  allowing it, since the Eon setting accepts `widgets = []`.
- Contract wording approved by Lucca before commit.

## Implementation Notes

1. Parse the input next to `--eon-version`. Hold it as an ordered list of a small Venus enum,
   and pass it to the scene instead of growing more `Option` parameters.
2. In the scene, fit by fixed priority and then place in input order, reusing today's two-step
   fit-then-place shape.
3. Extend `readings_yield_after_the_clock_and_have_no_actions` and the version and clock tests
   rather than adding parallel ones. Add one test that reorders items, including a quota chip
   after a reading.

## Verification

- `nix develop -c eon-test -p yazelix-venus` passes, including the new ordering test. It should go
  red when the input order is ignored.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --locked -p yazelix-venus --all-targets -- -D warnings`
  are clean (run inside `nix develop`).
- Portability disposition: neutral (no platform API).

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask Lucca if placing a quota chip between readings needs a change to quota
  compaction.
- Stop if the cited scene code has drifted materially since `0d27a46`.
- Stop before adding any EONW field.

## Maintenance Notes

- Item names are shared with Eon's `[bar] widgets` names (child 2). Keep one spelling and let
  Runtime pass the list through unchanged, with no translation table.

title: Replace [bar] show_version with an ordered [bar] widgets list
description:
## Why

The parent epic's design: one `[bar] widgets` ordered list sets the Eon Bar's order and which
items show, and replaces `[bar] show_version` before 1.0, so 1.x promises one setting.

## Evidence

- `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/managed_environment.rs:52-63`: `BarSettings { show_version }`
  with `deny_unknown_fields`, `show_version(root, defaults)`, and `Defaults::show_version`.
- `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/supervisor.rs:407-408`: passes `--eon-version` only when
  `show_version` holds, read per window launch. Tests at `supervisor.rs:1712-1746` and `:1968`.
- `eon/crates/eon/src/product.rs:14` and `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/fixtures.rs:16`: the
  `show_version: true` default.
- `eon/crates/eon/tests/workspace_control.rs:2140`: invalid `show_version` value case.
- `docs/CONFIGURATION.md:7-8,37-40`, `docs/CONTRACTS.md` EON-C25 (`show_version`), EON-C29 and
  EON-C30 ("always on, with no Eon configuration"), `runtime/README.md:25`,
  `venus/docs/LAUNCH.md:73`.

## Scope

In scope:
- `[bar] widgets`: an array of unique names from `codex_quota`, `claude_quota`, `cpu`, `ram`,
  `clock` and `version`. Eon owns the default, today's order, in `product.rs`. Runtime parses and
  validates it in `managed_environment.rs` when a window opens, and passes it to Venus through
  child 1's launch input. `--eon-version` is passed only when `version` is listed.
- Remove `show_version`. A config that still sets it fails with an error naming `[bar] widgets`.
  This is a breaking change before 1.0, so it gets a CHANGELOG line.
- New EON-C contract for the setting (next free ID), plus edits to EON-C25, EON-C29 and EON-C30.
  Also `docs/CONFIGURATION.md`, `runtime/README.md`, `venus/docs/LAUNCH.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`.

Out of scope:
- Stopping quota polling (child 3). In this bead a quota chip that is off is only left out of
  the launch input.
- New widget names, per-widget options, live reload without reopening the window, Ratconfig
  schema work (report it if Ratconfig needs a schema update to edit the list).

## Acceptance

- Omitting `widgets` gives today's bar. A reordered list reorders the installed bar on the next
  window open. `widgets = []` shows only tabs and controls.
- An unknown or duplicate name, a non-string, or a leftover `show_version` fails through the
  existing startup or replacement handling, and live terminals survive.
- Contract wording approved by Lucca before commit.

## Implementation Notes

1. Replace `BarSettings::show_version` and `Defaults::show_version` with the list. Keep
   `deny_unknown_fields`, but give `show_version` its own error instead of the generic
   unknown-field one.
2. Rework the supervisor tests at `supervisor.rs:1712-1746` and `:1968` for the list, keeping
   their invalid-input cases.
3. Update `workspace_control.rs:2140`'s case.

## Verification

- `nix develop -c eon-test` (the workspace and installer suites) passes. A focused red/green for
  the parser: unknown name, duplicate, `show_version` present.
- Installed (AGENTS.md "Installed runtime, UI, or product-configuration interaction"): profile
  refresh plus one isolated installed observation. A reordered list with `cpu` left out shows
  that order on window open, and a leftover `show_version` shows the error without killing live
  terminals.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if child 1's launch input is not merged.
- Stop and ask Lucca if EON-C28's stability wording lists `show_version` by name, since removing
  it would then change the stability contract text.
- Stop if Ratconfig validation of Eon's config needs a schema file that this repository doesn't
  own.

## Maintenance Notes

- Runtime passes the names through to Venus unchanged. Don't add a second mapping.

title: Stop polling a provider whose quota chip is off
description:
## Why

The parent epic's decision is that a quota chip turned off in `[bar] widgets` also stops Runtime
polling that provider, so Eon doesn't call CodexBar, and through it the provider, for data nobody
sees.

## Evidence

- `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/supervisor.rs:783`: the workspace supervisor starts
  `quota::Quotas::start(&inputs.codexbar)` once, at supervisor start, for both providers.
- `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/quota.rs:189-223`: `Quotas::start` and `start_every` spawn one
  worker per provider (Codex every 60 units, Claude every 300 after a failure), and
  `Quotas::apply` fills the snapshot's `codex_quota` and `claude_quota`.
- `quota.rs` tests `workers_isolate_failure_and_bound_output_timeout_and_shutdown` and
  `claude_waits_300_units_after_a_failed_read_while_codex_reads_every_60`.
- `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` "Agent quota", and the EON quota contracts in `docs/CONTRACTS.md`.

## Scope

In scope:
- Start only the workers for providers whose chip `[bar] widgets` (child 2) lists, and leave a
  disabled provider's snapshot field empty.
- The timing rule: the setting is read when a window opens (child 2), but workers start with the
  supervisor. Recommended rule for Lucca to approve: re-evaluate on each window open, starting a
  newly enabled provider's worker and stopping a newly disabled one, so polling always matches
  what the bar shows. The alternative, which is simpler but stale until restart, is to read it
  once at supervisor start.
- Contract text in the quota contracts and `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` "Agent quota".

Out of scope:
- New providers, CodexBar changes, refresh intervals, how chips render.

## Acceptance

- With `claude_quota` left out, no Claude CodexBar process runs, and the snapshot carries no Claude
  quota. With both left out, no quota worker runs.
- Re-enabling takes effect under the approved timing rule, without restarting live terminals.
- Contract wording approved by Lucca before commit.

## Implementation Notes

1. Give `Quotas::start` the enabled set, and keep one worker per enabled provider.
2. Add a fake-CodexBar case that proves a disabled provider is never invoked. Extend the existing
   worker test rather than adding scaffolding.

## Verification

- `nix develop -c eon-test -p eon-runtime` passes, including a red/green check that a disabled
  provider is never spawned.
- Installed: one isolated observation with one provider off, showing no chip and no CodexBar
  process for it.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if child 2 is not merged.
- Stop and ask Lucca for the timing rule before coding if it isn't recorded on this bead.
- Stop if stopping a worker mid-read can leave a CodexBar child unreaped (AP-FAILURE-001): report
  the shutdown path first.

## Maintenance Notes

title: Close the gap inside the CPU and RAM chips
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-21 (screenshot of the installed bar): the CPU and RAM chips show a visible gap,
`CPU  10%` and `RAM  34%`, and "we also have to fix this gap". VEN-C28 requires it today: each
label is "padded to the width of `CPU 100%` with the value right-aligned"
(`venus/src/system.rs:62,106`, `format!("CPU {:>4}", ...)`), so any value under 100% opens a hole
between the name and the value.

## Decision (Lucca, 2026-10-21, chosen as recommended)

One space between name and value (`CPU 10%`, `RAM 5%`), centered in a chip that keeps the width
of `CPU 100%`, so neighbouring items never shift as values change and the slack splits evenly on
both sides. Rejected: natural width (the clock and version shift one cell when CPU crosses 10% or
100%); trailing pad (lopsided chip).

## Scope

In scope: VEN-C28's label text and geometry sentence (contract change approved in substance
above; show the exact wording to Lucca before commit), the label text in `venus/src/system.rs`,
the scene/chrome geometry that sizes and places the CPU and RAM text in their chips, their tests
(`system.rs:130-187`, `accessibility.rs:1371-1373`), and `venus/CHANGELOG.md`.

Out of scope: hover and AccessKit descriptions (already single-spaced), quota chips, the clock,
the version label, width-fitting priority, item order (VEN-C29).

## Acceptance

- Installed bar shows `CPU 10%` and `RAM 34%` with one space, each centered in a chip as wide as
  `CPU 100%`; at 5% and 100% the chip width is unchanged and neighbours don't move.
- Width fitting still hides clock, RAM, CPU, version in that order.

## Verification

- `nix develop -c eon-test -p yazelix-venus`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --locked -p
  yazelix-venus --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- One isolated installed observation of the bar (see the eon-igae.14.1 proof for the headless
  Sway recipe). Portability disposition: neutral.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask Lucca if centering needs a half-cell offset that the chrome renderer can't place
  (monospace grid only); propose rounding the slack to the leading side instead.
close_reason: Gap closed: one-space CPU/RAM labels centered in fixed-width chips; proven on tree 511fa92f (see proof comment)

title: Show icons in the Eon Bar's CPU, RAM and GPU chips
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-21: use icons for the Eon Bar's CPU and RAM chips, and for the GPU chip too
("yeah / gpu too", on eon-52's recommendation). The quota chips already lead with a provider logo,
so the readings become the same family, and an icon is narrower than the `CPU ` / `RAM ` text, so
the readings survive narrower windows before width fitting hides them. The clock gets no icon:
`20:12` already says what it is (eon-52's recommendation, not contested).

## Design (recommended, glyphs to confirm with Lucca from the capture below)

- Each reading chip shows an icon, a space and the value (`<icon> 12%`), with the icon drawn from
  Symbols Nerd Font Mono, which Eon already ships as the first `font_fallbacks` entry and which
  Venus's font tests already require. No new asset or dependency.
- The chip keeps a fixed width, that of `<icon> 100%`, with its text centered (the rule
  `eon-igae.14.4` sets for the text labels), so neighbours never shift.
- Hover and AccessKit text is unchanged ("CPU use 12%, all cores, over the last 2 seconds",
  "RAM use 43% of 31.3 GiB"), so no meaning is lost.
- Candidate glyphs: CPU `nf-oct-cpu` (U+F4BC) or `nf-md-cpu_64_bit` (U+F0EE0); RAM `nf-md-memory`
  (U+F035B); GPU `nf-md-expansion_card` (U+F02AE) or `nf-md-gpu`-style alternatives. The three
  must be told apart at bar size.

## First step (spike, before contract wording)

One isolated installed capture showing the candidate glyphs side by side at the default font size
and at the minimum (6 px) and at scale 1.25, so Lucca can pick. If CPU and RAM glyphs blur together
at bar size, stop and ask Lucca whether to keep the text labels.

## Scope

In scope: VEN-C28's label text and chip-width sentence (contract change; exact wording to Lucca
before commit), `venus/src/system.rs` labels, the scene width rule (`venus/src/scene.rs`, the
`"CPU 100%"` floor), centering in `venus/src/render/chrome.rs`, tests in `system.rs` and
`accessibility.rs`, `docs/USAGE.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `venus/CHANGELOG.md`. Width-fitting checks
must still pass with the new widths. Record the chosen GPU glyph on
`eon-gpu-widget-eon-bar-ri16` so that chip uses it from the start.

Out of scope: a clock icon, the GPU chip itself (`eon-gpu-widget-eon-bar-ri16`), quota logos,
item order (VEN-C29), configurable icons or a text/icon setting.

## Prerequisites

`eon-igae.14.4` (the one-space centered text) is committed first; this bead reuses its fixed-width
centering.

## Acceptance

- Installed bar shows `<cpu icon> 12%` and `<ram icon> 43%`, centered in fixed-width chips; values
  from 0% to 100% never move the clock or version.
- Hover and AccessKit text unchanged; width-fitting order unchanged (clock, RAM, CPU, version).

## Verification

- `nix develop -c eon-test -p yazelix-venus`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --locked -p
  yazelix-venus --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- One isolated installed observation per accepted batch (headless Sway recipe in the
  eon-igae.14.1 proof). Portability disposition: neutral (font glyphs, no platform API).

title: Rename the component graph's eon-alpha product ID before 1.0
description:
## Why

The component manifest's product graph ID is still `eon-alpha` (`components/eon-alpha-v3.json:4`).
`eon-versioning-beta-bfyf` kept it "until the next graph version, because renaming them changes
the component report that live generations compare". 1.0 should not ship with "alpha" in its
version report, and renaming after the stability promise would be a breaking change.

## Evidence

- `components/eon-alpha-v3.json:4`: `"id": "eon-alpha"`.
- `flake.nix:68`, `flake.nix:727`, `eon/crates/eon/src/product.rs:8`,
  `eon/crates/eon-manifest/src/lib.rs:424`, `demo/record.rs:75`: file path consumers.
- `docs/DEVELOPMENT.md:43`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:10,239`, `docs/CONTRACTS.md:21`: doc links.
- `runtime/crates/eon-workspace-protocol/src/v2.rs..v6.rs`: historical `"eon-alpha x86_64-linux"`
  fixtures. Leave historical EONW fixtures alone (runtime/AGENTS.md: preserve history).

## Scope

In: a new graph version with a non-stage product ID (propose the name to Lucca, e.g. `eon`),
the manifest file name, its consumers and docs. Out: changing EONW historical revisions.

## Acceptance

- `eon versions` reports the new ID; no current product text or report says alpha.
- A live generation started before the rename stays discoverable, attachable as before, and
  stoppable from the new build (the comparison the versioning bead warned about).

## Verification

Component manifest route (AGENTS.md "Verification"): full affected Rust and Nix surfaces:
`nix develop -c eon-test`, `nix build --no-link .#default .#eonbase`, plus one installed
observation of an old live generation being listed and stopped by the new build.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if the rename forces an EONW revision or breaks old-generation discovery; ask Lucca.
close_reason: Product graph ID is eon in components/eon-v4.json; old generations stay listed and stoppable from the new build

title: Show a RAM widget in the Eon Bar
description:
## Why

Lucca chose CPU, RAM and clock widgets for 1.0 (2026-10-20), matching Nova's bar
(`~/pjs/nova/nova-upstream-theme/crates/yzx-config/src/catalog.rs:54` lists `cpu`, `ram`).
`eon-cpu-widget-eon-bar-acxs` builds the shared sampling and chip path; RAM rides on it.

Lucca, 2026-10-21: Venus samples locally (no Runtime sampling, no EONW revision), and the chip
format is `RAM 43%`, matching `CPU 12%`. See the CPU bead for the full design and reasons.

## Scope

In: whole-machine memory use as a read-only `RAM 43%` Eon Bar chip, parsed from `/proc/meminfo`
(used = MemTotal - MemAvailable) in the CPU bead's Linux-only Venus sampling module, on its 2 s
cadence, with hover and an accessible label. Contract: extend the CPU bead's `EON-C30`/`VEN-C28`
rather than adding new IDs; the wording needs Lucca's approval before commit.
Out: per-process or per-Eon attribution; GPU and IO (1.x).

## Acceptance

- The chip follows every failure rule of the CPU bead's contract: no chip on an invalid sample
  (never 0), no layout or resize churn on refresh, and the width-pressure order (clock, then
  CPU/RAM, then quota chips).
- The contract extension is approved before code.

## Verification

Focused parser test for `/proc/meminfo` parsing (red/green) plus the Venus build, and one isolated
installed dogfood observation of the chip.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask Lucca if `/proc/meminfo` lacks `MemAvailable` on a supported kernel, since the used
  figure would then need a different formula.

title: Show a clock in the Eon Bar
description:
## Why

Lucca asked for a clock in the Eon Bar for 1.0 (2026-10-20): quick and helpful.

## Scope

In: a read-only clock chip in the Eon Bar showing local time, with an accessible label.
Decide the owner before code (recommendation: Venus formats local time as presentation, Eon
owns the on/off default and any 12/24-hour setting; no EONW field is needed if Venus owns it).
Out: date pickers, calendars, time zones other than local.

## Acceptance

- The clock updates at minute boundaries without replacing attachments, scroll positions or
  sending an Orbit resize, and yields to required tabs and controls under width pressure, with
  an agreed order against quota and metric chips.
- Contract text approved by Lucca before code.

## Verification

The cheapest consuming check (a Scene golden or unit test for formatting and priority) plus the
affected build, and one isolated installed dogfood observation.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if Venus needs a per-minute timer that wakes the renderer when idle in a way that costs
  measurable CPU; record the measurement and ask.
close_reason: Local Eon Bar clock shipped under VEN-C27/EON-C29; proof and ledger recorded in comments.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Decisions (Lucca, 2026-10-21, via eon-53): (1) Venus owns the clock; local time zone from jiff =0.2.38, default-features off, features std + tz-system (Venus forbids unsafe, so no libc localtime_r; chrono rejected as more crates for the same responsibility). (2) Local 24-hour HH:MM, always on, no configuration, no runtime/EONW change; an on/off or 12-hour setting is a later bead if wanted. (3) Placement after the quota chips, before Shortcuts/Close; under width pressure the clock disappears first, then quota compacts and drops, then tabs and controls keep VEN-C21 priority. Reason: desktop panels usually show a clock; quota is Eon-only information.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Contract approved (Lucca, 2026-10-21): VEN-C27 and EON-C29 'Local clock in the Eon Bar'. Read-only local 24-hour HH:MM label after quota chips and the version label, before Shortcuts/Close; updates within a second of each minute boundary; hover and static AccessKit label give time, date and UTC offset ('Local time 14:05, Wednesday 21 October 2026, UTC−03:00'). Uses only spare drag-region space and keeps its minimum; shown only while every quota chip is full-width; hides before the version label, quota compaction, tabs or controls. Unknown local zone: no clock (no silent UTC). Clock-only updates do not replace attachments, recenter tabs, cancel scroll or send an Orbit resize; no action, focus target or drag behavior; after suspend or a clock change it corrects within one minute. Owners: Venus Scene text/geometry, application minute wake, jiff zone resolution (TZ, /etc/localtime). Boundary: no EONW/runtime change, configuration, 12-hour mode, calendar, other zones, widget framework. EON-C29: full Eon ships VEN-C27 always on with no Eon configuration.

Reference gate (consequential: new dependency).
- Behavior owner: Venus (VEN-C27); Eon only ships it (EON-C29).
- Routes read: venus/docs/REFERENCES.md 'Native Eon Bar workspace header' and 'Codex quota fact chip'; VEN-C21/C22/C25/C26; venus/docs/CRATES.md.
- Comparable: Waybar clock module, Alexays/Waybar tag 0.14.0 (41de8964f1e3278edf07902ad68ca5e01e7abeeb) src/modules/clock.cpp:141 sleeps 'interval - now.time_since_epoch() % interval' (default 60 s), i.e. wakes on wall-clock boundaries, and formats a zoned_time from the local zone. Adopted: wake at the next wall-clock minute computed from SystemTime, not Instant+60s drift. Rejected: Waybar's thread, locale/format configuration, calendar tooltip.
- Crate: jiff 0.2.38 (crates.io 2026-10-06, Unlicense OR MIT, crate sha256 b2b005715dcbeb0089a3c0dab99f2ff1cc3b2525323552703d648585d342a383). Features std, tz-system, tzdb-zoneinfo; adds only jiff-core on Linux/macOS (windows-link is Windows-only). src/tz/system/mod.rs caches the system zone with a 5-minute TTL; TZ env, then /etc/localtime (symlink name via TZDIR/zoneinfo, else TZif contents). Rejected: libc localtime_r (Venus forbids unsafe_code), chrono Local (iana-time-zone plus its own parser for the same job), time crate (local offset refused on multithreaded Unix).
- Version policy: exact pin like Venus's other direct deps; upgrade only with a reason. Exit condition: remove if Venus drops the clock or the platform host gains a safe local-time source.
- Decision check: Scene unit tests (format, placement, drop order, no-zone → no clock) plus one isolated installed observation.

title: Integrate accepted Venus cell-buffer memory reduction
description:
## Contract

For Eon and EonTerm users launching the refreshed Nix profile, select accepted Venus 541a9cb43c155b8b97069904593dc81c73682613 and its reduced per-cell allocation through the canonical component graph. Preserve terminal rendering, configuration, exact Orbit/protocol identity and bounded launch failures. Existing live supervisors and Sessions retain their processes and old generation; profile refresh does not restart them. Preserve EON-C1/C2/C4/C11/C19 and qualified Venus proof records; no new product contract.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

User selected this integration on 2026-09-08 after the Venus source and acceptance commits were pushed. ven-profile-venus-memory-u3o is closed at accepted source 541a9cb; Eon currently pins ec80e36625dec73544c0cb64becf4b135c932a63. Orbit remains accepted 91999d79546422b49bdbc124166a65859d0bd872. Required evidence before edits: Eon instructions, relevant contracts/distribution/reference routes, canonical manifest and Nix source/wrapper ownership; Venus exact source diff, locked Cargo inputs and retained memory proof; preceding Eon pin-refresh implementation as comparison. No new dependency or rendering mechanism is selected.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Manifest, exact flake input and lock select accepted Venus 541a9cb; all other component, protocol and existing contract-proof identities remain exact and unchanged.
- Both affected downstream packages build and their active profile elements resolve to the current working-tree artifacts. Installed versions and wrapper/source identity prove the selected child.
- Isolated native Wayland dogfood covers both installed products: actual 120x30 loaded Unicode, baseline/candidate pixel equivalence, and three paired fresh-process PSS/USS measurements per product. Use retained private Sway/pixman/lavapipe harness with fixed workload/environment and exact old/new package paths. No active-desktop windows. A failure or unexpected memory regression blocks acceptance; retain raw observations and limits, without extrapolating to COSMIC/hardware GPU results.
- Preserve pre-existing user runtime PID/start identities; stop only owned disposable generations. Update changelog, canonical proof and README LOC; verify Beads and diff.

## Scope

One exact child-pin integration, both local profile refreshes and bounded installed proof. No Eon Rust mechanism, Venus/Orbit changes, new settings, schema, dependency, broad benchmark matrix, new platform, public distribution, channel promotion or live-user Session interruption. Do not mutate child issues or widen fractional-scale, compositor, non-systemd, GPU-memory, throughput or long-running-growth claims.

title: Investigate slow Anima animations in Eon versus Nova
description:
## Contract and outcome

Investigate the user's report that some Anima animations perform terribly in Eon while the problem does not occur in Nova. Produce a reproducible comparison, measured bottleneck and responsible owner, with the smallest justified correction recommended for separately chosen implementation. This is investigation of the current x86_64 Linux native-Wayland product, not a new performance guarantee.

## Evidence and prerequisites

User report on 2026-10-07: severe animation-specific slowdown in Eon; Nova is the unaffected comparison. The affected style names, launch path and exact environment are not yet identified; establish them during reproduction rather than inventing a workload or assuming every animation is slow. eon-anima-startup-5el records accepted startup, caller-terminal CLI and popup integration. The current Eon manifest pins Anima 0.2.0 at b3133f057fa0029b3e06c85301161168c48bb799. Functional playback acceptance does not establish frame cadence or responsiveness.

No implementation prerequisite blocks read-only diagnosis. Select exact installed Eon/Runtime/Orbit/Venus/Anima and Nova artifacts before measuring; preserve live terminals and desktop focus. Existing lifecycle repairs remain separate work on the sequential implementation frontier.

## Reference gate and owners

Read docs/REFERENCES.md's Anima route, EON-C1/C3/C4/C10/C18, Anima's exact CLI and screen runner, and current accepted Eon/Nova launch and configuration paths. The integration comparison used Nova e476ca8065cc8b2c02ea611ae7edeeb0989c0c23; identify the user's actual current Nova revision and terminal stack instead of assuming it matches that historical reference.

Eon owns composition, launch and popup policy; Anima owns animation generation/playback; Orbit owns PTY ingestion and terminal state; Venus owns presentation. Trace the complete affected path and measure before attributing blame. Nova is comparison evidence, not a renderer/dependency selection or compatibility target.

## Acceptance

- Identify at least one reliably affected animation and an unaffected control, with exact style/arguments, launch path, component revisions, artifacts and reproducible observation. If the report cannot be reproduced, retain the negative evidence and state the missing conditions; do not claim a resolved performance defect.
- Compare the same Anima workload in Eon and Nova on the same host under controlled geometry, requested frame rate, duration and relevant rendering settings. Match Anima version and deterministic seed where supported, or disclose unavoidable differences. Capture the native hardware/compositor/backend environment; a software-rendered test alone cannot establish the user's hardware behavior.
- Distinguish animation generation/output cost, Orbit processing/transport, Venus rendering/presentation and Eon launch/settings effects using the smallest measurements that discriminate them. Quantify observed frame cadence/stalls and responsiveness plus relevant resource cost over repeated fixed-workload samples; retain distributions or bounds and raw evidence needed to reproduce costly measurements.
- Record the observed Nova/Eon gap, actual bottleneck and owner, supported conclusions and unresolved confounders. Screenshots, compilation, code inspection or average FPS alone do not prove smooth playback. Compare launch surfaces only as needed to isolate the affected boundary; avoid an arbitrary style/platform benchmark matrix.
- Recommend the minimum owner-specific correction and its falsifying before/after check, or state that further evidence is required. Preserve unaffected animations, dismissal, terminal-mode cleanup, picker handoff and peer work as constraints on any future fix.

## Scope boundary

Investigation and recommendation only: no runtime fixes, component-pin/config/default changes, copied Anima rendering, new animation styles, replacement renderer, dependency, protocol, benchmark framework, CI job or performance/support promise. No Nova product change, new platform, distribution work or automatic creation of follow-up beads. Record measured findings here and let the user choose implementation. Investigation completed on 2026-10-08; measured findings and the separately recommended Venus correction are recorded in the closure evidence. No runtime implementation is authorized by this investigation.
notes: Measured Venus font-fallback bottleneck; direct native Intel Wayland plasma comparison reproduces ~5 visible changes/s in Eon versus 20–23 in installed Nova. Proof: /home/lucca/.local/state/eon/proofs/anima-performance-2026-10-08/report.txt. Proposed half-block rectangle path remains separately chosen implementation; live COSMIC/original launch surface not proved.
close_reason: Investigation completed: native hardware reproduction, profiles, control and limitations recorded. Venus half-block rendering correction recommended for separate user selection; no runtime fix claimed.

comments.text:

The user identified plasma, physarum and aquarium. Exact Anima source shows that all three use its shared colored half-block output. Dense plasma reliably reproduced the slowdown; sparse matrix was an unaffected discovery control. The private Venus plasma CPU-core profile had 437 samples, 70.31% in cosmic-text FontFallbackIter::next through Renderer::render → build_scene_text → push_text → Buffer::shape_until_scroll. Aquarium showed the same dominant stack. Venus currently bypasses shaping only for the one-cell full block █; Anima's colored ▀/▄ runs reach the text path. title: Show an IO widget in the Eon Bar
description:
## Decision
Lucca, 2026-10-17: add an IO widget to Eon, alongside CPU and GPU.

## Contract (provisional; needs Lucca's approval before code)
- Consumer: a full-Eon user on native x86_64 Linux Wayland.
- Result: the Eon Bar shows a read-only IO chip with whole-machine disk read and write throughput
  (for example `R 12M/s W 3M/s`), through the chip path the CPU widget bead establishes.
- Failures: unreadable or invalid samples show no chip, never zero; counter wraps and device
  hot-plug do not produce spikes.

## Ownership
As in the CPU widget bead: Runtime samples behind the Linux platform seam, EONW carries typed facts,
Venus presents.

## Open decisions (recommendations)
1. What "IO" means: disk read/write throughput from `/proc/diskstats` (recommended, what btop and
   Waybar's disk modules show); IO pressure from `/proc/pressure/io` (answers "is the machine
   stalling on IO" but is a less familiar number); network throughput (a separate widget if wanted).
2. Device set: whole physical disks only, excluding partitions, loop, zram and device-mapper layers
   that would double count (recommended).
3. Units and width: compact binary units with a fixed width so the bar does not jitter.

## Reference gate (consequential if the CPU bead's EONW field must change)
Record btop, bottom and Waybar's disk module at exact revisions: device filtering, wrap handling
and units kept or rejected; the chosen source and its check.

## Prerequisites
`eon-cpu-widget-eon-bar-acxs` (collection, EONW field and chip path).

## Acceptance
Focused sampler red/green (device filtering, deltas, wrap, hot-plug, invalid input); EONW round-trip
if the field changes; Venus chip test; `eon-test`, fmt, clippy, nix build; isolated capture under a
real disk load; review loop; profile refresh.

## Scope boundary
Aggregate disk throughput only: no per-device or per-process view, IOPS, latency, graphs, network or
actions. Linux only.

title: Play a sound when a coding agent finishes
description:
## Why

Lucca, 2026-10-21: Eon should play a short sound (a "ding") when a coding agent finishes, so a
user supervising agents across tabs, or working in another window, knows to come back without
watching the screen. Eon has no audio output today, and no agent "done" signal yet.

## Evidence

- `eon-agent-sidebar-yx8.2` builds the Eon-owned attention state for Claude and Codex launched in
  a tab's Agent popup (working / needs input / done / unknown-or-stale) and carries it over EONW.
  Its done transition is the natural trigger; this bead adds no second state owner.
- `eon-bell-accent-appearance-2t2z` (deferred) records an earlier, never-activated audio-bell
  request. A terminal BEL needs Orbit's ordered-effects channel (`orb-ll1`), which does not exist.
- `venus/AGENTS.md`: Venus isolates native host mechanics (event loop, window, clipboard,
  accessibility host, application lifecycle) at the native host boundary; audio output would be a
  new mechanism there. Eon owns persistent configuration.

## Contract (proposal; needs Lucca's approval before code)

- Consumer: a full-Eon user running Claude or Codex in a tab's Agent popup.
- Trigger: that agent's attention state becomes `done` (per yx8.2's contract).
- Result: Eon plays one short completion sound, once per transition.
- Failures: no audio device or playback failure is silent and never blocks or delays the terminal;
  repeated or out-of-order `done` reports for the same run do not repeat the sound; unknown or
  stale state never dings.
- Contracts: extend the yx8.2 attention contract (EON-C / VEN-C IDs it settles) or add new IDs;
  stop for approval first.

## Open decisions (recommendations)

1. Trigger source: yx8.2's provider attention `done` (recommended: it means "the agent finished",
   explicitly reported) rather than the terminal BEL (needs `orb-ll1`, and any program can ring it).
2. Also ding on `needs input`? Recommend yes, with the same sound: an agent waiting on the user is
   the more costly case to miss. Lucca asked only for done; decide before code.
3. When to stay quiet: recommend no sound when the Eon window is focused and the agent's tab is the
   active tab (the user is already looking at it).
4. Default and setting: recommend on by default with one Eon configuration switch to turn it off
   (Eon owns configuration; Venus receives it as a startup input).
5. Mechanism: the freedesktop sound theme's `complete` event through the desktop's sound service
   (libcanberra or `canberra-gtk-play`), versus an owned audio path (for example `rodio` with a
   bundled sound) versus spawning `pw-play`/`paplay`. Run the AP-DEPENDENCY-001 gate; prefer the
   option that respects the user's sound theme and volume and adds no audio stack to Venus.

## Scope

In scope:
- The ding on the attention transition, its quiet rule, the off switch, and the audio mechanism.

Out of scope:
- Attention state itself (yx8.2), the sidebar (yx8.3), terminal BEL handling (`orb-ll1`), visual
  bells and accents (`eon-bell-accent-appearance-2t2z`), desktop notifications, per-agent or
  custom sounds, volume control.
- Never take focus or raise the window (AGENTS.md Desktop Focus).

## Acceptance

- One ding per `done` transition of a Claude or Codex run, none while its tab is active in a
  focused window, none with the switch off, and silent failure without audio.
- Contract and mechanism approved by Lucca before code; reference gate and dependency decision
  recorded here.

## Verification

- Focused test of the trigger rule (transition once, out-of-order and repeated reports, quiet rule,
  switch off) in the owning crate via `nix develop -c eon-test -p <crate>`.
- Affected builds, fmt and clippy for changed Orbit/Venus crates.
- One isolated installed dogfood with a real Claude or Codex run reaching done, observing the
  sound request (for example through the sound service's log or a stub sink), plus a run with no
  audio device.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop if yx8.2's attention contract has no stable `done` transition to consume.
- Stop if the mechanism needs a new runtime dependency before Lucca approves it.

## Maintenance Notes

- Portability disposition must be recorded at activation (audio is a platform seam; Linux only).

- Quiet rule (decision 3) maps onto EON-C31's Seen: a raise seen at once because its terminal is focused in an attached, focused window should not ding.
- Desktop notifications are the sibling eon-2kvr (now P2, undeferred); decide the two together so one setting family covers sound and notifications (Configurability: one setting per value).
- The Workspace hint: attention spans hidden workspaces (EON-C33), so a finish in a hidden workspace should ding too.

Open decisions 1-5 above stay for Lucca; decision 1 is now settled by the code shape (EON-C31 finished raise, not BEL).

title: Decide whether Eon needs an extension system
description:
Contract disposition:
This decision creates no compatibility surface or runtime contract. Eon remains configuration-first and has no general plugin system. If the user later chooses an extension system, approve and index a separate EON contract before implementation.

Current product direction:
Proceed in order: finish and dogfood the core Eon workspace; prove one Eon-owned semantic action registry and make the `eon` CLI its canonical human and agent projection; let one declarative Eon configuration schema and external programs consume those actions; then reconsider plugins only if real recurring needs remain unsolved. Human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output are views of the same action owner, not separate APIs. The action surface and its private local control transport are not a plugin ABI, and configuration must not become an accidental programming language.

Goal:
After eon-pxn proves the workspace, action surface, and declarative-profile boundary, decide whether built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, configuration, or child-owned extension systems are insufficient and a stable Eon extension boundary is justified.

Prerequisites:
- eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove and dogfood the Eon workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative profile.
- Dogfood records at least two concrete recurring extension cases from different workflows and routes each through the existing owners first.
- The user explicitly activates this decision work; it does not become an implementation frontier automatically.

Ownership:
Eon may own product orchestration, workspace metadata, semantic actions, one product configuration schema and apply policy, and, only if later approved, extension installation, grants, activation, and compatibility. Ratconfig owns reusable configuration editing while consuming the Eon-owned schema and model. Orbit remains plugin-free and owns PTYs, sessions, terminal state, and ORBS/ORBF. Venus owns native rendering and may render only host-defined declarative contributions. Helix and Yazi keep their own extension mechanisms.

Scope:
Research and decide only. Do not add a runtime, SDK, manifest format, extension host, marketplace, plugin API, child-protocol capability, or production code. Do not let external automation or extensions receive raw PTY or protocol frames, fabricate provider state, inject arbitrary UI trees, or bypass separately approved Orbit observation contracts.

## Reference gate

At activation, read the exact accepted workspace, semantic-action, CLI, local-control, configuration, and declarative-profile contracts and their dogfood evidence. Inspect the two concrete unmet extension cases and the current primary documentation for only the credible candidate boundaries they require. Compare no extension system, first-party owner code, ordinary external executables over accepted actions, and—only if demonstrated needs survive—WebAssembly Components or an embedded runtime. Record security, grants, lifecycle, compatibility, portability, dependency/toolchain weight, owned LOC, upgrade and removal cost, and meaningful rejections.

## Acceptance criteria

- At least two recurring unmet cases from different workflows survive routing through existing owner code, configuration, the canonical CLI/actions, ordinary external programs, and child-owned extension systems.
- One explicit adopt, defer, or reject decision names the user value, owner, trust boundary, lifecycle, compatibility promise, platform scope, proof, and reversal condition.
- A positive decision selects the smallest sufficient boundary and requires a separately approved indexed EON contract before implementation; it does not create an SDK, marketplace, guest-language promise, or raw child-protocol access by implication.
- A defer or reject decision records what evidence would justify reconsideration.
- The user explicitly accepts the decision. Closing this bead creates no implementation, dependency, repository, protocol, configuration language, or compatibility surface.
design:
Decision ladder:
1. Continue core product work. First-party workspace, tab, pane, attention, graphics, mouse, accessibility, and presentation needs are not plugin evidence.
2. Prove one excellent Eon-owned semantic action registry and its canonical `eon` CLI in eon-pxn. The running supervisor alone owns live workspace and action state behind a private Eon local control endpoint. The CLI exposes stable semantic identities, context-sensitive available actions, typed arguments, structured results, unavailable-action reasons, cancellation, and bounded errors through human-readable output and deterministic `--json` output. It does not address child protocols directly, and begins explicitly versioned and experimental; no stable 1.0 or plugin compatibility promise is implied.
3. Prove one bounded declarative configuration system over the same owner-authored actions. It may describe workspace and launch profiles, keybindings, named action sequences, explicit environment and working-directory inputs, and accepted presentation choices. It has one Eon-owned schema and Ratconfig editing. It does not gain loops, mutable variables, asynchronous callbacks, arbitrary code, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or a second state owner. External commands using the action surface are the escape hatch.
4. Reopen the plugin decision only when two recurring cases cannot be expressed safely by the first three rungs or a child-owned extension system.

Required comparison:
A. Keep built-ins plus child-owned extension mechanisms.
B. Use the canonical `eon` CLI and the same narrow action protocol from external tools or commands without Eon-owned extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, SDK promises, or plugin compatibility.
C. Use schema-backed declarative Eon configuration over the action API.
D. Add a plugin system using one of the credible architectures below.

Plugin architecture candidates, only after dogfood earns them:
1. Out-of-process extension executables over the same bounded framed local action protocol. Their implementation language is private and unrestricted; Eon promises the protocol, not supported languages or SDKs. This is the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions because it reuses the action owner, fits Eon process supervision and Nix-pinned executables, and isolates crashes. Process separation alone is not an authority boundary; ambient user authority and OS sandboxing remain explicit.
2. WebAssembly Components with WIT and a credible runtime only when demonstrated cases require portable untrusted distribution, default-deny capability imports, or resource isolation that the selected process boundary cannot provide. Multiple guest languages are not themselves a product requirement. Record runtime weight, build and startup cost, standards maturity, toolchains, Linux/native-Wayland support, and removal cost.
3. An embedded language runtime only when the demonstrated cases require synchronous or high-frequency in-process callbacks that the external action protocol cannot satisfy. At that point compare no runtime with exact credible languages and require the selected runtime to remove a complete Eon responsibility. Do not choose a language for syntax taste, agent novelty, or programmable configuration alone.

Language and runtime disposition:
Zero, Roto, Steel, Lua, Luau, and other languages remain discovery inputs rather than standing candidates. Zero is useful comparison evidence for semantic graph inspection, checked edits, typed facts, explicit effects, and agent-facing diagnostics, but its current experimental compiled toolchain is not an Eon extension host, stable compatibility boundary, or security sandbox. Reconsider a named language only when a demonstrated extension case and exact current evidence make its runtime uniquely credible.

Native Rust dynamic-library plugins are not a default candidate because they couple compiler and ABI choices to the host and place extension failure in the Eon process. Reconsider them only if exact evidence makes that coupling advantageous.

Reference gate:
Begin with the demonstrated cases, the exact accepted eon-pxn action, CLI, and configuration contracts, and the exact owner mechanisms they consume. First test whether built-ins, child-owned extensions, `eon` CLI composition, bounded wait or events, configuration, or an ordinary external process solve each case. Inspect an out-of-process extension-host precedent only if Eon-owned installation and activation remain necessary. Inspect WebAssembly Components, WIT, and a selected runtime only for a demonstrated untrusted portable-code requirement. Inspect a named embedded language only for a demonstrated synchronous in-process requirement. Compare no new dependency, existing process and protocol facilities, release health, licenses, Linux/native-Wayland support, dependency and compile weight, security posture, owned LOC, compatibility burden, and removal cost. Agent-authoring ergonomics are secondary to ownership, failure isolation, security, portability, and compatibility.

Security and lifecycle gate:
Default-deny filesystem, environment, process spawning, network, clipboard, secrets, raw terminal or protocol data, GPU, windows, webviews, and background execution. Separate read-only observation from mutation. Define memory, wall-time, queue, message, result, log, storage, concurrency, activation, cancellation, crash, restart, and shutdown bounds. An extension-host crash must not terminate Orbit or Venus, and safe mode must disable third-party extensions.

Distribution and compatibility gate:
Start with local or Nix-pinned immutable bundles only. Identity is publisher, name, version, API version, and content hash, never a Nix store path. Permissions match imported capabilities and re-prompt when expanded. Defer a marketplace, arbitrary panels, custom widget trees, remote installation, signing infrastructure, and a multi-language support promise. Define the selected API version policy and make no stable compatibility promise before an explicitly approved 1.0 API.

Stop conditions:
Stop with no plugin feature if built-ins, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, or child-owned plugins cover the demonstrated needs. Stop if the design needs Orbit plugins, raw ORBS/ORBF access, duplicated terminal or provider state, speculative capability negotiation, ambient authority presented as sandboxing, or a marketplace before local extensions prove value. Stop for explicit user choice before creating a contract or implementation bead.
acceptance_criteria:
1. eon-pxn and its activated owner children prove the core workspace, deterministic action surface, and bounded declarative-profile boundary before this decision starts.
2. Dogfood supplies at least two independent recurring extension cases and explains why built-in owner code, the action API, external commands, declarative configuration, and child-owned plugins do not solve them. First-party tabs, panes, overlays, status items, graphics, mouse behavior, accessibility, and presentation do not count as extension demand.
3. The record distinguishes the Eon-owned action registry and canonical CLI from a plugin system: actions expose semantic state and behavior through human-readable and deterministic structured projections, while extension discovery, installation, activation, hosting, grants, SDK promises, and compatibility remain absent unless explicitly approved. The running supervisor is the sole live action-state owner, and the CLI or external clients never bypass it by speaking child protocols directly.
4. The configuration candidate has one Eon-owned schema and apply policy, is edited through Ratconfig, consumes accepted semantic actions, and contains no arbitrary executable language, loops, mutable callbacks, custom widget trees, raw terminal control, or duplicate state.
5. The comparison grades continuing with built-ins, API plus external tools, declarative configuration, and a plugin system against product value, human and agent usability, architecture, security, portability, dependency cost, compatibility burden, and removal cost.
6. If plugins remain justified, the reference and crate or tool gates start with out-of-process executable extensions over the accepted Eon action protocol. They evaluate WebAssembly Components only for demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation needs, and a named embedded runtime only for demonstrated synchronous or high-frequency in-process needs that the external protocol cannot meet. They compare no new dependency and record why Zero or any other language is or is not credible at its exact current revision. Eon makes no supported-language, SDK, or multi-language promise merely because executable or Wasm boundaries permit several implementations.
7. The decision names one owner for identity, installation, activation, grants, actions, UI contributions, state, failures, and compatibility while preserving Orbit, Venus, Ratconfig, Helix, and Yazi ownership.
8. A threat model and capability table cover filesystem, environment, process, network, clipboard, secrets, terminal observation, UI, storage, and background work with deny-by-default behavior. Process separation is not claimed as authority isolation without an OS sandbox.
9. Resource, lifecycle, crash-isolation, safe-mode, Linux/native-Wayland, distribution, upgrade, removal, and API-version policies are explicit and falsifiable.
10. Any proposed plugin proof contains exactly the two demonstrated first-party extensions and checks useful behavior, permission denial, runaway execution, extension crash, incompatible API version, and clean removal.
11. The record estimates owned LOC, dependency weight, compile and runtime cost, maintenance, and permanent compatibility cost and names evidence that would reverse the recommendation.
12. The user explicitly chooses keep built-ins and the CLI/action API only, add declarative configuration only, use a narrow out-of-process extension contract, adopt WebAssembly Components for a demonstrated portable untrusted-code or isolation requirement, adopt a named embedded runtime for a demonstrated in-process requirement, reject plugins, or defer.
13. Closure creates no runtime code, dependency, manifest, protocol change, marketplace, SDK, or compatibility promise.
notes:
User-approved planning direction on 2026-08-08: sequence core product work, a narrow high-quality action API, schema-backed declarative configuration, and only then a plugin decision if dogfood still demonstrates unmet needs.

Current judgment:
- Continue core workspace work: A for the present frontier.
- One Eon-owned semantic action registry with the canonical `eon` CLI for humans and agents: A+, the preferred control and extensibility backbone.
- Bounded declarative configuration and ordinary external programs consuming the same actions: A, the preferred customization and automation layers.
- General plugin system: D at the current product stage, with an A- ceiling only after concrete demand and successful ownership, security, lifecycle, portability, and compatibility gates.

If plugins are later earned, out-of-process executables over the accepted action protocol are the preferred first candidate for trusted local extensions. Their language remains a private implementation detail rather than an Eon support promise. WebAssembly Components are conditional on demonstrated untrusted portable-code or isolation requirements. An embedded runtime is conditional on demonstrated synchronous in-process requirements that external actions cannot meet. No architecture, SDK, supported guest language, or durable second language is selected by this planning decision.

Priority P4 remains intentional. This work follows the eon-pxn workspace and action proof rather than competing with Orbit, Venus, or the first Eon workspace frontier.

Feature-horizon boundary: eon-pxn owns bounded native horizontal tabs, visual vertical accordion panes, semantic actions, and declarative workspace or profile pressure as first-party product architecture. Generic overlays, floating terminal popups, arbitrary split trees, fixed status items, semantic mouse routing, accessibility focus, and graphics remain first-party owner concerns rather than plugin evidence.

Planning effort M; implementation risk HIGH because every published capability becomes a security and compatibility surface. Confidence HIGH in API-first and configuration-first sequencing, HIGH in deferring plugins, and LOW that an embedded runtime is justified before concrete cases exist.

First-principles language disposition approved on 2026-08-08:
- Eon needs one semantic action owner and canonical CLI, not an Eon-specific plugin language.
- Zero is retained as high-value comparison evidence for agent-queryable semantic interfaces, not selected as a dependency or extension runtime.
- Syntax elegance, static typing, and single-language ecosystem preferences do not outrank child ownership, crash isolation, security, portability, protocol stability, and removal cost.
- A language or runtime becomes credible only when dogfood supplies a case that the CLI, external actions, configuration, and child-owned mechanisms cannot solve.

Repository-wide prime — 2026-09-17: `eon-pxn` is an organizational product horizon, not a requirement that every optional workspace outcome close. The edge is therefore `related`. Activation remains hard-gated by the issue text on exact proved and dogfooded workspace, semantic-action, and declarative-profile outcomes; add owner-sized blocking edges when those concrete beads exist. No extension work is ready.

title: Evaluate a built-in editor popup
description:
## Why

Lucca asked (2026-10-26) whether Eon should ship an editor popup: Helix as a popup entry next to Git, Files and Agent. He dropped a fixed Alt+Shift+E key ("never mind alt shift e"); the key is a configurable detail. He is dogfooding a custom popup first: `[popups.editor] command = ["hx"], label = "Editor", keybinding = "Alt+Shift+O", keep_alive = true` in `~/.config/eon/config.toml` (custom popups are already supported, `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` Popups). Bead kept open for later (Lucca, 2026-10-26).

## Evidence

- `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` Popups section: custom `[popups.<id>]` entries with command, keybinding, label, keep_alive.
- `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/cli.rs:1198` (`parse_edit_arguments`) and `runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/workspace.rs:5213`: `eon edit -- FILE` and Files' Enter on a text file open Helix in a new pane.
- Pinned Helix is 25.07.1 (`helix --version` in the Eon closure).

## Questions to answer

1. Whether Lucca reached for the custom popup during dogfood (ask him; this decides whether a built-in is worth it).
2. Whether Helix 25.07.1 (or a newer upstream release) can receive a file from outside a running instance (server/remote open). Without it, Files' Enter and `eon edit` cannot target the popup, and a built-in would give Helix two homes that share nothing. Cite upstream issues/PRs with revisions.
3. If a built-in is still worth it: how Files and `eon edit` interact with it, the CLI path by ID (AGENTS.md Humans and Agents; gap `eon-agent-parity-a9g0`), the default key (configurable; check pinned Helix, Yazi, lazygit, shells and agent CLIs for conflicts), and the owning EON-C/VEN-C clauses for popup entries.
4. Lighter alternative: document the custom-popup recipe in `docs/CONFIGURATION.md` instead of a built-in.

## Scope

In scope: reading code, docs, contracts and upstream Helix; one bead comment with findings, options and a recommendation; on Lucca's choice, an implementation bead filed per the create-beads size rule.

Out of scope: code, configuration or contract changes.

## Acceptance

- A bead comment records the answers above with sources and a recommendation.
- Lucca's choice (built-in, docs recipe, or drop) is recorded with the date; then this bead closes, with an implementation bead if chosen.

## Verification

- Planning-only route (AGENTS.md Verification table): bead state and the comment.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop and ask Lucca before any contract change, new popup kind, or wire message.

Reference and dependency gate — canonical raster icon packaging

Question: How should Eon turn one luminous raster master into a clean canonical Linux desktop icon without launcher resampling artifacts or duplicate source assets?
Contract: existing EON-C1 desktop-icon identity only.
Sources and revisions: user-selected assets/icon-concepts/icon_eon_3.png (1254x1254 sRGB RGB, SHA-256 1bc63f18c821520e9a3b5e09f1c8bd5e33b5a87da85179523cb22bc1fb0d9786); Freedesktop Icon Theme Specification 0.13, current official page inspected 2026-08-09; Desktop Entry Specification 1.5 current official page; Eon flake.nix at HEAD 2b8fef19bb09d7ea0d1e891720eb36c838cbd237; Nixpkgs makeDesktopItem and comparable exact packages losslesscut/obsidian/blockbench at pinned revision 567a49d1913ce81ac6e9582e3553dd90a955875f.

Freedesktop requires at least a 48x48 PNG in hicolor/48x48/apps and permits additional exact raster sizes; scalable/apps is the SVG route, so the current 1254px PNG there is rejected. One canonical source asset owns identity; derived installed sizes are build outputs.
Options compared: keep one large PNG under scalable (rejected: wrong raster location and reproduces arbitrary COSMIC downsampling); check in seven derived PNGs (rejected: duplicate generated truth and manual synchronization); trace SVG (rejected: changes the selected 3D identity); generate exact raster sizes at build time with pinned ImageMagick (selected).
Dependency gate: ImageMagick 7.1.2-23 from the existing pinned Nixpkgs revision, Apache-2.0, is build-only and owns deterministic high-quality raster resizing. Its standalone Nix closure is 218.1 MiB, but it adds zero bytes to Eon runtime closure. No local image-resizer code, script, or second language is checked in. Decision: rebuild a clean transparent canonical master through the image workflow, install exact 16/24/32/48/64/128/256/512 PNGs using ImageMagick from that one source, and remove the temporary alternate launcher. title: Honour OSC 10/11 default colours and answer their queries
description:
## Why

Found by eon-mac-launch-kz4p.36 (2026-10-29): Eon ignores OSC 10/11 on every platform. A program
that sets the terminal's default background or foreground (`printf '\e]11;#808080\e\\'`), as some
themes, editors and tools do, changes nothing, and OSC 110/111 have nothing to reset. A program
that queries the background (`\e]11;?\e\\`) to choose a light or dark theme gets no reply, so it
falls back to guessing. Users reasonably expect both (AGENTS.md "Happy Users").

Cause (kz4p.36's analysis, unverified by the overseer): Orbit only sets libghostty's default
palette (orbit/src/pty.rs:200-206), never a default foreground or background. libghostty (ghostty
521cf2c5) stores OSC 10/11 as overrides, but its render state (src/terminal/render.zig:1052-1066)
copies fg/bg only when both are set, so with no default foreground an OSC 11 never reaches
Orbit's frame colours, and Venus keeps its background. The OSC 11 query goes unanswered
(Terminal.zig:189).

## Contract

Likely a new or changed ORB-C (Orbit owns terminal state and replies, ORB-C2), and possibly an
EON-C for a configurable default fg/bg. Needs Lucca's approval of the contract text before code.

## Change (shape, to plan)

Orbit gives the libghostty terminal a default fg/bg (from product config or Venus's theme
colours, one owner), so OSC 10/11 set and 110/111 reset reach frames and Venus, and queries
answer. Decide the source of the defaults (Configurability rule), reattachment behaviour, and
how Venus renders a changed default background with background_opacity.

## Acceptance

- Real-PTY Orbit check: OSC 11 set, query reply, OSC 111 reset; survives reattach.
- Installed dogfood: a program's OSC 11 changes Eon's background; OSC 111 restores it.
- Afterwards the macOS scenario's translucency step can go back to a grey probe
  (eon-mac-launch-kz4p.36's accepted gap).

## Scope

Orbit (and Venus/Runtime only if the defaults' source needs them). Not on the macOS launch path.

title: Closing tab 1 closed the whole window, tab 2 included
description:
## Report

Lucca, 2026-10-21 ~20:29 -03: "i close tab 1 in an older eon, and the entire window closed,
including tab 2".

## Evidence (eon-52, 2026-10-21 20:37 -03)

- The window belonged to supervisor `g1-62066c6e2a8666d073e678c90a66bb3d` (PID 2021541,
  started 17:58:05, EONW 13, `/nix/store/l5ss1z32rbzzk13qgl4aqqaiv6m2jn35-eon-0.1.1`).
- After the close, that supervisor and tab 2's terminal stayed alive: Orbit `orbit.sock`
  (PID 2022048) still runs nu -> Claude Code (PID 2022912). No Venus child remains, so the
  window, not the workspace, ended. Tab 1's terminal is gone.
- The supervisor's stdout/stderr go to /dev/null, so it left no log of why Venus exited.
- Lucca then opened a new Eon window at 20:29:17 (COSMIC scope `app-cosmic-eon-2642696`).

## Unknown, to establish first

- How tab 1 was closed: tab close control, Alt+W on its last pane, `exit` in its last shell, or
  `eon tab close`. Ask Lucca if not recorded here.
- Whether edge (EONW 14) still does it. Reproduce on edge in an isolated headless Sway
  (two tabs, close tab 1 the same way), and check whether Venus exits, crashes, or the
  supervisor drops the presentation.

## Expected

Closing a non-final tab removes only that tab; the window and the other tabs stay (EON-C contract
for tab close; `eon tab close` says "Close the active non-final tab").

## Scope

Find and fix the cause at its owner (Venus or Runtime) with a red/green regression check at the
cheapest harness that reproduces it. Out of scope: logging Venus stderr (file separately if the

title: Deliver long, pixel-smooth kinetic Eon scrollback
description:
## Chosen product contract

Deliver useful retained terminal history and responsive native-Wayland scrolling without moving terminal authority out of Orbit or adding a second scheduling/rendering architecture.

Consumer: one installed Eon/EonTerm user on supported x86_64 Linux native Wayland.
Trigger: primary-screen history owns scrolling and the user moves a precision/continuous surface or discrete wheel.
Result: Orbit retains a measured useful byte budget and applies bounded signed whole-row movement atomically; Venus presents direct fractional pixels, bounded release momentum only when the native phase supports it, three rows per discrete logical step, and compositor-paced FIFO redraw; Eon composes exact accepted child revisions and records installed dogfood.
Important failures: terminal-owned input keeps its canonical physical routing and receives no synthetic momentum; all motion is interruptible; history edges stop firmly; background output never produces stale/invented rows; profile refresh preserves live Sessions.

When measured safe choices are otherwise equivalent, prefer the more responsive/lively behavior while preserving 1:1 low-speed precision, exact distance, bounded stopping, routing, and authority.

## Owner beads and sequence

This epic is a planning container and is never claimed for implementation.

1. Finish the existing active Eon Sessions lifecycle frontier.
2. Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-history-byte-budget-ykn`: measure and set the Orbit-owned history byte budget.
3. Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-signed-scroll-batch-x12`: extend `ORB-C8` and the next canonical ORBS version with one atomic bounded signed history commit.
4. Eon Desktop `ven-venus-kinetic-touchpad-scroll-5sl`: revise `VEN-C7` for fractional presentation, native input interpretation, minimal elapsed-time physics, batching, pacing, and honest metrics.
5. Eon `eon-kinetic-scrollback-bjs.1`: pin exact accepted children, refresh the active Nix profile without restarting live Sessions, and dogfood the installed candidate.
6. After that first installed dogfood, Eon Desktop `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` records the explicit choice to keep pinned winit, backport narrowly, adopt a stable release, or—only with user approval—use an exact unreleased revision. It does not block owner implementation or the first candidate, but it precedes final epic closure.

Cross-repository relationships are recorded by exact IDs rather than duplicated Beads. The two Orbit beads share a workflow prerequisite but no false technical dependency; Eon Sessions still implements only one active frontier at a time.

## Reference decision

Inspected 2026-08-24:

- Orbit `bad068a775140a1a4c4a157a0b9b64fba46f8202` and pinned Ghostty `a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083`: current `max_scrollback: 1_000` is bytes, not rows; existing `ORB-C8` already owns authoritative adjacent preview, routing, viewport movement, and frames.
- Venus `082ecb7e9e2a8dde009db28e481a68bee2d3ace6`: current path truncates native movement to rows and may amplify one event into repeated requests/frames; existing winit, wgpu FIFO, glyphon, and event loop remain the chosen owners.
- Pinned winit 0.30.13 fork `fb45fbf901fbe70cc9a877b5d651d0b60c206b08`: Wayland exposes line versus pixel deltas and phases but discards axis source, native event time, and useful device identity. Core policy is therefore based only on observable delta/phase.
- Winit master `874a1e31f194d11313c1ac133b28037b99db3e19` has unreleased hold gestures and newer high-resolution wheel support but still lacks source/time/device guarantees. Defer selection until hardware dogfood identifies whether those capabilities matter.
- Wayland pointer semantics: https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland
- GTK's current frame-clock and elapsed-time kinetic model, Kitty's pixel/momentum behavior, winit redraw/presentation notification, WGPU FIFO latency, libinput scrolling, Ghostty history semantics, and Alacritty's useful-history/wheel defaults are routed in the owner beads.

Adopt: 16 MiB as a measured starting hypothesis; one-row authoritative preview as the architecture ceiling; one signed batch in flight; fractional rendering; phase-complete precision momentum; direct discrete wheels; actual elapsed-time decay; compositor callbacks; existing glyphon first; honest event-delivery-to-submit metrics.

Reject for the first slice: rows as the history unit, nominal fixed 60 Hz timers, fixed per-frame decay, device/source guesses, synthetic discrete-wheel inertia, velocity stacking, bounce, one frame per row, multi-row overscan, custom renderer/shader, refresh discovery, actual-presentation protocols, public tuning, new mouse bindings, worker threads, physics dependencies, or unreleased-winit adoption before dogfood.

## Epic acceptance

1. Both Orbit beads and the Venus bead close with exact accepted revisions, contract/docs alignment, focused owner proof, and full affected shared-protocol surfaces.
2. `eon-kinetic-scrollback-bjs.1` proves the exact installed component graph and profile artifact, retains live Sessions during refresh, and records real supported-Wayland hardware behavior across the agreed gesture, wheel, edge, live-output, routing, cancellation, resize, reconnect, and lifecycle cases.
3. The accepted metrics demonstrate control and identify the actual bottleneck: no lost distance, stale/invented rows, runaway tail, bounce, unbounded queue, terminal-routing regression, or misleading physical-input/visible-presentation claim.
4. Available 60 Hz and 120+ Hz surfaces are observed without promising a fixed cadence. If required hardware is unavailable, the proof records that gap rather than inferring it.
5. After first installed dogfood, `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` records the user's explicit source decision. Any selected dependency change receives its own authorization and proof; “keep pinned” is a valid complete decision.
6. The user accepts the installed scroll length, sensitivity, smoothness, acceleration, stopping distance, and interruption behavior.

## Scope and stop conditions

In scope: the four owner slices above, exact composition, installed proof, and the post-dogfood winit decision.

Out of scope: scrollbar/search UI, persistent history, compression lifecycle, multi-row overscan, terminal cells owned by Venus, renderer replacement, public tuning/configuration, new mouse-button gestures, momentum inside terminal applications, display-refresh guarantees, X11/Xwayland/macOS, additional architectures, or init/service-manager work.

Stop and return to the user if the one-row preview is insufficient; a new dependency/thread/timer/renderer/public configuration appears necessary; protocol work expands beyond one bounded commit and atomic response; real hardware cannot be handled from existing observable events; per-device policy becomes necessary; or measurement cannot identify a bounded existing-owner fix.
close_reason: All Orbit, Venus, installed-composition, hardware-dogfood, and post-dogfood winit decisions are accepted; kinetic scrollback is complete.

title: Accept installed Eon kinetic scrollback
description:
## Outcome and contract routing

Compose the exact accepted Orbit and Venus kinetic-scrollback revisions into Eon and record one installed native-Wayland acceptance. This refreshes the proofs for `EON-C1` through `EON-C4`; it adds no Eon-owned scrolling, input, rendering, or terminal state.

Consumer: one installed Eon/EonTerm user on supported x86_64 Linux native Wayland.
Trigger: the accepted child revisions are available and Eon selects them in its canonical component graph.
Result: the Nix profile resolves to the just-built exact component set, existing live Sessions are preserved until the user restarts them, and a fresh installed surface exposes Orbit-owned useful history plus Venus-owned direct pixel scrolling, bounded kinetic release, discrete-wheel behavior, and compositor-paced presentation.
Important failures: incompatible pins/builds fail before profile activation; profile refresh does not restart a live supervisor; dogfood must not claim physical-input-to-screen timing or guaranteed display cadence unavailable from the accepted APIs.

## Prerequisites and references

Accepted child work:

- Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-history-byte-budget-ykn`: measured retained-history byte budget.
- Eon Sessions `orb-orbit-signed-scroll-batch-x12`: accepted canonical ORBS v7 bounded signed history commit.
- Eon Desktop `ven-venus-kinetic-touchpad-scroll-5sl`: exact protocol consumer, fractional renderer, input policy, physics, pacing, and instrumentation.

Accepted rollout source `b44d968e38474fc5b75a41bcde2ad750da0d1e3e` pins Orbit `baf8aa28dcaa50484cd221aa7730defedc2356bb` with ORBS v7 and Venus `f13dc7ac2e9a24c5cff5bb7e618436783ec76dbf`.

The post-dogfood winit decision `ven-decide-winit-scroll-gestures-mfz` is deliberately non-blocking. Run it after this installed runtime is dogfooded; do not expand the first slice to an unreleased dependency beforehand.

## Acceptance

1. The canonical manifest, lock identities, Venus protocol import, and Nix composition name the exact accepted Orbit and Venus revisions with no compatibility probe, adapter, duplicate schema, or copied child mechanism.
2. Full affected Rust and Nix surfaces pass because the work crosses the shared ORBS protocol and installed UI. Refresh the active `eon` profile from the working tree and verify it resolves to the resulting store artifact.
3. Preserve running supervisors and Sessions during profile refresh. With explicit user authorization to stop/restart or after natural closure, launch one fresh installed Eon/EonTerm surface for outermost proof.
4. Installed dogfood covers: retained-history usefulness; slow sub-row precision; weak and strong releases; detented and rapid wheels; history edges; background PTY output; semantic-key live return; selection and mouse buttons; cursor/focus/occlusion loss; resize; pane/session changes; reconnect; terminal mouse tracking; and repeated launch/close lifecycle.
5. On available 60 Hz and 120+ Hz displays, retain the child metrics for event-delivery-to-redraw/present-submit, redraw cadence/missed callbacks, requested/applied distance, Orbit batch/frame time, renderer preparation/submission, coalescing, fling duration, and stopping distance. Report unavailable hardware honestly and make no refresh-rate guarantee.
6. The user accepts that movement is exact, responsive, controllable, and sufficiently long-lived, with no lost distance, stale/invented rows, runaway tail, bounce, queue-pressure notice, terminal-routing regression, or lifecycle regression.
7. `docs/CONTRACTS.md`, component records, changelog, README LOC scorecard, exact installed artifact, and Beads proof all agree at the same revisions.

## Scope boundary and stop conditions

In scope: exact child pinning, canonical composition, Eon and EonTerm profile refresh, exact Eonova downstream pin/profile refresh, installed proof, and user acceptance.

Out of scope: Eon-owned scroll policy or state, winit selection, renderer/protocol redesign, public tuning, new platform support, init/service-manager work, or any child fix copied into Eon.

Stop and return to the user if a child contract is not accepted, the profile cannot resolve the exact built artifact, installed behavior contradicts child proof, live Sessions would need automatic interruption, or dogfood reaches a recorded child stop condition.
close_reason: Accepted exact installed ORBS v7 and Venus kinetic scrollback through native-Wayland dogfood; composition, profile, ownership, and failure boundaries are proved.
