title: Let users and agents name Eon windows
description:
## Why

eon-n77e: Eon windows have random hex IDs and no name. The OS title is the selected terminal's title (venus application.rs:3898-3902), so a picker of windows is unreadable.

The references keep a stable ID with a separate label (Rex: ID > label > position, and an ambiguous target exits without acting; tuios: `set-session-name`). Name-as-identity breaks in Zellij (non-atomic rename) and kitty (basename collisions).

## Contract (proposed; bring the exact EON-C23 amendment to Lucca before code)

A user or agent can give an Eon window a name:

- `eon window rename [ID] NAME` names a window; without an ID it names the caller's window.
- `eon window new --name NAME` names a window as it opens.
- An empty NAME clears the name.

`eon windows` (from the previous bead) shows the name. `window attach` and `window stop` accept an ID or an exact name; a name that matches more than one window fails without acting. The ID stays the identity, and names need not be unique.

The name lives with the window's runtime state, so it ends when the window stops. Keeping names across a reboot belongs to eon-reboot-restore-im8y.

## Scope

In scope: the name store, the CLI, the listing field, name targeting, contract/USAGE text, CHANGELOG.

Out of scope: the picker, a rename action inside the picker or Commands (add one only if the contract review asks), the window title, persistence across reboot.

## Acceptance

- Renaming a detached window shows the new name in `eon windows`.
- Attaching it by name works.
- With two windows of the same name, attaching by that name fails, leaves both untouched, and names the matching IDs.

## Verification

Focused tests through `nix develop -c eon-test`, plus the affected build. One installed observation in the switching batch. Codex on every code change.

title: Replace a kept Down scroll preview whose rows output rewrites near live
description:
## Problem

Found by the fresh Claude reviewer of eon-preview-kept-in-history-after-prune-li45 (2026-10-27), by
source reading, not yet observed. A Down scroll preview taken while the viewport is in history but less
than one screen from live (`rows_from_live < dimensions.rows`) holds rows from the active screen. Orbit's
viewport_preview reads the rows below the viewport (orbit/src/frame.rs, about lines 372-380). Output
can rewrite those rows in place without changing either ScrollPosition count: a progress bar, or the
half-written cursor row when `rows_from_live == 1`. SessionModel::preview_may_be_stale
(venus/src/model.rs) is true only at live and at the oldest retained row. So a held sub-row Down
remainder near live keeps drawing the outdated active-screen row until something else replaces the
preview.

## Expected

A kept Down preview whose rows overlap the active screen is replaced through the same paced and held
path (h7y0's next_request gate: at most once per PREVIEW_ANSWER_GRACE, one outstanding preview). First
confirm it in an isolated headless Sway: scroll a few rows up from live while a program redraws its
bottom line, leave a sub-row Down remainder, and capture the bottom edge.

## Contract

VEN-C7. Any change to contract text stops for Lucca's approval.

## Prerequisites

eon-preview-kept-in-history-after-prune-li45.

## Scope

In scope: the staleness gate in venus/src/model.rs, plus any test in venus/tests/canonical_scene.rs or
venus/src/application/scroll.rs. Out of scope: Orbit.

## Acceptance

- A Venus test with a kept Down preview near live over a frame that rewrites the active screen.
- One isolated installed observation, or a recorded reason that the case cannot occur.

## Portability disposition

neutral.

title: Add Neuralink input support to Eon
description:
## Contract
A Neuralink user can operate Eon through a verified Neuralink computer-input interface: open a workspace, select a directory, enter and run terminal text, switch tabs/panes, scroll, and select/copy text. Preserve focus and normal keyboard/pointer behavior. An unavailable or disconnected input source must not inject stale actions or prevent ordinary input.

## Prerequisites and first decision
Verify the actual interface exposed by Neuralink, supported operating systems, access/licensing requirements, and available hardware or participant collaboration. Do not assume a public SDK or Linux compatibility. First check whether Neuralink’s existing computer control already supplies the pointer and text input Eon consumes; support may require only qualification and documentation. If access or a compatible platform is unavailable, record the concrete prerequisite and defer implementation without claiming support.

## Reference gate
Read current official Neuralink technology and Telepathy material, then any vendor documentation available for the chosen interface:
- https://neuralink.com/technology/
- https://neuralink.com/updates/two-years-of-telepathy/
Review docs/ARCHITECTURE.md ownership boundaries and EON-C7, EON-C8, EON-C18 and EON-C20. Compare with an application actually operated through the same Neuralink interface. Record exact versions, input capabilities and limitations before choosing an adapter or dependency. Official material was consulted on 2026-10-11; SDK availability and Eon-platform compatibility remain unverified.

## Ownership and scope
Prefer existing OS pointer, keyboard/text-entry and accessibility paths. Venus owns native input, focus and accessibility; Orbit owns terminal input/state; Eon owns product configuration, exact component selection and installed qualification. Fix a demonstrated gap at its owner and consume an accepted exact revision. This bead does not authorize implant drivers, neural decoding, raw neural-data storage, a generic BCI framework, or an additional supported platform. Any needed platform expansion requires a separate user decision.

## Acceptance
1. Identify a usable supported interface and platform, or record the exact external blocker; research alone does not complete the support goal.
2. Complete the contract’s workflows in an installed Eon with real Neuralink output and record device/software versions, exact Eon/child revisions and observed limits. A simulated input stream can validate an adapter but cannot establish Neuralink support.
3. Verify loss/disconnection and recovery without unintended input or lost workspace state; existing input remains usable.
4. Document setup, supported capabilities and known limitations. Add only the smallest proven integration needed, if any, and make no broader hardware or platform claim.

title: Open an independent Eon workspace in a new window
description:
## Contract routing
EON-C23 owns the product action; VEN-C23 consumes the exact Eon executable supplied by the supervisor for the native shortcut. Consumer: one installed full-Eon user on x86_64 Linux Wayland. Trigger: explicit New Window from CLI, desktop launcher action, or Alt+Shift+N in a live Venus window. Result: a second native Eon window starts a fresh directory picker and has its own Eon supervisor, tabs, focus, and durable Orbit Sessions. The first window and its Sessions remain unchanged. A stable window ID makes each window discoverable, attachable after detach, and separately stoppable. Bare eon continues to present the current default workspace. Important failures: a collision, invalid/private-runtime path, failed child readiness, or stale target must leave existing windows and Sessions untouched; Stop must target the chosen identity.

## Ownership and prerequisites
Eon owns window identity, private runtime namespace, launch, discovery, attach/stop policy, CLI action, and desktop entry. Venus owns only the fixed native shortcut and its visible help; Orbit keeps Session authority and one presentation client per Session. Start from accepted EON-C1/C8/C11/C15 and VEN-C8/VEN-C20; retain accepted Orbit b6cecf8f2ee35570b41cfdc578b095889d917fe2 and consume accepted Venus source a23f9eed95120ca4acea8789bf7d32d2472d84ce.

## Reference gate and decision
Inspect Eon's generation, supervisor, CLI, EONW, installed launcher, and existing lifecycle tests; inspect Venus's shortcut dispatch and one-window contract before changing it. Canario's current published spaces workflow and Ghosthub 0.7.0's independent native windows/detach policy are comparable product evidence, not code sources. Reuse Eon's generation validation and add a short private runtime root for each window. Reject a second view onto the same Orbit Session (one presentation client) and randomizing the build generation (it is component identity). The check is two simultaneously live installed Eon windows with distinct Session endpoints and independent detach/reattach/Stop.

## Scope
Nix-only x86_64 Linux Wayland full Eon. No shared tab or focus state, arbitrary multi-window renderer, new Orbit behavior, generic instance framework, another distribution channel, macOS proof, or change to existing bare-eon presentation semantics.

## Acceptance Criteria
1. New Window creates a distinct private runtime and fresh picker without replacing or stopping the first window. Concurrent requests get distinct IDs; an immediate failed launch reports its private log; uncertain startup retains its ID and process for safe inspection.
2. CLI and desktop action open a window. Alt+Shift+N is discoverable in native shortcut help and triggers the same Eon-owned action. The new window can be listed, reattached after its Venus closes, and stopped by exact ID; batch Stop includes all owned windows without retargeting another generation.
3. Closing either Venus window detaches only its Sessions. Stop of one window leaves the other's Sessions and presentation intact. Existing bare eon, attach, run, and generation behavior remain valid.
4. Focused red/green lifecycle checks, full affected EONW/Rust/Nix checks, exact child pins, and one isolated installed native Wayland observation establish the contract. Refresh the active eon profile without restarting live supervisors; update docs, shortcut help, CHANGELOG, and README LOC.
close_reason: EON-C23 batch Stop ordering and confirmations proved on installed native Wayland artifact

title: Start new tabs at home and keep them when the picker is dismissed
description: Consumer: full Eon user creating a later tab through Alt+Shift+T or eon tab create. User chose on 2026-10-12: new tabs start in home; Escape dismisses the picker into a first pane at home instead of deleting the tab; explicit tab close is how to give up. Contract: new pending tabs and Project picker start in the native current-user home directory. Dismissing/exiting a pending picker keeps that tab and starts exactly one first pane at its starting directory; initial workspace still uses the validated launch directory. Selection still commits the selected path. Explicit close of a non-final pending tab stops/removes it without spawning a pane. Preserve background focus, existing tabs/panes, Alt+Z established-tab behavior and final-tab protection. Resolve home through std::env::home_dir (nonempty HOME then Unix account lookup), validate through the existing bounded absolute-directory owner before mutation; unresolved/invalid home or picker startup failure leaves topology unchanged. No hardcoded /home path, new setting, dependency, wire version or shell injection. Runtime owns workspace state/mechanism; Eon owns chosen product contract and exact consumer selection. Prerequisites: accepted Orbit 427cf2d, Venus 1897526, Runtime e8ec71d, canonical EONW b8f18b4. Reference gate: C17/C18 and all workspace/picker/close callers; Rust current_dir and home_dir docs; Nova e76ae565 explicit workspace roots; Zellij 910339e and Kitty 5441649 explicit launch directories. Preserve spawn-boundary enforcement; reject pane-CWD inference and configuration frameworks. Acceptance: focused red/green real-executable check proves new-tab home and picker spawn cwd; owner checks cover invalid/unresolved home atomicity, pending dismissal versus explicit close, background focus and replacement-start failure. Affected Runtime/Eon Rust/Nix surfaces pass; exact runtime pin with unchanged codec/children; refreshed profiles and isolated installed native Alt+Shift+T then Escape observe same tab, one pane and shell cwd at home; explicit pending-tab close creates no shell. Preserve ambient terminals/focus. Update C17/C18, usage/changelog/LOC and exact proofs. Excludes first-workspace/window default changes, ranking changes, picker removal, tab persistence and platform expansion.
close_reason: New tabs start at native home; picker dismissal keeps the tab with its first pane; explicit close removes it without a pane. Rust/Nix checks, exact profile refresh and private installed Wayland shortcuts/browser/cwd proof pass; ambient terminals preserved.

title: Tell a running window when a newer Eon is installed
description:
## Why

After eon-cli-old-window-after-upgrade-mno4 (landed d56c373), a running window is one build: its terminals run that build's `eon`, and new windows opened from it (Alt+Shift+N, the launcher's New Eon Window) use the running build. Lucca chose to keep that (2026-10-23, answering the overseer's "New window after an upgrade: keep the running build, plus a 'newer Eon installed, restart to update' notice as a follow-up" with "agree to everything"). The cost is that after a profile upgrade, a user keeps running the old build with nothing telling them a newer one is installed. Every edge build reports version 0.1.1, so the version badge can't show it.

## Goal

When the installed Eon differs from the build a window runs, the window says so once, unobtrusively: for example a small Eon Bar marker or tooltip, "A newer Eon is installed. Restart the window to use it."

## Contract (bring the exact text to the overseer or Lucca before code)

- How a running supervisor learns that a different build is installed, without constructing store paths, querying the Nix store or invoking an evaluator (AGENTS.md Composition and Distribution). Candidates to compare at the reference gate: the new build's CLI leaving a marker in the shared runtime dir when it runs; or the supervisor resolving its own launcher path again and comparing build identities. Name the owner (Eon Runtime, or Eon's launch policy) and how it reaches Venus (an EONW field implies a version bump).
- What "differs" means: a generation or build identity, not the version string.
- Presentation in Venus: where it shows, that it never steals focus, and that it never shows when the builds match.

## Scope

In scope: the reference gate, the contract text, the mechanism, the presentation, and tests.

Out of scope: restarting windows automatically, migrating terminals between builds, and n5qv's reattach work.

## Acceptance

- After a profile upgrade, a window started earlier shows the notice, and a window started after it doesn't. That's one installed observation across a real upgrade, in isolation.

## Verification

The affected Rust and Nix surfaces (wider if EONW changes), converge plus Codex, and the isolated installed observation.

title: Choose which install comes next: Nix-free Linux or Apple Silicon
description:

title: Initialize host mise in Eon's managed Nushell and Bash
description:
## Decision
Lucca, 2026-10-19: Eon's managed shells should initialize mise automatically, as Yazelix Nova
does, in Nushell and Bash. Found while fixing eon-amo0 (mise trust errors in hooks).

## Contract change (stop for Lucca's approval before code)
EON-C9 (Managed shell environment) excludes it today: its Boundary lists "automatic
Direnv/Mise". Proposed change, smallest form:
- Consumer: a full-Eon user whose inherited PATH has `mise`.
- Trigger: an interactive managed shell (`eon-nu`, `eon-bash`) starts.
- Result: the shell evaluates host `mise activate nu` / `mise activate bash` output after Eon's
  packaged configuration and before the user's native configuration (Nova's order for Nu), so
  mise-managed tools resolve per directory in Eon terminals as in the user's own shell.
- Failures: `mise` missing or `mise activate` failing is skipped silently (Nova's rule); the shell
  still starts. A per-project mise error (e.g. an untrusted config) is mise's own message, not
  Eon's.
- Boundary kept: Eon still writes no user files, installs no mise, and adds no Direnv. Decide
  whether a `[shell]` boolean turns it off (recommended: a `mise` boolean defaulting to true, like
  the existing Starship, Zoxide, Atuin and Carapace booleans).

## Reference (Nova, ~/pjs/nova/nova at 0c3fa126)
- `runtime/yzx-nu.rs` `host_mise_init()`: runs `mise activate nu` with the runtime PATH; uses
  stdout only on success and non-empty output; otherwise skips.
- ARCHITECTURE.md Nu row: "Packaged -> optional host `mise activate nu` -> optional user Nu";
  docs/runtime-notes.md and docs/configuration.md describe it; `checks/yzx-contracts.rs` tests it
  with a fake `mise` that accepts only `activate nu`.
- Nova does this for Nu only; Bash is new here, so check Eon's managed bashrc order
  (`bash_rc`, runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/managed_environment.rs) the same way.

## Reference gate (consequential: changes EON-C9's lifecycle and trust boundary)
Record before code: which `mise` runs (the inherited PATH's, not a pinned one) and when (once per
shell start; cost of `mise activate` on startup), how its PATH edits interact with Eon's one
child-private managed PATH prefix (EON-C9 `session_path_contains_one_managed_prefix`), and
whether activation runs inside Eon's popups and `eon run`.

## Prerequisites
Lucca's approval of the EON-C9 text.

## Acceptance
A red/green check with a fake `mise` (as Nova's) for each shell: activation output evaluated in
order, missing and failing `mise` skipped; the shell-environment Nix check; `nix develop -c
eon-test`; one isolated installed observation that a mise-pinned tool version resolves in a fresh
Eon terminal in a project directory; CHANGELOG entry; review loop; profile refresh.

## Scope boundary
Nushell and Bash managed shells only. No Direnv, no mise installation or trust management, no
change to arbitrary argv commands.

comments.text:
Approval and reference gate (claude-w3, 2026-10-21). Lucca pre-approved every decision in this session, including the EON-C9 text change below.

Contract (EON-C9): new [shell] mise boolean, default true, beside the Starship/Zoxide/Atuin/Carapace booleans. When enabled and the inherited PATH has a mise executable, an interactive managed shell evaluates host 'mise activate nu|bash' output after Eon's other integrations. A shell that already activated mise is left alone. Missing or failing mise is skipped silently; mise reports its own per-project errors. Boundary now reads 'automatic Direnv, mise installation or trust management'.

Reference: Nova ~/pjs/nova/nova at 3325ef5d (bead cited 0c3fa126), runtime/yzx-nu.rs host_mise_init(): runs 'mise activate nu', uses stdout only on success and non-empty, then writes it into a generated config.nu. Kept: the success-and-non-empty rule and silent skip. Rejected: Nova's generated config file, because Eon's Nu activation is a fixed store tree (NU_VENDOR_AUTOLOAD_DIR, one path, per Nu 0.113.1 eval_const.rs) and Eon writes no startup files. Nu 'source'/'use' need a parse-time path. Nushell's string hooks are parsed when they run and keep definitions, as the overlay-activation pattern in Nu's hook docs shows.

Mechanism:
- Nu: a snippet appended to every vendor-autoload mask file, gated at runtime by EON_SHELL_MISE (no new mask bit, since nothing in it must be kept from parsing). It runs 'mise activate nu' at config time and prepends a one-shot pre_prompt string hook: 'module mise { <output> ; export def --env "eon apply" [] { mise_hook } }; use mise; mise eon apply'. The 'eon apply' call (added only when the output defines mise_hook) applies the directory's env before the first command. Without it, mise's own hook fires only from the second prompt (observed).
- Bash: last in eon.bashrc, so Eon's Starship check still sees only the user's PROMPT_COMMAND: 'eval "$(mise activate bash)"' on success and non-empty output. mise's bash output already calls _mise_hook.
- Already-active guard: per-shell state, not MISE_SHELL. An inherited MISE_SHELL (Eon started from a mise-activated shell) would otherwise skip every terminal. Nu: 'which mise | where type == custom | is-empty' (67 µs, measured), checked at config time and as the hook condition. Bash: no _mise_hook function.
- Which mise and when: the inherited PATH's mise, once per interactive shell start. 'mise activate' takes milliseconds; mise_hook then runs on each prompt and PWD change, as mise does in the user's own shell. Non-interactive 'eon-nu -c' and scripts load no config, and bash -c reads no rcfile, so 'eon run' and argv popups are unaffected. Interactive popup shells (Agent and Git run their tools, not shells) behave like terminals.
- PATH: mise's hook-env prepends its tool dirs to the PATH it saw at activation, which already holds Eon's one managed prefix. Project-pinned tools win over Eon's managed names only for tools mise manages. session_path_contains_one_managed_prefix covers the launch environment, which is unchanged.

Observed candidate (PTY-driven nu 0.113.1, real mise 2026.7.0, project with [env] EON_MISE_PROBE): env present at the first command, MISE_SHELL=nu, mise is a custom command, the env clears after cd out. An inherited MISE_SHELL=nu still activates. EON_SHELL_MISE=0 activates nothing.

title: Show an attention inbox ordered by agent state
description:
## Why
Rex has a priority inbox of sessions needing you; herdr a picker filtered by agent state. Eon has
"next agent" (Alt+G / Alt+Shift+G) and the agent sidebar, but the sidebar lists tabs in tab order
(VEN-C30 "Contents"), so nothing shows every agent needing the person in priority order, and nothing
filters by state. Source: competitor audit eon-r6yt (2026-10-29), reports in
~/pjs/refs/competitor-audit-2026-10/. Lucca, 2026-10-29: "file the beads". Filing only; no work is
approved yet beyond planning.

## Correction to the filed framing
The order already exists and has one owner: EON-C31's queue (docs/CONTRACTS.md, "NextAttention and
PreviousAttention") holds every terminal of every workspace of the window whose most urgent record
is needs input, an unseen error, or finished, ordered by class (needs input, error, finished), then
oldest change time, then workspace, tab and terminal position. The filed "blocked > needs input >
finished" was wrong: blocked is needs input, and error sits between. The inbox shows that queue; it
must not define a second order in Venus.

## Contracts
EON-C31 (Agent attention: the queue, EONW fields, CLI JSON rule Q8), VEN-C30 (Agent sidebar) or a
new VEN-C for the view, EON-C10 (CLI), EON-C28 (JSON fields freeze at 1.0).

## Children
1. eon-ngwf.1: expose the queue, in order, to Venus and the eon CLI (Runtime; blocked by
   eon-agent-parity-a9g0.2, which amends the same Q8 rule).
2. eon-ngwf.2: the inbox view with a state filter in Venus (blocked by .1).

## Acceptance (epic)
With three agents in different states, the inbox lists them in queue order and jumps to each; the
CLI returns the same order. Children closed.

## Scope
Reference route: docs/REFERENCES.md "How should Venus direct human attention across many
agent-bearing workspaces without becoming their source of truth?" (cmux).

title: Highlight and open plain-text URLs in terminal output
description:
## Decision

Lucca, 2026-10-19: plain-text URLs in terminal output should highlight on hover and open like
explicit links. This covers shell output and agent TUIs such as Claude Code, which print URLs as
plain text in Eon. Today Venus highlights only explicit OSC 8 links. VEN-C5's Boundary says "No
heuristic detection", so this reverses that clause.

Evidence (eon-wt2g, 2026-10-19, edge 5dbd53c, isolated headless Sway): OSC 8 hover, highlight,
target preview, Ctrl+click and Ctrl+Shift+C all work. Plain URLs printed by the shell and by Claude
Code never highlight. Ctrl+click on them opened links only where the program itself handled the
click, with no Venus notice.

## Contract (draft; show Lucca before code; VEN-C5 change)

- Consumer/trigger: a Venus user hovers, or Ctrl+clicks, a URL that appears as plain text in a
  visible terminal row.
- Result: the same presentation and actions as an explicit link: outline, escaped target preview,
  Ctrl+click Open, Ctrl+Shift+C Copy, and the same opening limits (ASCII HTTP/HTTPS, a host, no
  credentials, 4096 bytes). An explicit OSC 8 link on a cell always wins over detection.
- Failures: unchanged from VEN-C5. Frame, geometry, scroll and focus changes retire actions. Nothing
  opens on hover.
- Contract edits: VEN-C5 Boundary and Result, venus/docs/INTERACTION.md ("ordinary URL-looking
  text is not detected"), USAGE/README if they mention it, venus/CHANGELOG.md and CHANGELOG.md.

## Open decisions (recommendations)

1. Owner: Venus Scene derives detected spans from the projected visible cell text, the same place
   it derives OSC 8 spans today. This needs no Orbit or protocol change and is not a second
   emulator (AP-TERMINAL-001: it reads projected text). Alternative: Orbit detects and publishes
   spans, which changes the protocol. Recommend Venus.
2. Scope: http:// and https:// only, matching what the opener accepts. Trim trailing punctuation
   and unbalanced closing brackets. Join soft-wrapped continuation rows so a wrapped URL is one
   target. Recommend this.
3. When to highlight: on plain hover, the same as OSC 8 today. Ghostty-style highlighting only
   while Ctrl is held is the alternative. Recommend plain hover, for consistency with VEN-C5.
4. Accessibility: whether detected links join the AccessKit Open/Copy nodes (possibly many per
   screen). Recommend yes, keeping VEN-C5's per-target pair, after checking the node count cost.
5. Complement, not a replacement: setting FORCE_HYPERLINK=1 for Orbit children would make
   supports-hyperlinks-based programs emit real OSC 8. It covers only those programs and is a
   separate Orbit or Eon decision; record it, do not bundle it.

## Reference gate (consequential: contract change)

Before code, inspect at exact revisions and record in this bead: Ghostty's link detection (default
URL regex, hover and modifier highlight rules, wrapped-row handling) and one other terminal (for
example WezTerm hyperlink_rules or foot url-mode). Note what is adopted and rejected.

## Acceptance

- Scene tests: detection on a plain row, a soft-wrapped URL, trailing punctuation and brackets, an
  OSC 8 cell overriding detection, non-HTTP text ignored, wide cells.
- One isolated installed dogfood observation: hovering a plain URL in shell output highlights it,
  shows its target, and Ctrl+click opens it through the Venus opener (the notice appears).
- Profile refresh.

## Scope boundary

Detection and presentation in Venus only. No file paths, custom schemes, Orbit or EONW change,
URL rewriting, or FORCE_HYPERLINK change.

Portability: neutral (Venus Scene).

title: Improve Nova Helix default settings
description:
## Goal and contract
Improve the default Nova Helix editing experience shipped with Eon. With no personal Helix configuration, a fresh editor should have a small, coherent set of useful defaults for readability, navigation and editing feedback. Explicit user settings remain authoritative; preserve existing configuration files, normal Helix keybindings, workspace-trust boundaries and save safety.

"Make them better" authorizes reviewing and improving defaults, not a predetermined settings list. Identify concrete friction, record each selected before/after behavior and rationale, and keep the change small. Do not label subjective preferences as confirmed bugs.

## Current evidence
- Eon `components/eon-alpha-v3.json` pins `Yazelix/nova-helix` at `817dcbca8b99c3db35ea66ded7492673d1a397ad`.
- Eon `flake.nix:346` consumes `yazelix_helix`; `EON_HX` points directly to that package. It does not consume Nova's managed Helix configuration.
- Nova Helix `helix-term/src/config.rs` owns configuration loading, default keymaps and user/workspace layering. `helix-view/src/editor.rs:1190` owns editor defaults; the inspected baseline disables cursorline, color modes and soft wrap. These are review candidates, not agreed replacements.
- Nova `defaults/helix/config.toml` is a useful comparison for theme, buffer visibility, cursor shapes, diagnostics, indent guides, wrapping and statusline. It also contains Nova-specific reveal commands, paths and remappings that must not be copied into Eon or standalone Helix.
- Nova Helix has no local Beads tracker; this issue lives in Eon's backlog. Existing Eon native-editor/keybinding research is deferred and is not a prerequisite.

## Scope and ownership
Review the actual zero-config packaged experience and a few representative editing tasks. Prefer existing configuration/package facilities over Rust changes. Keep generic editor behavior at Nova Helix and Eon-specific selection/composition at Eon; record the chosen owner before editing. Do not change Nova's managed-session policy, add plugins or language-server bundles, redesign keymaps, or begin the deferred native editor.

## Reference gate and prerequisites
Read current owner instructions, configuration documentation, loading code and relevant references; compare upstream Helix and Nova's managed defaults. Record exact inspected revisions, selected defaults, rejected candidates and override precedence. No unmet dependency identified. If a child revision changes, publish and verify that child before composing its exact accepted revision into Eon.

## Acceptance and verification
- Record a short justified defaults set and demonstrate its effect in a fresh packaged editor with an isolated empty config home.
- Exercise a representative file, multiple buffers and diagnostics where applicable; verify usability in a narrow pane and the Eon terminal. Check effects rather than merely asserting configured literals.
- An explicit user override still wins, existing user files are unchanged, and ordinary edit/save/reopen behavior remains safe.
- Build the affected package; for Eon composition use `nix build .#eon --no-link`. If native Helix code changes, run `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo check -p helix-term`, and focused owner tests.
- Align affected documentation/changelog and verify the installed artifact after refreshing Eon's active Nix profile. Use an isolated fresh workspace and preserve running terminals and desktop focus.

## Stop boundary
Stop at a useful settings pass. Additional editor capabilities, dependencies, compatibility promises or a broad fork refactor require separate scope.

title: Enable native Nushell clipboard commands in Eon
description:
## Contract and outcome

Extend EON-C9 for Eon-managed Nushell. A user in a new default Eon Session or running eon-nu can pipe a value to clip copy or clc, and read the native clipboard with clip paste or clp. The aliases expand to the native Nushell commands. When clipboard access is unavailable, Nushell reports its own failure; Eon does not claim a remote or headless clipboard bridge.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

Preserve the accepted EON-C9 native configuration and user-autoload order, the exact Nushell 0.113.1 manifest identity, and the current Orbit and Venus pins. The pinned Nushell source at 7b7df4aa has native clip behind the opt-in native-clip experimental flag: without the flag the installed eon-nu cannot find clip, and with it both help commands resolve. Nova at 6fceb4e uses that flag in runtime/yzx-nu.rs, defines clc and clp in defaults/nu/config.nu, and checks their expansions in flake.nix. Before editing, inspect those exact sources, Eon managed_environment.rs and nuVendorAutoload in flake.nix, and Nushell clipboard and alias precedence semantics.

## Ownership and scope

Eon owns the managed Nushell opt-in and default aliases; Nushell owns native clipboard behavior and errors. Reuse the existing managed launcher and startup layer. Keep user files and global environment unchanged, preserve user startup precedence, and leave Bash, Zsh, Fish, arbitrary shell commands, Orbit, and Venus alone. Add no clipboard dependency, EONW or OSC52 bridge, compatibility layer with Nova, or claim of macOS, remote, or headless clipboard support from Linux proof.

## Acceptance

From the built and installed eon-nu, both native help commands resolve and clc/clp expand to clip copy/clip paste. In one isolated native Wayland Eon Session, copy then paste a known value through the full commands and aliases. Verify user startup precedence and that a missing clipboard surfaces a native failure. Update EON-C9 current-state docs, configuration help, changelog, and README LOC. Run the affected package and shell checks, refresh the active eon profile from the accepted tree without restarting live Sessions, and record the exact artifact and installed observation.

title: Decide whether Eon earns a durable native semantic editor
description:
## Contract Routing

This is the product decision gate for a possible Eon-native durable semantic editor engine. It changes no product contract and authorizes no implementation, dependency, repository, protocol, or Helix removal. EON-C4 currently preserves Helix as the sole owner of editing, language integration, and editor state. A positive decision requires explicit user approval, an updated ownership architecture, and new or revised indexed EON and owner-repository contracts before code.

User constraint recorded 2026-08-12: if Eon adopts its own editor engine, it must provide Helix-like modal editing and preserve most Helix default keybindings regardless of whether it reuses `helix-core`. `eon-specify-helix-modal-semantics-3kl` and `eon-preserve-helix-keybindings-uca` make that requirement falsifiable.

## Why

A native editor is justified only if it unlocks a user-visible contract that opaque terminal-hosted Helix cannot supply: authoritative addressable documents and revisions, durable unsaved editor state, transient Venus attachment, semantic native presentation, and explicit human/agent edit-conflict boundaries. Native appearance, fewer visible processes, code ownership preference, or the existence of reusable Helix crates are insufficient.

The important question is not “Can Eon render text?” It is whether Eon can earn the permanent editor-feature, language-support, compatibility, security, durability, and maintenance burden while remaining more valuable than Helix running inside an Orbit Session.

## Current Evidence

Repository evidence:

- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:16` assigns editing, language integration, and editor state to Helix; `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:69` forbids Eon from implementing editor behavior under the accepted architecture.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:18` proves EON-C4's no-duplicate-child-state boundary. `README.md:249` exposes managed Helix as `eon-hx`.
- Orbit already proves a real PTY plus authoritative terminal state and complete structured attachment revisions; this does not expose Helix documents, selections, undo, diagnostics, or semantic commands.
- Venus already consumes host-authored snapshots while remaining transient. A future editor projection must preserve that ownership lesson without reusing the terminal grid as an editor schema.

Exact Helix evidence:

- Official Helix `079a789e8cb08ead67f19e1971a1b7438b37354b` (2026-07-23), MPL-2.0.
- `docs/architecture.md` describes `helix-core` as functional Rope, Selection, Transaction, and Syntax primitives, but says `helix-view` is currently tied to the terminal UI.
- `helix-term/src/keymap/default.rs` owns the default Normal, Select, and Insert tries. `helix-term/src/commands.rs` is 7,228 lines and owns substantial mappable-command behavior. Reusing `helix-core` alone therefore does not preserve Helix modal behavior or keybindings.
- `helix-core` is a credible candidate mechanism; `helix-view` and `helix-term` are not an accepted native-frontend seam at this revision.
- Recheck upstream issue #5555, issue #312, and PR #13468 at decision time for an accepted command/view/client split; their observed open work is discovery, not a supported contract.

External architecture evidence:

- CodeMirror 6 System Guide, https://codemirror.net/docs/guide/: accept immutable state and transaction lessons; reject its browser and extension architecture as an Eon requirement.
- Neovim UI protocol, https://neovim.io/doc/user/api-ui-events/: external clients are viable, but its terminal-like grid and multigrid model are a semantic ceiling Eon should not copy for a native editor.
- Kakoune client/server design, https://kakoune.org/why-kakoune/why-kakoune.html: session-owned editing with attachable clients is useful precedent; reject multiplayer and shell-extension scope by default.
- Xi retrospective, https://raphlinus.github.io/xi/2020/06/27/xi-retrospective.html: process-separated frontend/core RPC, pervasive async, CRDTs, and plugin processes consumed excessive novelty and coordination cost. Eon needs a process boundary only when dirty-buffer survival or attachment demonstrably requires it.
- Zed CRDT architecture and DeltaDB, https://zed.dev/blog/crdts and https://zed.dev/blog/introducing-deltadb/: fine-grained concurrent edit and conversation lineage are not unique Eon differentiators. Reject CRDTs and concurrent writers until a real multiplayer requirement exists.
- Agent Client Protocol at pinned Eon reference `9ef3e3800b4070632b54846b5ddf310fc4b35b03`: structured agent communication is preferable to ANSI scraping, but provider sessions remain adapter-owned and distinct from editor documents and Eon work.

## Smallest Observable Decision

Consumer: one local Eon user, with Venus as a transient native client.

Trigger: the user opens or reattaches to one editor surface after the native client was absent.

Candidate result if replacement is earned: one authoritative editor owner supplies a coherent complete semantic document/view snapshot at revision N followed by ordered revisions; accepts semantic modal commands against explicit base revisions; preserves approved Helix-like behavior and keybindings; retains bounded dirty document, selection, and undo state across Venus loss; saves safely; and reports stale edits, external file conflicts, engine loss, incompatible clients, and corrupt recovery state explicitly.

Non-result: this does not promise exact process survival, remote access, cloud sync, multiplayer, CRDT convergence, a plugin system, Helix configuration compatibility, machine-restart recovery, a standalone application, or a supported third-party client. Eon-wide reboot and machine-loss policy remains `eon-decide-eon-session-durability-qhf`.

## Candidate Shapes

1. Keep Helix as an opaque Orbit-hosted child. This remains the default and wins unless dogfood demonstrates a replacement-only contract.
2. Consume a supported upstream Helix semantic or native-client boundary if one exists at decision time. Do not build against an open PR or private fork contract.
3. Reuse selected Helix crates, especially `helix-core`, behind an Eon editor owner while implementing modal command, lifecycle, language, attachment, and Venus projection layers. Apply the dependency and MPL-2.0 license gates to exact files and artifacts.
4. Implement the minimum accepted editor primitives independently, using Helix behavior as a reference corpus. Estimate parity and maintenance honestly.

A full Helix fork, terminal-screen scraping, Neovim-style grid protocol, `helix-view` extraction by assumption, CRDT-first engine, plugin system, cloud service, or distributed process mesh is rejected unless evidence overturns the smaller candidates.

## Ownership Constraints

- The editor engine owns canonical document text, revisions, selections, modal state, transactions, undo, syntax, language integration, safe save, external-change conflicts, and bounded editor recovery state.
- Venus owns native text shaping, drawing, IME, accessibility, pointer input, focus, and ephemeral geometry. It consumes semantic editor projections and never reconstructs document authority from cells or pixels.
- Eon owns workspace topology, product policy, component selection, and references to editor surfaces; it does not implement editing mechanics.
- Orbit retains PTY, process, terminal, history, and terminal-input authority and owns no editor state.
- Provider adapters own provider sessions. Future agents may submit base-revision proposals, but direct agent mutation, isolated worktrees, context manifests, and run provenance remain separately routed through `eon-pxn` and `eon-az9` rather than being prerequisites for the first editor proof.
- Logical ownership does not imply one process per component. Prefer the fewest process and protocol boundaries; require lifecycle evidence before separating the editor engine from the long-lived local workspace host.
- Nice-to-have portability: keep the editor core free of Eon, Orbit, and Venus product types when that does not enlarge the first proof. Eon integration should enter through a narrow adapter, and Venus should be an initial client rather than an engine dependency. This prefers future embedding or a standalone client without promising or building either.

## Prerequisites

- The accepted Helix-based Eon composition remains dogfoodable and supplies concrete limitations caused by the terminal/editor boundary.
- `eon-specify-helix-modal-semantics-3kl` selects the required semantic behavior.
- `eon-preserve-helix-keybindings-uca` selects the binding coverage and workspace-shortcut collision policy.
- The user explicitly activates this decision; deferred status does not make it the active implementation frontier.

## Decision Work

1. Record exact terminal-bound limitations from dogfood and distinguish replacement-only needs from configuration, structured run records, agent worktrees, native review surfaces, or an upstream integration.
2. Reinspect exact current Helix source, relevant upstream client/server work, license, and release/API stability.
3. Compare the four candidate shapes on contract fit, owned and reused LOC, direct/transitive dependencies, language/tooling parity, keybinding and modal fidelity, security, durability, Linux/native-Wayland behavior, upgrade burden, upstream drift, and removal cost.
4. Produce before-and-after owner and data-flow maps. Select one canonical document owner and the minimum semantic projection; do not create a universal UI or action protocol.
5. Define the smallest falsifiable proof: one document, one client, open/edit/save, approved modal corpus, semantic detach/reattach, bounded dirty-state recovery, stale revision rejection, external-change conflict, and Venus-native input/presentation.
6. Decide whether process separation is necessary. If not, keep the editor owner in the smallest long-lived host; if yes, define start, attach, crash, restart, incompatibility, shutdown, cleanup, queue, and persistence semantics.
7. Obtain an explicit user decision: keep Helix, defer, integrate upstream, reuse selected Helix crates, or authorize an independent engine. Do not implement in this Bead.

## Acceptance

- Exact dogfood evidence identifies at least one valuable contract that requires editor authority, or the decision keeps Helix.
- The keep, upstream integration, selected-crate reuse, and independent-engine shapes are compared at exact revisions with license, dependency, LOC, parity, portability, security, lifecycle, and reversal costs.
- Modal semantics and keybinding continuity decisions are complete and included in every positive cost estimate; reuse of `helix-core` is never treated as automatic behavioral compatibility.
- One owner map covers document text, revisions, selections, modal state, undo, syntax, language services, saves, external changes, workspace references, native projection, terminal state, and provider sessions without duplicate authority.

Both slices satisfy the retained aggregate development acceptance below; the closure review and remaining gates are recorded in notes. eon-qualify-nix-free-linux-public-beta-lm9p owns subsequent wider public-beta qualification. Retain the existing comparison of dist, a small owned assembler and credible maintained tooling, including the recorded Doodlestein/local-release evidence and spending constraints. Select no bundler from its availability alone.

Eon owns assembly and install/upgrade/remove policy. Children retain runtime mechanisms and artifact ownership. Every path consumes the canonical component manifest; no hidden component substitution, copied child behavior or second graph.

## Success Criteria

Both slices are accepted for the same exact graph: the useful manual Nix-free Linux bundle first, then the thin installer with verified delivery and active-work-safe upgrade/rollback/removal. Wider public-beta qualification remains separate.

## Acceptance

- Produce one immutable x86_64 Linux archive, checksum and signature or attestation binding the artifact, with exact graph/provenance and retained size/closure observations. Release assets are authoritative; website installation copy points to them.
- Manual extraction runs useful Eon on a clean native-Wayland machine/user environment without a host Nix installation/store, Nix daemon/evaluator, development checkout or undeclared machine-local references. - Partial download, verification, extraction or activation failure leaves the prior installation usable. Removal affects only owned installation/integration points and preserves configuration/data; preserve any version payload still needed by live retained work or stage its removal. Switching current never silently stops live supervisors/terminals; retained work remains usable with its prior executable under accepted generation contracts.
- Direct and Nix artifacts report the same accepted exact graph and runtime semantics. Verify fresh install plus active-work upgrade/rollback/removal at the outermost delivery boundary, with the cheapest checks for introduced deterministic logic. Record exact artifact/environment/result and limitations; align current install/usage/contract docs and LOC at implementation acceptance.
- Prepare yazelix.com installation copy without making it binary authority. Public publication/promotion requires the ordinary explicit user decision on the reviewable candidate.

## Scope boundary

One Linux bundle and small installer only. No extra architecture, macOS, X11/Xwayland, Home Manager, AppImage, Flatpak, deb/rpm, containers, system repositories, service-manager requirement, auto-updater, live handoff or restart-persistence promise. Deferred channels remain separate. This completed epic records the two accepted development slices. Public-beta qualification, release trust, redistribution clearance and publication retain separate gates.

title: Define the canonical Eon component manifest
description:
Contracts:
EON-C2 and EON-C3.

Goal:
Define one small, human-reviewable manifest that pins exact child revisions, compatibility contracts, and declared package or artifact inputs. Nix consumes this graph during alpha. Later distribution tooling must extend the same graph instead of replacing it.

Reference and tool gate:
Inspect current child release and package metadata plus at least one comparable multi-component manifest. Compare a small hand-owned schema with using existing Nix metadata directly. Record versioning, validation, local LOC, maintenance, and the point at which external release tooling becomes useful. Defer cargo-dist, portable-bundle, and installer evaluation to the direct-distribution gate.

Acceptance:
- The alpha schema names project, revision, contract version, target, package or artifact input, and launch inputs.
- A focused validator rejects incompatible or incomplete component sets.
- One fixture pins the exact owner revisions and contracts required by the alpha: ORB-C1 through ORB-C9, VEN-C1 through VEN-C4, and VEN-C7, their canonical ORBS v2 and ORBF v1 package boundary, plus Helix, Yazi, and Ratconfig. Additional proved contracts may be recorded without becoming activation prerequisites. If preactivation hardening advances an owner proof, pin the final accepted proof rather than preserving an obsolete candidate.
- Eon receives resolved component paths without constructing store paths or invoking a Nix evaluator during normal use.
- Product state records stable component identities instead of resolved store paths.
- docs/CONTRACTS.md records exact proof evidence.

Scope:
Do not require portable artifacts during Nix-only alpha. Do not create a second dependency graph for a package manager or rebuild child behavior in Eon.

First-principles decision:
- The validator is durable policy: it defines which component graphs Eon accepts. Language consistency therefore affects ownership, review, build reproducibility, onboarding, and removal cost, not just initial LOC.
- Rust gives compile-time schema ownership, one project toolchain, one test/format/lint path, and a reusable library boundary for the later Nix composition without making Nix or shell reinterpret the graph.
- Python would save initial code but introduce a second durable toolchain and split conventions for one small repository. That lifecycle cost exceeds its local brevity here.
- Go would add a second compiled ecosystem with no concurrency, deployment, or service advantage. TypeScript would add Node/package-manager state without a web runtime. - serde 1.0.228 with derive, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: owns typed deserialization and unknown-field rejection.
- serde_json 1.0.150, exact crates.io pin, MIT OR Apache-2.0: owns standards-compliant JSON parsing and serialization for mutation tests.
- Normal dependency closure from the already accepted Ratconfig lock and local crate sources is two direct crates plus ten unique transitive crates: serde_core, serde_derive, proc-macro2, quote, syn, unicode-ident, itoa, memchr, and zmij (the direct/unique count includes the shared serde_core only once). All are pure Rust; no native, runtime, Nix service, network, accessibility, input-method, Linux-specific, or macOS-specific behavior is added. The Cargo lock will pin the complete closure. title: Prove Home Manager and direct-release parity with Nix Eon
description:
Contract:
EON-C6.

Goal:
Keep the proven Nix package as a supported channel after direct distribution and let Home Manager consume that same package and product contract.

Prerequisites:
- eon-ohh proves the first direct Linux bundle against the same canonical component manifest and accepted runtime semantics.

Inspect the exact supported Home Manager revision and its official package, module, option, activation, state-version, upgrade, and removal contracts. Compare no Eon-specific integration with `home.packages` consumption and the smallest thin Eon module justified by demonstrated configuration needs. Record Linux target support, evaluation and activation failures, ownership of user files, dependency weight, local LOC, compatibility policy, and removal cost. Reject any shape that creates a Home-Manager-only component graph, settings owner, runtime behavior, or release identity.

## Acceptance Criteria
- The original Nix package, Home Manager integration, and direct release consume the same exact component revisions and compatibility metadata.
- Version diagnostics match across channels.
- Runtime behavior and configuration ownership remain channel-independent.
- A clean Nix profile and Home Manager evaluation pass without requiring the direct installer.
- Direct-install users need no Nix evaluator or store.

Scope:
Do not maintain a Home-Manager-only component graph, runtime contract, or feature. This bead does not expand the Nix-only alpha surface.

title: Make Open Eon independent of launcher PATH
description: Harden EON-C1. Consumer: a Linux user invoking the installed Open Eon desktop action. Trigger: the desktop launcher executes the packaged entry with a PATH that does not contain the Nix profile bin directory. Result: the entry invokes the exact installed Eon executable and starts or presents the current generation; live Sessions remain untouched. Failure: package construction must fail if the generated entry cannot be rewritten exactly. Scope: Eon flake desktop packaging, current contract/changelog/LOC, exact artifact build and profile refresh only; no runtime, protocol, child repository, launcher-specific integration, or supervisor restart.
close_reason: Published candidate accepted: Open Eon invokes its exact packaged executable, the profile resolves the immutable artifact, restricted-PATH launcher dogfood passed, and live Sessions were preserved.

comments.text:
Reference gate — 2026-08-23

Question: which owner should make Open Eon launch reliably when a desktop session PATH omits the user Nix profile?

Inspected the installed desktop artifact, flake.nix makeDesktopItem/copyDesktopItems package path, EON-C1 launcher contract, README install/current-generation behavior, docs/DISTRIBUTION.md Nix-alpha ownership, the exact current profile target, generation state, and live process identities.

Evidence: Eon owns desktop-entry metadata and Nix owns installation. The runtime is healthy when invoked by exact path; Orbit and Venus are not involved until Eon starts. The generated entry alone uses a PATH-dependent command. The package output already owns both the entry and wrapped executable.

Decision: after copyDesktopItems installs the entry, use Nix substituteInPlace --replace-fail to replace only Exec=eon with Exec=$out/bin/eon. Cheapest proof is the exact built artifact plus launch through the refreshed installed entry.

title: Deliver trustworthy OpenCode Go quota in the Eon Bar
description:
## Contract

A full-Eon user with OpenCode Go can see authoritative subscription quota in the existing native Eon Bar when the selected read-only source supplies it. Show remaining allowance, actual periods and reset details with explicit freshness and account/model scope. Missing or unsupported data stays absent or visibly unavailable; failures never block terminals or appear as fresh quota.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

Reviewed 2026-10-13: https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/console/go/ (redirected from https://opencode.ai/docs/en/go/). Official docs describe five-hour, weekly and monthly limits with model-dependent allowances, console usage visibility and optional spending from a separate balance after subscription limits. They do not establish a supported machine-readable quota query.

First falsifier: inspect the exact OpenCode release/source and provider usage implementation, then obtain a real authoritative read-only quota observation without an inference turn. Record source revision/license, endpoint or CLI stability, auth ownership, supported account class, reset semantics and whether models share accounting pools. Reinspect current docs and one comparable implementation before selecting a mechanism. Prefer an existing provider-owned read boundary; explicitly select any direct credential/API access before code. A model catalog, inference endpoint, local token tally or session cost is not subscription quota.

Resolve model/bucket selection and presentation of all applicable five-hour, weekly and monthly limits before protocol/UI changes. Do not force three windows into the existing two-window Claude/Codex projection or invent a combined percentage. Keep Go allowance separate from Zen/pay-as-you-go balance and direct subscriptions to underlying model providers. Do not hardcode plan prices, model catalogs or allowance tables as quota truth.

## Ownership and sequencing

Eon owns product policy and exact composition; Eon Runtime owns collection, normalization, freshness and bounded lifecycle; canonical EONW owns versioned typed facts; Venus owns native presentation, hover and accessibility. OpenCode owns auth/billing semantics. Orbit remains terminal authority.

Accepted EON-C21/C22/C26 provide the baseline. Index the selected product contract before implementation. Keep one active integration frontier: prove Runtime/EONW, then Venus, then Eon against exact accepted child revisions. Grok delivery is not a technical prerequisite.

## Scope and stop boundary

One read-only OpenCode Go quota feature for a verified account/source class on the accepted x86_64 Linux Wayland alpha. Claim Go Plus compatibility only with separate evidence. No paid inference, provider-configuration mutation, billing actions, login UI, credential-refresh owner, browser-cookie import, transcript scanning, provider bundling, generic widget framework, new bar row, website work or platform/distribution expansion. Keep secrets and raw account/billing payloads out of EONW and logs.

If no acceptable authoritative source exists, record the exact blocker and leave delivery incomplete; an unavailable-only chip does not satisfy the goal.

## Proof

Use source/parser red-green checks for meaningful failures, followed by full affected Rust/Nix proof for protocol/dependency changes. Delivery needs exact revision/artifact identities, affected profile refresh and isolated installed native real-source dogfood with failure and narrow-width cases. Preserve live terminals, provider configuration and desktop focus. Align contracts/docs/changelog/LOC with the implemented outcome.
acceptance_criteria:
1. An exact recorded OpenCode version/account class supplies real authoritative quota through an explicitly selected read-only source without inference or provider mutation. Actual account/model pooling, periods and reset semantics are verified.
2. The selected presentation exposes every applicable five-hour, weekly and monthly limit honestly, with accessible period/reset details; other balances/subscriptions and local costs/tokens are never treated as Go quota.
3. Missing/incompatible source, auth changes, malformed/oversized input, timeouts/provider loss and stale/reset-expired data have bounded handling and cleanup without blocking Eon or republishing obsolete facts.
4. Canonical versioned EONW carries bounded normalized facts. Native Venus presentation preserves the existing single-row layout, hover/accessibility and priority of tabs/required controls alongside accepted quota chips.
5. Exact accepted owner revisions, meaningful source/failure checks, affected Rust/Nix proof, profile refresh and isolated installed real-source observation pass. Docs state only the proved account/platform scope; existing user state is preserved.
notes: User authorized this single planning bead on 2026-10-13. Open and unclaimed. No implementation, authenticated provider query or configuration write was performed. The authoritative-source gate remains unresolved.

title: Send each hyperlink URI once per frame so a long link stays whole
description:
## Why

eon-frame-budget-links-m62b (2026-10-23) keeps a terminal alive when hyperlinks push a frame past the 4 MiB budget: cells keep their text, and links are kept in reading order while they fit. ORBF sends the URI in every linked cell, so a single ~2 KB link covering about 2000 cells (an unclosed OSC 8, or a tool that prints a long URL as its own link text) uses up the budget. After m62b, the first ~2000 cells keep the link and the rest show as plain text. A user clicking near the end of such a link gets nothing. The trigger is rare (a URI over ~1.7 KB covering about 2000 cells), but the result is a link that only half works.

## Scope

In scope:
- Send each distinct URI once per frame, with cells referencing it by index, so a long link stays whole within the budget.
- This is an ORBF wire change (v3) that Venus, bend-orbit and any other ORBF consumer must follow. Bring the compatibility choice (version negotiation, or lockstep with an Orbit and Venus bump inside one Eon build) and the ORBF and ORB-C6 wording to the overseer or Lucca before code.
- Keep m62b's reading-order rule as the fallback when distinct URIs alone exceed the budget.

Out of scope: link opening in Venus, and the text-only overflow (eon-frame-budget-text-kzze).

## Acceptance

- One ~2 KB link covering a full 100x24 screen reaches the client linked on every cell, within the budget.

## Verification

The full affected Rust and Nix surfaces for a wire change (Orbit, orbit-protocol, Venus), converge plus Codex, and an installed observation of a long link clicked near its end.

Portability disposition: neutral.

title: Start an Orbit child at its session's real size so a popup's first program reads it
description:
## Why

Orbit spawns every child at 80x24 with zero PTY pixels (orbit/src/host.rs:448 `Orbit::spawn(..., 80, 24)`, orbit/src/platform.rs open_pty) before any client sends a size; Eon Runtime's `orbit_command` (runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/sessions.rs:1249-1290) passes no size. orb-j2i.1 observed the first program in a popup read 24x80 with 0x0 pixels. A program that reads its size once at startup, such as an image preview at launch, lays out for the wrong size until the client's first Resize brings SIGWINCH. After orb-j2i.4 the pixel fields and CSI 14t/16t answers are zero until then (honest, but useless for that first program).

## Scope

In scope:
- Give Orbit the session's real size (cols, rows, cell pixels) before it spawns the child: either a `serve` size option that Eon Runtime fills from the pane or popup geometry it already knows, or Orbit spawning the child at the first client Resize. Pick one in the bead with its reference gate (it changes Orbit's command line or the session lifecycle, so it is consequential).
- A real-PTY check that the child's first TIOCGWINSZ and 16t answer carry the given size.

Out of scope: ORBF/ORBS changes; Venus.

## Open question

Does Eon Runtime know a popup's or pane's cell size before Venus reports it? If not, the second shape (spawn at first Resize) may be the only honest one; it changes ORB-C1's lifecycle (a session with no client yet has no child) and needs Lucca's choice.

## Acceptance

The first program in a new popup reads its real cols, rows and text-area pixels from TIOCGWINSZ at startup.

## Prerequisites

orb-j2i.4 (text-area pixel fields and size answers).

title: Find and fix the orbit-clipboard check's early peer close flake
description:
## Why

The `orbit-clipboard` Nix check failed once and passed on an immediate rerun of the same
derivation. A check that fails at random makes landing proofs need reruns and can hide a real
ORB-C11 regression.

Source: eon-overseer's morning report 2026-10-27, question 5 (the run is recorded in the
qkq8.1 landing commit message and the overnight log, not as a bead comment). Approved by Lucca
2026-10-27 (morning report question 5): "5. ok", accepting the recommendation "file a small flake
bead". Relayed by eon-overseer.

## Evidence

- Run: the landing proof of eon-configurability-qkq8.1 on its landed tree, commit 15134ee
  (2026-10-27, about 05:20 UTC), one `nix build --keep-going` of `.#default` plus 49 checks;

  Derivation /nix/store/w55dfbfw45d7wn0wf1bgnpwv64mmwmq8-orbit-clipboard.drv; the full build log
  may still be readable with `nix log` on it.
- Failure: `test clipboard ... FAILED`, `thread 'clipboard' (8) panicked at
  orbit/tests/real_pty/support.rs:480:26: peer closed before a complete ORBS message`, after
  0.86 s.
- orbit/tests/real_pty/support.rs:480: `Peer::receive_within` panics when `fill()` returns 0
  (EOF) before a whole ORBS message.
- orbit/tests/real_pty/clipboard.rs:22: the test's `run()` (an observer peer plus an attached
  client, released through `Gate`); its script is selected by `CLIPBOARD_SHELL`.

- Also recorded at /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/eon-overseer/overnight-log-2026-10-26.md
  (Notes, first bullet) and the 15134ee commit message. The same check passed on the first run
  in orb-j2i.6's and eon-9rtt.4's proofs.

## Contract

ORB-C11 (Ordered terminal-authored clipboard writes) is what the check proves. A test-only fix
needs no contract change. If the cause turns out to be a product defect whose fix changes
ORB-C11 or other ORB-C/EON-C text, stop and bring the wording to Lucca for approval first, as
AGENTS.md requires.

## Prerequisites

None.

## Scope

In scope:
- Find which peer (observer or client) saw EOF and why: the server ending early, the script
  exiting before the expected writes, or a race in the test's gate sequence.
- A test-side fix in orbit/tests/real_pty/clipboard.rs or support.rs, or, if Orbit itself

- `cargo fmt -p yazelix-orbit --check` and `cargo clippy -p yazelix-orbit --locked --all-targets

title: Fix the Orbit Ready-claim lock race behind a flaky test
description:
## Decision
Lucca, 2026-10-15: fix the flaky Orbit Ready-claim test at its owner and establish whether the
Orbit server shares the race.

## Contract
- Consumer: anyone running `nix develop -c eon-test`, and Orbit's management publication path.
- Result: `platform::tests::management_ready_claim_has_one_winner_and_survives_record_removal`
passes deterministically under the full parallel workspace run. If the server can fork while
`RecordGuard::publish` holds its claim, management publication cannot fail spuriously because of it.

## Evidence (edge d8eafff)
- One full `eon-test` run failed this `yazelix-orbit` test with `Error: "WouldBlock"`; 30/30
isolated runs, 5/5 Orbit binary suite runs and five other full runs passed
(`eon-sandboxed-test-command-w3jy`).
- `RecordGuard::publish` (`orbit/src/platform.rs`) opens the record through `ready_claim` with
O_CLOEXEC, `try_lock`s it (flock), writes, and replaces the record atomically; the test then expects
its own `claim.try_lock()` and a second publish to succeed.
- Likely mechanism (inference, unproved): a concurrent test thread forks a child (PTY spawn) while
the claim descriptor is open. The child shares the open file description, and so the flock, until
it execs, so a later `try_lock` sees WouldBlock.
- Production publication: `orbit/src/management.rs:126`; PTY spawns at `orbit/src/runtime.rs:258`
and `:1317`. Whether these can overlap in one process is unverified.

## Approach
1. Reproduce deterministically (for example a test helper that forks while the claim is held) and
confirm or reject the mechanism.
2. Fix at the owner. Candidates: make the test robust to transient foreign holders without
weakening its one-winner assertion, or, if the server shares the race, use a lock whose ownership
does not leak through fork (for example OFD locks) or serialize spawn against publication. Record
the choice.

## Prerequisites
A change to Orbit's lock or lifecycle behavior touches its management and lifecycle contracts:
stop for Lucca's decision before changing them. Classify any `orbit-protocol` impact (none
expected) and name consumers.

## Acceptance
Deterministic reproduction recorded red, then green; the full `nix develop -c eon-test` passes
repeatedly (at least ten consecutive full runs); Orbit `cargo fmt --check` and clippy green.
Portability disposition recorded (flock vs OFD lock semantics on Linux and Darwin).

## Stop boundary
No change to the management wire format or Orbit's single-attachment model.
close_reason: Fixed in the test: a concurrent PTY fork briefly shares publication's locked claim; the test retries try_lock for up to 5s. The Orbit server forks only before publication, so it does not share the race. Proof and ledger in comments; 10 consecutive full eon-test passes (runs 9-18).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Proof (revision: the commit that carries this comment; x86_64 Linux, `nix develop` shell, eon-test bubblewrap sandbox).

Mechanism confirmed. Another test in the yazelix-orbit test binary forks a PTY child (`Pty::spawn`) while `RecordGuard::publish` holds the flock on its claim. The child shares that locked open file description until exec closes the O_CLOEXEC descriptor, so the test's next `claim.try_lock()` sees WouldBlock.
- Red: a temporary test-only fork in `RecordGuard::publish`, with the child holding the lock 300ms, made `nix develop -c eon-test -p yazelix-orbit --bin yazelix-orbit management_ready_claim` fail with `Error: "WouldBlock"`, the same error as the original flake.
- Green: with the fix, the same reproducer passed in 0.30s.
- A holder kept for 8s still failed the fixed test after 5.01s with WouldBlock. The reproducer is removed.

Fix (test-only, `orbit/src/platform.rs`): after the second publication, the test retries `claim.try_lock()` on WouldBlock every 10ms for up to 5s. The one-winner check while the claim is held and the record-removal checks are unchanged.

The server does not share the race, so there is no production, ORB-C* or orbit-protocol change and no consumer impact. `yazelix-orbit` is single-threaded. Its only fork, `Pty::spawn` (runtime.rs:258), runs before management publication (runtime.rs:281). With `pre_exec`, std `Command::spawn` returns only after the child has exec'd (CLOEXEC error pipe).

Rejected: OFD locks. They are also shared through fork-inherited descriptors, they are Linux-only, and they do not work together with eon-runtime's flock on the same claim. Serializing every forking test behind one mutex was also rejected, because future forking tests would have to remember to take it.

Portability: neutral. std `File::try_lock` is flock on both Linux and Darwin, with the same fork semantics, and the change is test-only.

Checks:
- Orbit `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings`: green.
- Full `nix develop -c eon-test`: 18 runs. Run 8 failed on an unrelated eon flake, `failed_or_stuck_startup_anima_reports_and_continues_to_picker` (workspace_control.rs:396, exit 1 where 0 was expected); Orbit's suite did not run in that run. Runs 9-18 were 10 consecutive full passes. The Ready-claim test passed in all 17 runs that reached it.
- `nix build --no-link .#default`: ok.

Review ledger: 1 pass (codex exec, read-only, fresh context): nothing blocking, no nits; the implementer's own pass also found nothing blocking.

title: Fix the latent ETXTBSY race in the Orbit startup-failure test
description:
## Why

A latent ETXTBSY flake of the same class as eon-supervisor-stderr-test-flake-ixne, eon-1fxc and eon-ven-new-window-test-flake-66gm.

## Evidence

- At a5a819f, `sessions::tests::startup_failure_names_the_orbit_log` (runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/sessions.rs, about line 2168) writes its fake Orbit launcher with `fs::write` in the test process, chmods it, and `start_orbit` execs it at once. A child forked meanwhile by a parallel test inherits the write descriptor until it execs, so the exec can fail with "Text file busy (os error 26)".
- No failure of this test has been observed yet. ixne's reproduction of the same pattern (write, chmod, then exec at once, while four threads fork and exec) hit ETXTBSY in 149 and 148 of 2000 rounds; see ixne's red/green comment of 2026-10-27.
- Seen by reading at a5a819f, outside eon-runtime and not checked further: installer/src/tests.rs:212-221 and orbit/tests/real_pty/support.rs:129-133 also write a script with `fs::write` and exec it right after. Fix them here if they share the cause, or file them separately.

## Scope

- Test-only: write the launcher from a child shell (`printf '%s' "$1" > "$0"`) and chmod by path, as supervisor.rs's `script` helper (ixne, `/bin/sh`) and quota.rs's (the `sh` on PATH) do. A shared `pub(crate)` helper in `sessions::tests`, which supervisor.rs's tests already import from, may replace ixne's local copy.
- Out of scope: production code.

## Acceptance

- `nix develop -c eon-test -p eon-runtime --lib` passes; eon-runtime fmt and clippy -D warnings clean.
- No literal mirror test; the existing test's exec is the check.

Filed by eon-2f on 2026-10-27 from eon-supervisor-stderr-test-flake-ixne.
close_reason: Test-only fix landed: shared sessions::tests::script, installer child_writes; Orbit real_pty does not race

comments.author: lucca
comments.text: Filed by the eon-supervisor-stderr-test-flake-ixne session as eon-wh2b in its worktree; eon-overseer recreated it here through br at landing (2026-10-27).

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Implementation and evidence (eon-4v2w session, 2026-10-27).

Not consequential under AGENTS.md's code-shape rule: test-only, no dependency, protocol, contract or lifecycle change, so no reference gate.

Change (test code only, no production code):
- runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/sessions.rs: `sessions::tests::script` (pub(crate)), ixne's helper moved here: a child `/bin/sh` writes the file (`printf '%s' "$1" > "$0"`), then chmod by path. `startup_failure_names_the_orbit_log` uses it.
- runtime/crates/eon-runtime/src/supervisor.rs: ixne's local `script` copy removed; `orbit_stderr_is_logged_and_owner_loss_names_the_file` imports the shared one.
- installer/src/tests.rs: `child_writes` runs a child that writes a file a test then executes. `fixture_version` copies the test binary with a child `cp` (was `fs::copy`), and `smoke_timeout_stops_wrapper_and_child` writes its wrapper with a child `sh` (was `fs::write`).
- orbit/: unchanged (see look-alike 2).
- quota.rs keeps its own helper (the `sh` on PATH). Moving it is outside this bead.

Look-alikes checked:
1. installer/src/tests.rs races, at two sites, by reading. `select` runs `smoke`, which spawns `timeout` to exec the version's `eon`. Two tests call `select` (`selection_and_removal_preserve_payloads_and_unrelated_files` and `failed_selection_and_locking_leave_current_usable`), and `smoke_timeout_stops_wrapper_and_child` spawns `sh` and `timeout`. All of them run in parallel in one test process. (a) `fixture_version`'s `fs::copy` writes `nix/eon`, which `select` then execs through `timeout`. ETXTBSY there shows up as timeout's exit 126, so `select(..).unwrap()` panics. (b) `smoke_timeout`'s `fs::write` of its wrapper, which `smoke` then execs. The `fs::write`/`fs::copy` at tests.rs:128 and :135 (before this change) cannot flake: :135 is never execed, because `entrypoint` rejects a non-link first, and :128 is expected to fail its exec anyway.
2. orbit/tests/real_pty/support.rs `executable()` cannot race, by reading. Every #[test] in that binary is generated by main.rs's `checks!` macro and runs through `support::serial`, which holds one process-wide mutex for the whole check. All of a check's forks (`Process::spawn` and friends) happen on the check's own thread, after `executable()`'s `fs::write` has closed its descriptor. The only other threads (pipe collectors in `Process::spawn`, `management_lease`'s two `acquire_as` racers, the watchdog) never fork. The checks are also #[ignore]d, and nix/orbit-checks.nix runs each one alone (`--ignored --exact NAME`). An edit to `executable()` was tried and then reverted, so Orbit is unchanged.
3. Other `from_mode(0o7..)` sites in the repo (generation.rs, diagnostics.rs, lib.rs, socket.rs, lifecycle.rs, venus application.rs, workspace_control.rs) set directory modes. managed_environment.rs's popup preflight writes executables but never execs them. venus application.rs:7157 already writes through a child shell.

Evidence. Pattern reproductions, not reproductions of these tests. No failure of the four affected tests has been observed. The reproducer, /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/4v2w-work/repro/repro.rs (rustc -O, edition 2024), runs four threads that fork and exec /bin/true in a loop while the main thread writes an executable and runs it at once. Results at loadavg about 3.4 to 5.2, on this tree's machine:
- write (fs::write + chmod + direct exec; the sessions.rs and installer smoke_timeout pattern): ETXTBSY in 168 of 2000 rounds. With a child /bin/sh writing instead: 0 of 2000.
- copy (fs::copy of the 686 KB repro binary, then exec through timeout(1); the installer fixture_version + smoke pattern): ETXTBSY in 1 of 2000 and 2 of 4000 rounds, identified by timeout's 126 exit and "Text file busy" on stderr. With a child cp instead: 0 of 2000 and 0 of 4000.
The copy window is smaller than the write window because fs::copy's descriptor is open only during one copy_file_range. The installer's test binary is larger, so its window should be wider. That is reasoned, not measured.

comments.author: lucca
comments.text:
Correction, review and proof (eon-4v2w session, 2026-10-27).

Corrections to the implementation comment above:
- Look-alike 1: the installer write that is expected to fail its exec is at tests.rs:131 before this change (`fs::write(bad.join("eon"), "invalid executable")`), not :128. One more site cannot flake: pre-change :139 (`fs::write(prefix.join("bin/eon"), "user command")`), because `select` rejects it through `bin_owned` before `smoke` runs. The conclusion is unchanged.
- Look-alike 2: the threads that never fork also include interactive_pressure.rs:47's flood sender, which only writes to a socket. The conclusion is unchanged.

New surface:
- `sessions::tests::script` (/bin/sh) is eon-runtime's shared test helper for writing an executable. quota.rs:524 keeps its own copy (the `sh` on PATH); merging the two is outside this bead.
- `installer/src/tests.rs::child_writes` writes any file an installer test later executes. Those tests now need `cp` on PATH, in addition to `sh` and `timeout`, which they already needed. The supported harnesses (eon-test's dev shell and the Nix build) supply coreutils.

Proof, on candidate tree aeea0639810ff98b4a381d5e1ab5361ed72a9141 (base a5c0d71, x86_64 Linux 7.1.5, rustc 1.95.0 from the dev shell, bubblewrap sandbox via eon-test), run by the fresh Claude reviewer with /home/lucca/.cache/eon-agents/4v2w-work/checks.sh (log: checks-review-c1.log):
- `nix develop -c eon-test -p eon-runtime --lib`: 120 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored. It includes `startup_failure_names_the_orbit_log` and `orbit_stderr_is_logged_and_owner_loss_names_the_file`. The sj0c flake did not occur.

- `cargo clippy --locked -p eon-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean. `cargo clippy --locked --manifest-path installer/Cargo.toml --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo fmt --check` for eon-runtime and the installer: clean.

The implementer's earlier run (checks-1.log) gave the same results on the same eon-runtime and installer code.

- Codex (gpt-6.1-sol, xhigh): no blocking findings; one nit, the thread list, corrected above.
- Fresh Claude reviewer, who also ran the checks: no code findings. One blocking text finding, the :128 line number, and nits, all corrected above. Its cp mode nit (umask) and its smoke_timeout double-sh nit were judged harmless and not changed.
