title: Prefer the current Eon runtime generation without orphaning live work
description:
## Contract routing

Add one user-approved Eon lifecycle contract before implementation:

> When Eon launches, it uses only a supervisor from the current runtime generation by default. Older live generations remain discoverable; compatible generations are explicitly attachable, generation-aware supervisors are explicitly stoppable, and changing generations never silently terminates Orbit-backed work.

The local user is the consumer. A bare Eon or desktop launch is the trigger. If a live supervisor has the exact current generation identity, Eon attaches to it. Otherwise Eon starts a fresh current-generation workspace in a separate private runtime namespace and leaves every older live generation running. Missing, corrupt, incompatible, ambiguous, or unreachable generation state produces a bounded explanation and never causes fallback to an unverified supervisor or implicit process termination.

This extends Eon's EON-C1/EON-C2 composition identity and EON-C8 lifecycle policy. Index a new EON contract before runtime edits and update EON-C10 only if the accepted minimum requires a protocol change. Do not silently widen EONW v1 or impose a compatibility window on Venus.

## Why and pipeline position

The current launcher treats the existence of one fixed `eon.sock` as proof that the running supervisor matches the installed Eon. After a runtime/profile update, bare `eon` can therefore attach current Venus to a stale supervisor or reuse stale Orbit/Venus policy. The user has already encountered this failure mode.

Implement this as the next P1 child of `eon-pxn`, after the completed workspace producer and Venus composition in `eon-pxn.3` and `eon-qat`. Complete it before the runtime/lifecycle, workspace-state, EONW, component-graph, and Nix-composition audits so those audits cover the final generation model rather than immediately becoming stale. It also precedes `eon-p93`: direct-distribution graduation already requires declared relaunch semantics and an upgrade path that never silently kills active work.

## Ownership

- Eon owns runtime-generation identity, current-generation selection, discovery, attach/stop policy, bounded cleanup, and user-facing diagnostics.
- Each running Eon supervisor remains the sole live owner of its own workspace topology and action state.
- Orbit remains the sole owner of every process, PTY, terminal state, retained history, attachment, and Session lifetime.
- Venus remains a transient client. It receives only an explicitly compatible Eon/Orbit endpoint pair and does not choose generations.
- Nix or another distributor may inject build inputs, but runtime behavior and identity remain distribution-neutral. A Nix store path, profile path, PID, socket pathname, or package-channel name is never a stable generation identity.

## Required evidence before code

- Current `crates/eon/src/main.rs` launch, attach, socket, supervisor, shutdown, and stale-endpoint paths; workspace control tests; the canonical component graph and validator; EON-C1, EON-C2, EON-C3, EON-C8, EON-C10; and the exact accepted Orbit and Venus proofs.
- `eon-pxn`, `eon-p93`, the runtime/lifecycle, component-graph, Nix-composition, workspace-state, and EONW audit Beads, including their immutable-subject rules.
- The exact current Power Failure Resumer reference for discovery, ambiguity, idempotent recovery, and partial-failure reporting; the official XDG runtime-directory contract for the local namespace.
- Herdr live handoff is comparison evidence only. This slice does not select live handoff, migrate a PTY, adopt an old supervisor, or add restart persistence.

Record an Execution baseline and Reference gate before production, test, manifest, or generated-fixture edits. Prefer no new dependency. If generation identity cannot be derived from accepted stable Eon build/protocol/component identities without another owner or package-channel concept, stop for a dependency/ownership decision.

## Minimum complete slice

1. Define one opaque, distribution-neutral runtime-generation identity that changes whenever the Eon runtime behavior, canonical component graph, or consumed protocol compatibility changes. Report its meaningful source identities for diagnosis without treating resolved artifact paths as identity.
2. Give every generation a separate owned private runtime namespace. A bare launch attaches only to an exact current-generation supervisor; if none exists, it starts one. Multiple invocations of the same generation still converge on one live supervisor.
3. Discover previous generations without reconstructing workspace state from files. Filesystem records may locate candidate endpoints, but the live supervisor remains authoritative and must be contacted and validated before its state or capabilities are reported.
4. Project one deterministic human and `--json` view that distinguishes current, previous, legacy, dead, incompatible, and corrupt generations and reports stable generation identity, component/protocol identity, liveness, and whether attach or stop is available with an owner-authored reason.
5. Let the user attach an explicitly selected compatible previous generation. Never substitute a different generation after failure.
6. Let the user explicitly stop a selected generation only through its authoritative Eon owner, with bounded confirmation and exact affected live Session identities. Non-interactive structured mode never prompts. A pre-feature legacy supervisor may report stop unavailable; it must never be killed by PID guessing, socket deletion, or process-tree inference.
7. Automatically remove only owned dead endpoint metadata or an empty, already-stopped generation. Never auto-stop a live supervisor or Orbit Session. Keep cleanup bounded and idempotent.
8. Prove the first upgrade transition from the current single fixed runtime namespace. Preserve and identify the legacy live workspace; attach it when its accepted EONW/Orbit contracts are compatible, otherwise keep it visible with an exact incompatibility reason.

Do not add a global manager daemon, durable topology storage, machine-restart recovery, live supervisor/PTY handoff, background updater, second component graph, Nix query, plugin API, remote runtime, or automatic age/count eviction. Do not change Orbit or Venus to compensate for an Eon-owned lifecycle problem. Stop and route an exact cross-repository gap if an accepted child contract is insufficient.

## Acceptance

1. The approved generation contract is indexed before implementation with consumer, trigger, result, failures, owner, exact commands, and honest proof state.
2. Same-generation bare launches attach to the existing supervisor; a changed generation starts a fresh supervisor and workspace while a long-running Session in the old generation remains alive and usable.
3. Current and previous generations can run concurrently without socket collisions, shared mutable topology, accidental cross-generation actions, or one generation cleaning another's live endpoints.
4. Listing is deterministic in human and JSON forms and validates live owners rather than presenting filesystem residue as authoritative state.
5. Explicit attach selects the requested compatible generation and supplies Venus one compatible Eon/Orbit endpoint pair. Missing or incompatible generations fail explicitly with no fallback.
6. Explicit stop affects only the selected generation, names the affected live Sessions, and routes through that supervisor. Cancellation or failure preserves every Session. Legacy stop remains unavailable unless it can be proved without guessing or a protocol compatibility promise.
7. Corrupt records, unsafe permissions, symlinks, stale sockets, owner mismatch, timeouts, partial startup, and concurrent launches have bounded deterministic outcomes and do not delete or terminate unrelated state.
8. Generation identity uses stable Eon build, canonical component, and protocol identities; normal runtime invokes no Nix evaluator and neither persistent product state nor the user-facing identity contains a Nix store/profile path.
9. Focused deterministic tests prove selection, ordering, validation, and cleanup. A process test runs generation A with useful long-lived Orbit work, launches generation B, proves B becomes the default while A survives, attaches both explicitly, and proves bounded stop/cleanup behavior.
10. Nix dogfood updates the installed Eon profile between two exact builds while the first generation has live work, then proves the same observable behavior. Record exact revisions, commands, platform, artifacts, and remaining compatibility limits.
11. Required Rust, manifest, Nix, and `git diff --check` verification passes; README/architecture/contracts/CHANGELOG and LOC accounting describe the accepted current behavior. After the proof-bearing commit, refresh and verify the active Eon runtime under the repository rule without stopping older user Sessions.
12. Closure records the exact proof revision and unblocks the runtime/lifecycle, workspace-state, EONW, component-graph, Nix-composition, and final integration audits plus the later direct-distribution decision. It does not claim machine-restart recovery, arbitrary historical compatibility, or live handoff.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if safe explicit stop requires guessing process ownership, deleting a live socket, or killing Orbit outside the authoritative supervisor.
- Stop for user approval before changing EON-C10/EONW, adding a compatibility window, adding a dependency, or changing an Orbit or Venus contract.
- Stop if the first complete slice requires a manager daemon, persistent duplicate workspace state, or distribution-specific runtime identity.

title: Remove a pane when its Orbit Session exits
description:
## Contract routing

Change EON-C8 under the user-approved 2026-08-10 lifecycle decision. Consumer: one local Eon user. Trigger: an Orbit Session process exits after its shell exits or fails. Result: Eon removes the pane mapped to that ended Session, selects the nearest remaining pane, removes an empty tab, and closes the Eon supervisor and Venus when the final pane exits. A following sibling at the removed index is nearest; otherwise select the previous sibling. The same rule applies to tabs after their final pane disappears.

Unexpected transport loss may remain visible through Venus current bounded connection notice until the next accepted workspace snapshot. Eon adds no notification protocol or stored tombstone. Unknown Session identities remain explicit internal failures and do not mutate topology.

Ownership: Eon owns topology pruning and selection. Orbit remains the sole owner of process, PTY, terminal state, and Session exit. Venus remains a transient renderer and follows EONW snapshots. Preserve EON-C1 through EON-C4, EON-C9, EON-C10, EONW v1 bytes, child contracts, and one expanded pane.

Out of scope: a user-invoked close/stop action, killing a live Session, close confirmation, exit-status persistence, restart, reopen, history retention after Session death, protocol changes, new dependencies, settings, remote behavior, or machine-restart recovery.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A known ended Session removes exactly its pane and never stops or changes another live Session.
2. Removing the selected pane chooses the following sibling at the same index, otherwise the previous sibling; removing an unselected pane preserves selected identity.
3. Removing a tab final pane chooses the following tab at the same index, otherwise the previous tab; removing an inactive tab preserves active identity.
4. The initial Session may exit while later Sessions remain; Venus and Eon remain live and expose the nearest surviving pane.
5. The final Session exit leaves no pane or tab and closes Venus and the Eon supervisor with the existing initial-status policy.
6. Unknown or repeated Session-exit notifications fail without mutation. EONW v1 and all explicit actions remain unchanged.
7. Deterministic unit tests fail before implementation and pass after it; a process test covers initial-Session exit with a surviving Session.
8. Current-state contracts, README, CHANGELOG, LOC, required Rust/Nix checks, installed-profile verification, and git diff checks pass while the pre-existing documentation cleanup remains preserved.

title: Package Nerd Font symbols for native tool glyphs
description:
## Contract routing

This bead hardens EON-C9 managed-environment packaging and preserves EON-C4 child ownership. It adds no new product contract and does not activate the deferred appearance slice. Eon owns the packaged font selection and closure; Venus continues to own native discovery, shaping, fallback, and rendering. If the packaged face is discoverable but Venus still cannot render representative glyphs, stop and route that demonstrated renderer gap to Venus instead of compensating in Eon.

## Smallest observable contract

Consumer: one local user running managed Yazi or another native terminal tool in packaged Eon.
Trigger: the tool emits a supported Nerd Font private-use glyph.
Result: the packaged runtime can discover and render that glyph from Symbols Nerd Font Mono without relying on an ambient host font installation.
Important failures: a missing package, undiscoverable face, or fallback box fails the proof explicitly; it must not prevent Eon or Yazi from starting.

## Evidence

- Eon currently builds Venus with a generated fontconfig containing only DejaVu and documents unsupported native-tool glyphs as a current gap.
- Nova revision 6c7174b4efca5f139a461d204186c5001d6457bd uses pkgs.nerd-fonts.symbols-only and maps private-use ranges to Symbols Nerd Font Mono.
- The requested defect is visible in managed Yazi, so this is current product credibility rather than speculative appearance work.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

Before manifest or production edits:
1. Confirm no active implementation frontier and compare pinned Orbit and Venus revisions with their latest accepted revisions.
2. Inspect the exact locked nixpkgs package metadata, contents, license, supported systems, and closure cost for nerd-fonts.symbols-only.
3. Inspect Nova revision 6c7174b4efca5f139a461d204186c5001d6457bd only for its symbols-only package and font-discovery mechanism.
4. Inspect the pinned Venus glyphon/cosmic-text discovery boundary only as needed to establish the cheapest consumer proof. Defer deeper renderer work unless a packaged discoverable face still fails.
5. Record the reference and dependency decisions, including no change and a full patched Nerd Font as rejected alternatives, before editing.

## Scope

In scope:
- The smallest Eon Nix composition change that exposes Symbols Nerd Font Mono to packaged Venus.
- One artifact-level discovery check and focused native Yazi visual dogfood.
- Current-state README, contract-gap, changelog, LOC scorecard, and proof updates required by the accepted behavior.
- Active Eon profile refresh without restarting or terminating live Sessions.

Out of scope:
- A full patched primary Nerd Font, font picker, user font configuration, explicit symbol-map API, emoji stack, theme, opacity, size, or broad appearance work.
- Venus renderer changes unless a separately routed Venus bead is approved after a demonstrated boundary failure.
- Nova compatibility or copied Nova configuration.

## Acceptance

1. The exact Eon artifact includes Symbols Nerd Font Mono from the locked nixpkgs input and Venus can discover it through its existing font path.
2. An artifact-level check proves representative BMP and supplementary private-use glyph coverage without ambient user fonts.
3. Fresh packaged Eon dogfood opens managed Yazi and its ordinary file and directory icons render without fallback boxes.
4. Eon and Yazi still start when optional user font configuration is absent; no ambient font, shell profile, or global fontconfig mutation is required.
5. The change adds no renderer code, second font schema, patched primary face, or unrelated appearance behavior.
6. Exact Nix build and flake checks, relevant existing checks, and git diff --check pass.
7. README and CONTRACTS describe current state, CHANGELOG records the visible packaging fix, and the LOC scorecard is current.
8. The active Eon profile resolves to the proof artifact while any existing supervisor and Orbit Sessions remain untouched.

## Platform and exit conditions

The first proof is x86_64 Linux. The selected packaged face must remain available for the repository’s credible macOS packaging path, but this bead claims no macOS runtime proof. Remove the dependency if Yazi stops using private-use icons or Venus gains a smaller accepted owner-supplied glyph mechanism.

Question:
How can packaged Eon render Yazi private-use icons without adding a font subsystem or depending on ambient host installation?

Contracts:

Sources and exact identities:

Only the symbols-only selection is adopted; Nova’s Mars-specific symbol-map, primary font, emoji stack, and configuration schema are rejected scope.
- Locked nixpkgs 567a49d1913ce81ac6e9582e3553dd90a955875f: nerd-fonts.symbols-only 3.4.0 is a stdenvNoCC data derivation fetched by exact archive hash. It installs SymbolsNerdFont-Regular.ttf and SymbolsNerdFontMono-Regular.ttf.
- Package licenses from exact nixpkgs metadata: OFL-1.1 and MIT, both free. Supported platforms include x86_64/aarch64 Linux and Darwin.
- Package cost: 4,949,240-byte Nix closure; two TTF files totaling 4,947,872 bytes; no runtime executable, native library, or transitive service.
- Pinned Venus 6ef19afddaedcbe2b9ed0996e31bc02df5d854ac: Renderer constructs glyphon FontSystem::new. Exact glyphon 0.12.0 consumes cosmic-text 0.19.0 and fontdb 0.23.0 with fontconfig enabled. fontdb reads FONTCONFIG_FILE and loads every configured directory.
- Managed Yazi 26.5.6 source uses representative Nerd Font glyphs including U+E5FF folder, U+F15B file, U+F489 command, and supplementary U+F0868 Docker.
- A realized candidate makeFontsConf containing DejaVu and symbols-only names the exact Nerd Font store directory. Current host font matches are not proof because this machine already has unrelated FiraCode Nerd Font in its user profile.

Options compared:
1. No change: rejected; it preserves the user-visible fallback-box defect and leaves Eon’s existing fontconfig derivation build-only.
2. Full patched primary Nerd Font: rejected; it duplicates text faces, changes primary-font policy, adds broader appearance behavior, and is unnecessary for Yazi icons.
3. Copy Nova’s explicit symbol-map: rejected; Mars owns that schema and Venus has no approved font-map surface.
4. Add symbols-only to Eon’s existing generated fontconfig and export that exact config from the installed Venus wrapper: selected. This reuses the current Nix and Venus owners and requires no renderer code.

Code-shape consequence:
Keep the existing FONTCONFIG_FILE derivation variable, add pkgs.nerd-fonts.symbols-only to its fontDirectories, and pass that variable through wrapProgram. Do not add the font to the canonical component manifest because it is presentation-package data, not an independently versioned Eon component. Expected production change: two flake lines and no new source module.

Platform:
The proof is x86_64 Linux. The font package itself supports Darwin, but cosmic-text’s macOS system loader does not consume FONTCONFIG_FILE; a later native macOS bundle must supply the face through its platform packaging or an explicit Venus font source. The Linux wrapper remains an isolated packaging seam rather than a cross-platform contract.

Cheapest proof:
Inspect the built Venus wrapper for the exact FONTCONFIG_FILE; inspect its closure for nerd-fonts-symbols-only; use that config to verify the two named faces and representative BMP/supplementary codepoints; then fresh packaged Yazi visual dogfood.

Exit condition:
Remove the package when managed tools no longer emit PUA icons or an accepted smaller Venus-owned glyph source replaces font fallback.

title: Decide Eon boundary for agent-driven terminal software testing
description:
Contract routing:
- This is a planning and architecture decision. It changes no EON-C*, ORB-C*, or VEN-C* contract and creates no runtime behavior, protocol, dependency, module, or compatibility promise.
- Eon owns the decision because it owns agent-run policy, authorization, workspace composition, lifecycle, and product actions.
- Orbit remains the sole PTY, process attachment, terminal-state, semantic-input encoding, and terminal-query authority.
- Venus remains the native rendering and input materialization owner. Any new Venus module or capture contract requires separate user approval.
- Any implementation outcome must be activated later as owner-specific child Beads after exact contract approval. This decision claims no implementation frontier.

Why:
The qwertty ecosystem demonstrates a credible automated terminal-engineering loop: a terminal application library, TUI library, terminal emulator, deterministic capture or test harness, and agent harness. Eon already owns durable workspace composition around Orbit and Venus, but it has no accepted boundary for terminal-test automation. Without a decision, later work may duplicate Orbit PTY or emulator authority, make pixels the primary state source, or accidentally add a second interactive client.

Evidence:
- `eon-pxn` already routes Eon AgentRun, action, authorization, and workspace work and explicitly leaves bounded terminal observation to `orb-p92`.
- `../eon-sessions/docs/CONTRACTS.md:30,34-35` keeps PTY lifetime, semantic input, and rich terminal presentation authoritative in Orbit.
- `../eon-desktop/README.md:29,50` routes complete frames through one reducer and permits only one presentation client per Session.
- qwertty `829539399b4dcfd95f85758a285f5200f1bc711c` demonstrates app-side terminal ownership, ordered output, semantic input, and policy gates.
- qwertty-term `9021f511bf053ec4155298e43a65de4365a13f80` demonstrates an embeddable terminal emulator and deterministic VT-bytes-to-PNG capture.
- Betamax `7fbaa1598e3601ccb60f244a8c669d60a6d780db` demonstrates PTY-driven tape scripts, bounded screen waits, structured state, screenshots, and animations.

Decision question:
Should Eon own any agent-driven terminal testing component, or are external tools plus accepted Eon and Orbit surfaces sufficient?

In scope:
- Compare external black-box tooling, an exclusive headless Orbit presentation client, a bounded read-only Orbit observer combined with Eon actions, and no Eon-owned harness.
- Decide whether structured Orbit observations are sufficient and when pixel capture adds unique evidence.
- Name one owner for authorization, lifecycle, input, observation, rendering, artifacts, and cleanup.
- Select at most one smallest end-to-end proof or explicitly decide that external tools are sufficient.

Out of scope:
- Implementing a harness, tape language, MCP server, plugin, provider adapter, remote service, CI job, screenshot API, new Venus module, or new Orbit role.
- Embedding Betamax, qwertty-term, or another PTY or terminal emulator inside Eon.
- Multiple input-capable Orbit clients, raw PTY access, OCR as authority, durable transcripts, arbitrary shell execution, and automatic secret-redaction claims.
design:
Decision method:
1. The earlier planning activation was deferred again; this decision requires renewed user selection. Before starting the decision, confirm the current cross-repository implementation frontier is clear, then reread exact accepted Eon, Orbit, and Venus contracts and the current `eon-pxn` and `orb-p92` plans.
2. Inspect qwertty, qwertty-term, and Betamax at the pinned commits. Treat their mechanisms as evidence, not dependencies or ownership authority. Record license implications only for any proposed reuse; comparison alone approves no reuse.
3. Compare these shapes:
   A. External black-box tool owns its own PTY and emulator and tests Eon or terminal applications from outside the product.
   B. External agent harness composes accepted Eon actions with authorized bounded `orb-p92` observations; Eon ships no testing component.
   C. One exclusive headless Orbit presentation client temporarily occupies the existing input-capable attachment role, sends canonical semantic input, and inspects bounded canonical state while Venus is detached.
   D. A separate concurrent input-capable automation role or second terminal owner. Presumptively reject unless a demonstrated workflow cannot be satisfied by A through C and the user approves a new Orbit contract.
4. Start with structured authoritative observations. Permit pixel evidence only for a named rendering or visual-quality question that structured state cannot answer. Any native image path must reuse the accepted Venus frame-to-draw path and cannot become a second renderer, schema, or terminal owner.
5. For each credible shape, define consumer, trigger, result, failure semantics, authorization, capability expiry and revocation, bounds on sessions, input, observations, time, bytes, artifacts, retries, cancellation, cleanup, and sensitive terminal content.
6. Evaluate one representative loop: create or select a disposable workspace, start a terminal application, send semantic interaction, wait on bounded authoritative state, optionally capture supplementary pixels, let an agent make one correction, rerun, and tear down. The proof must use disposable state and cannot interrupt durable user Sessions.
7. Prefer no Eon-owned component when an external tool or accepted Eon and Orbit surfaces satisfy the loop. If product code is justified, select one smallest owner-specific vertical slice and request explicit contract approval before creating implementation children.

Verification for the decision record:
- `br show eon-pxn.7 --json` shows one deferred, unclaimed planning decision related to `eon-pxn`, without requiring closure of the whole product-horizon epic with no implementation assignee.
- `br show eon-pxn --json` and, in Eon Sessions, `br show orb-p92 --json` confirm owner routing and exclusions.
- `rg -n "ORB-C1|ORB-C5|ORB-C6" docs/CONTRACTS.md` in Eon Sessions confirms the cited terminal owners.
- `rg -n "VEN-C1" docs/CONTRACTS.md` in Eon Desktop confirms the canonical frame-to-draw owner.
- `git ls-remote` for all three references confirms their recorded commits when the decision activates.
- `br dep cycles --json`, `br lint`, and `git diff --check` pass in every planning repository touched.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The record states whether Eon owns any terminal-testing component or whether external tools and accepted product surfaces are sufficient.
2. The comparison covers external black-box tooling, an external harness over Eon actions plus bounded Orbit observation, one exclusive headless Orbit presentation client, and the presumptively rejected concurrent automation role.
3. Orbit remains the sole PTY, process-attachment, terminal-state, terminal-query, and semantic-input-encoding owner. No selected shape reparses raw PTY bytes, instantiates another emulator inside Eon, or maintains another Orbit schema.
4. Eon alone owns product authorization, AgentRun and workspace selection, lifecycle policy, action routing, capability issuance, expiry, revocation, and cleanup. Venus alone owns native rendering and input materialization.
5. The selected observation path is bounded, source-labeled, revision-consistent, and explicit about lossiness. Structured state is primary; screenshots are supplementary and justified by a named visual question.
6. The one input-capable Orbit attachment invariant remains intact unless the user separately approves a changed Orbit contract. An exclusive headless client cannot run concurrently with Venus.
7. The decision defines authorization and deterministic failures for unauthorized, expired, revoked, malformed, oversized, stale, cancelled, timed-out, disconnected, child-exited, and shutdown cases without exposing terminal content on denial.
8. The decision bounds sessions, concurrent work, messages, bytes, time, retries, artifacts, retained data, cancellation, teardown, and pressure on Orbit, Venus, and Eon owner loops.
9. The decision selects at most one disposable end-to-end proof or records explicit external-tool sufficiency. It names the cheapest falsifying check and evidence that would reverse the choice.
10. No tape DSL, MCP server, plugin system, provider integration, remote service, CI expansion, durable transcript, OCR authority, automatic redaction claim, dependency, or compatibility promise is bundled into the decision.
11. Any selected implementation names exact EON-C*, ORB-C*, and VEN-C* routing, cross-repository order, portability disposition, reference and crate gates, and separate owner-specific child Beads. Contract or module creation stops for user approval.
12. Closure records exact reference commits, adopted and rejected mechanisms, license or reuse disposition, security and lifecycle model, expected owned LOC and dependency cost, limitations, and the explicit user decision. Closure itself changes no runtime contract or code.
notes:
Initial recommendation: choose no Eon-owned terminal-testing component unless dogfood proves that an external harness over accepted Eon actions and bounded Orbit observations is insufficient. This is the Ponytail first rung and keeps terminal ownership singular.

Reference disposition as of 2026-08-13:
- qwertty `829539399b4dcfd95f85758a285f5200f1bc711c`: comparison-only evidence for explicit app-side terminal ownership, ordered IO, semantic events, capability evidence, and policy gates. It is not an Orbit replacement or proposed dependency.
- qwertty-term `9021f511bf053ec4155298e43a65de4365a13f80`: comparison-only evidence for embeddable deterministic byte-to-image rendering. Reject its PTY and terminal-emulator ownership inside Eon because Orbit already owns them.
- Betamax `7fbaa1598e3601ccb60f244a8c669d60a6d780db`: comparison-only evidence for bounded tape waits, structured snapshots, screenshots, and terminal-test ergonomics. Reject embedding it because its PTY plus libghostty state would duplicate Orbit.

Conditional children, deliberately not created:
1. Prove one exclusive headless Orbit automation client using canonical semantic input and bounded state predicates, with Venus detached.
2. Render accepted Venus scenes to deterministic images only after structured observation fails a named visual proof, reusing the real rendering path and adding no second renderer.
3. Prove one complete disposable agent build-run-inspect-correct loop after the owner slices exist.

Priority P2 deferred. Planning effort M. Implementation risk HIGH if selected because authorization, sensitive terminal content, pressure, and cross-repository contracts are involved. Confidence HIGH that the decision is needed before product work and HIGH that external sufficiency should be the default.

Readiness reconciliation (2026-08-19): The decision remains preserved but is not current frontier work. Reactivate when the user selects terminal-testing boundary work; it authorizes no implementation by status alone.

2026-09-08 evidence: eon-zlf's native benchmark was stopped after focus theft, then completed from existing observations without more GUI launches. Any later proof must honor AGENTS.md Desktop Focus. External/background or isolated surfaces remain the first candidates, and an alternate renderer/compositor proves only its named surface. This does not activate a harness, capture API or new owner.

- Exact source: Gaurav-Gosain/tuios revision 0047c409185f37e568933a566e0253b2a6e96a96, including docs/protocol.md, docs/TAPE_SCRIPTING.md, internal/session capture and wait handlers, and the tape runner.

title: Add direct tab close and workspace reorder shortcuts
description:
## Observable outcome

Consumer: one local full-Eon workspace user.

Trigger: the user invokes a direct structural shortcut while Eon owns the terminal key stream.

Result:
- `Ctrl+Shift+W` requests closing the active tab without entering a mode.
- `Ctrl+Alt+H/L` moves the active tab one position left or right.
- `Ctrl+Alt+K/J` moves the selected pane one position up or down.
- Reordering stops at the corresponding edge rather than wrapping.
- Existing `Alt+H/L` tab focus, `Alt+K/J` pane focus, `Ctrl+T` tab creation, and `Alt+M` pane creation remain direct and unchanged.
- Eon adds no Tab mode or Pane mode.

Important failures: an edge reorder changes nothing; unavailable pane movement changes nothing; shortcut handling never leaks a partial topology update, changes stable tab or pane identities, retargets a Session, or forwards a consumed Eon chord into the terminal application.

## Ownership

Eon owns semantic close and reorder actions plus ordered workspace topology. Venus owns exact shortcut recognition, precedence, and presentation. Orbit owns every Session and its stop result. A tab-close implementation must preserve the distinction between removing Eon topology and stopping Orbit Sessions; it may not orphan a live Session or claim atomic success after a partial stop.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- Finish and accept `eon-traverse-tabs-during-picker-nxp` before implementation because both slices change the same workspace action frontier.
- Reread EON-C8 and EON-C18, the current workspace action codec, workspace dispatch, picker gate, supervisor lifecycle, Session-exit pruning, CLI routing, and exact accepted Orbit and Venus revisions.
- Use Yazelix Nova revision `091f0ee0e09d4f6137fc642803cc60861272fb20` only as comparison evidence for its direct `Alt` focus layer and `Ctrl+Alt` structural-movement layer. Nova and Zellij are not compatibility targets.
- Recheck the exact pinned Helix keymap and Kitty keyboard encoding before consuming `Ctrl+Shift+W`; the current inspected Helix revision `7e6cd307d00783c16ad4cff99ed71936d34f6572` has no default or managed `Ctrl+Shift+W` binding and distinguishes it from lowercase `Ctrl+W`.
- Before contract approval, define durable-tab close, pending-picker close, last-tab close, multi-Session partial-stop, duplicate request, stale Session, and picker-active behavior. The shortcut decision does not silently choose those lifecycle outcomes.

## Scope boundary

In scope: the minimum Eon semantic actions and CLI projection, ordered tab and pane reordering, exact Venus shortcuts, required protocol evolution, lifecycle-safe active-tab closing, current contracts and docs, exact component pins, installed profile refresh, and focused installed dogfood.

Out of scope: Tab or Pane modes, keybinding configuration, pane closing, renaming, drag-and-drop, arbitrary index moves, moving panes between tabs, new layout shapes, Nova compatibility, dependencies, and platform expansion.

## Acceptance

The structured acceptance criteria are canonical.
design:
1. Update the EON-C8 lifecycle contract before code. Record the chosen close semantics for pending, durable, and final tabs and for partial Orbit stop failure.
2. Extend the existing semantic action owner and codec only as required. Reuse ordered workspace vectors for one-position swaps; add no mode state, generic command layer, or dependency.
3. Prove owner behavior before wiring the same actions through the canonical CLI and exact Venus consumer shortcuts.
4. Preserve picker identity and current shortcut precedence. Admit picker-active structural actions only where the approved lifecycle contract explicitly requires them.
5. Refresh the exact component graph and active Eon profile without restarting live supervisors, then dogfood the installed shortcuts.
acceptance_criteria:
1. `Ctrl+Shift+W` invokes the one Eon-owned close-active-tab action; `Ctrl+Alt+H/L` moves the active tab exactly one position; `Ctrl+Alt+K/J` moves the selected pane exactly one position. None enters a mode.
2. Tab and pane moves stop at ordered edges without wrapping or mutation. Every successful move preserves the moved stable identity, selection, tab directory, pane-to-Session mapping, picker binding, and unrelated order.
3. Before implementation, EON-C8 explicitly defines pending-picker close, durable-tab close, final-tab close, duplicate close, stale Session, and multi-Session partial-stop outcomes. Installed behavior matches that contract and never leaves an unrepresented live Session or reports complete closure while a required stop failed.
4. Existing direct focus and creation shortcuts retain their exact behavior. Exact `Ctrl+Shift+W` is consumed only by full Eon; lowercase `Ctrl+W` and unrelated Helix or terminal input remain untouched.
5. Picker-active admission is narrow and explicit. Rejected close or move actions leave topology, focus, directories, Sessions, and picker state unchanged.
6. Focused codec, workspace, lifecycle, process, and Venus shortcut checks pass; complete affected locked Rust/Nix surfaces pass; exact accepted Orbit and Venus revisions are pinned; the active profile is refreshed; and isolated installed native Wayland dogfood proves all five chords without restarting live Sessions.
7. No Tab mode, Pane mode, keybinding configuration, pane-close action, cross-tab pane move, arbitrary reorder, dependency, Nova compatibility promise, or platform expansion is introduced.
close_reason: Accepted runtime and installed shortcut proof are complete; canonical Eon Desktop policy now matches the accepted contract and proof.

title: Add non-wrapping workspace reorder actions
description:
## Observable contract

Consumer: one local full-Eon workspace user or semantic-action client.

Trigger: the consumer requests tab movement left or right, or pane movement up or down, through the canonical Eon action boundary.

Result:
- `eon tab move left|right [--json]` swaps the active tab with exactly one adjacent tab and keeps that same `tN` identity active.
- `eon pane move up|down [--json]` swaps the selected pane with exactly one adjacent pane in the active tab and keeps that same `pN` identity selected.
- Movement stops at the first or last position rather than wrapping.
- Stable identities, tab directories, pane-to-Session mappings, picker binding, Session lifetime, and unrelated order remain unchanged.

Important failures: an edge move, singleton axis, pane move in a pending pane-free tab, picker-active request, duplicate request, malformed direction, or EonTerm target changes no topology or process state and returns a bounded existing-style failure.

Ownership: Eon owns semantic movement, ordered topology, and failure policy. Orbit owns Session lifetime and is untouched. Venus remains an unchanged snapshot consumer; shortcut recognition is not part of this slice.

## Reference gate and decision

Inspected EON-C8/EON-C18, the EONW v3/v4 request codec, workspace dispatch and Session-exit pruning, CLI routing, current picker tests, exact accepted Orbit `a65e199e16e97330175e314cacf791fa00f53069`, and exact accepted Venus `a6e6846fe0c6039759b526b936704a3146fcad9c`.

Comparable evidence:
- Yazelix Nova `091f0ee0e09d4f6137fc642803cc60861272fb20` uses a direct `Ctrl+Alt` structural layer over its `Alt` focus layer.
- Yazelix Zellij fork `b9637022eaddb22855dc9914a0cc06762a124b8c` swaps adjacent tabs internally but rotates the full tab order at edges.

Decision: reuse Eon's existing ordered vectors and cardinal `Direction` with one semantic `Move(Direction)` action. Preserve EONW v3 wire behavior and add movement only to the current v4 request language. Reject a v5 bump, copied Zellij machinery, edge rotation, mode state, generic reorder indices, child changes, and dependencies.

## Scope boundary

In scope: EON-C8 movement contract, EONW v4 action encoding, workspace swaps, CLI commands, focused owner/process checks, current docs and changelog, README LOC, full affected Rust/Nix proof, profile refresh, and installed CLI dogfood.

Out of scope: tab closing, pane closing, Venus keybindings, Tab or Pane modes, picker-active movement, wrapping/rotation, direct identity/index targets, moving panes between tabs, drag-and-drop, persistence, child revisions, dependencies, and platform expansion.
design:
1. Extend EON-C8 before code with adjacent, non-wrapping reorder semantics and unchanged identity/session ownership.
2. Add focused red checks for v4 movement request round trips with v3 rejection and one workspace test covering every success and edge failure.
3. Add one `Move(Direction)` action, four v4-only request tags, direct `Vec::swap` transitions, and the two narrow CLI command families.
4. Reuse the current dispatch, snapshot, duplicate-request, picker gate, and process control paths unchanged.
5. Run the full shared protocol/runtime proof, refresh the active profile without restarting live supervisors, and dogfood only the installed CLI actions.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Current EONW v4 round-trips `Move(Left|Right|Up|Down)`; historical v3 rejects those actions and tags without changing any existing bytes.
2. A successful tab move swaps the active tab with one adjacent tab and follows its stable identity. A successful pane move swaps the selected pane with one adjacent pane in the active tab and follows its stable identity.
3. First/last edge, singleton, pane-free, picker-active, duplicate, malformed, EonTerm, and unsupported-version cases fail without changing topology, focus, directories, identities, Session mappings, processes, or picker state.
4. `eon tab move left|right [--json]` and `eon pane move up|down [--json]` are the complete new command surface and return the ordinary complete workspace snapshot.
5. Existing create, focus, directory-picker, Session-exit, lifecycle, human/JSON output, and exact Orbit/Venus behavior remain unchanged.
6. Focused protocol, workspace, parser, and process checks; complete locked Rust/Nix verification; installed profile refresh; installed CLI dogfood; contracts, README, changelog, LOC, Beads, and diff checks succeed without restarting live Sessions.
7. No close action, shortcut, mode, key configuration, edge wrap/rotation, arbitrary target/index, cross-tab pane movement, child edit/pin, dependency, or platform expansion is introduced.
close_reason: Accepted non-wrapping workspace reorder mechanics, complete proof, installed profile, and isolated dogfood are complete.

title: Decide Bend ownership of the AgentRun transition kernel
description:
## Outcome and decision contract

Decide whether Bend should become the sole owner of a future Eon AgentRun transition kernel, and choose exactly one outcome: Go for a separately authorized production slice, Defer pending a named Bend capability, or No-Go with the failed criterion recorded.

Consumer: the deferred `eon-pxn` agent-work horizon and a future Eon implementation decision.

Trigger: an explicit user action or fresh source-labeled provider event is presented with the current AgentRun state.

Candidate result: one pure Bend transition returns the next AgentRun state, a bounded list of authorized effect intents, and bounded presentation facts. It does not execute effects. Invalid, stale, contradictory, replayed, or unauthorized inputs return a bounded rejection and produce no effects.

This issue is a research and decision slice only. It creates no EON contract, production module, runtime dependency, provider promise, or shipped AgentRun behavior.

Impact: HIGH if Eon activates agent work because the kernel would own lifecycle and authorization invariants that are costly to reconstruct across adapters. Effort: M. Adoption risk: HIGH because Bend 2 is young and has no supported native library ABI. Confidence: HIGH that this is the best Eon responsibility to evaluate; MEDIUM that current Bend can meet the integration gate.

## Evidence

- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:70-120` requires one owner per Eon policy and keeps Orbit, Venus, and child mechanisms separate.
- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:174-191` places live workspace policy in Eon and the versioned client boundary in EONW.
- `docs/REFERENCES.md:249-428` routes agent work through explicit provider evidence, distinct work/attempt/provider/terminal/process identities, bounded actions, and user-visible disagreement rather than terminal inference.
- Deferred parent `eon-pxn` defines AgentRun as distinct from a pane, PTY, process, Orbit Session, provider thread, or durable Beads work item; no production AgentRun owner exists yet.
- `crates/eon/src/workspace.rs:94-966` shows that the existing Rust workspace reducer is already intertwined with accepted tab, pane, popup, directory, and Session operations. Rewriting that proven surface is a higher-risk first Bend adoption.
- Bend 2.0.5 release commit `38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7` checked the disposable Orbit attachment laws in about 0.09 seconds and rejected a deliberate successor-revision mutation; evidence is retained in `eon-sessions:orb-evaluate-bend2-orbit-proof-model-1re`.
- `bend2/README.md:213-251` records Bend limitations relevant here: affine values, termination requirements, linked-list strings, whole-program C output, slow native compilation, a young unaudited compiler, formalization mismatch, and limited tooling.
- `bend2/main.ts:1-7` exposes filled pure definitions through the JavaScript loader. A native probe using `bun bend2/main.ts demos/proof_insertion_sort/main.bend -o <tmp>/sort.c` produced a whole program with `int main` and no supported public library ABI. Production embedding must not assume callable native functions that Bend does not expose.

## Ownership under test

Bend would own:

- AgentRun and attempt lifecycle state.
- Typed distinctions among an opaque work reference, AgentRun, attempt, provider session, Orbit Session, and process reference.
- State-transition validity and terminal-state rules.
- Evidence source and freshness admission.
- Replay/idempotency policy.
- Authorization of bounded effect intents.
- The bounded presentation projection derived from the same state.
- Laws and proofs for those invariants.

Rust Eon would retain:

- EONW and any internal framing or transport.
- Provider adapters and provider-native semantic interpretation.
- Child process, filesystem, persistence, Nix, and platform effects.
- Execution of Bend-authorized effect intents and reporting their outcomes.
- Fail-closed lifecycle policy when the Bend boundary is unavailable.

Beads remains the durable work and authorization truth. Orbit remains the Session, PTY, process-lifecycle, and terminal-state owner. Venus remains the presentation and interaction owner. Bend must not become an autonomous scheduler, provider adapter, issue tracker, terminal controller, or UI owner.

## Laws to evaluate

At minimum, formalize and prove:

1. Work, AgentRun, attempt, provider-session, Orbit-session, and process identities cannot be substituted for one another.
2. Process exit, terminal detachment, output growth, silence, or provider-session end cannot by itself mark durable work successful.
3. Unknown or stale provider evidence cannot become authoritative working, needs-input, reviewable, or completed state.
4. Replaying an accepted event cannot emit a second non-idempotent effect.
5. A terminal attempt cannot resume; a retry receives a fresh attempt identity.
6. No launch, stop, focus, notification, or acceptance intent is emitted without a valid explicitly authorized transition.
7. State, retained evidence, rejection detail, and emitted effects remain within declared bounds.
8. Rejected input leaves the prior state observationally unchanged and emits no effect.

Do not add an at-most-one-active-attempt law or provider-specific lifecycle meaning without a separate product decision.

## Scope

In scope:

- A disposable, exact-revision Bend model of the minimum AgentRun state, events, reducer, effect intents, projection, laws, and proofs.
- Positive traces covering start, source-labeled activity, needs-input, review handoff, explicit acceptance or rejection, failure, abort, and retry only where the evidence supports those generic meanings.
- Negative mutations for identity confusion, stale-evidence promotion, process-exit-as-success, duplicate effect emission, terminal-state revival, and unauthorized effect creation.
- Comparison of three integration shapes: no production adoption, the supported JavaScript export surface, and a native one-shot subprocess. Compare a long-lived service only if measurement shows one-shot startup is inadequate.
- Exact source pins, license, build/runtime closure, cold-start and transition latency, output determinism, failure containment, Linux and Apple Silicon feasibility, owned LOC, debugging burden, upgrade cost, and removal cost.
- A Go, Defer, or No-Go recommendation recorded in this issue, followed by explicit user review.

Out of scope:

- Production Eon, Orbit, Venus, EONW, component-manifest, Nix-profile, or contract changes.
- Creating a new repository, component, runtime service, protocol version, provider integration, durable state format, scheduler, sidebar, UI, or implementation follow-up.
- Rewriting the existing Eon workspace reducer, EONW codec, Orbit runtime, or Venus scene/rendering.
- Retaining a Rust transition implementation as a second policy owner.
- Using `@unsafe` inside the pure reducer or its proof-bearing laws.
- Claiming that a proof covers Rust adapters, transport, persistence, foreign effects, the Bend compiler, or the generated runtime.

## Investigation steps

1. Freeze the Eon, parent Bead, Bend source, Bun, and clang identities; preserve the pre-existing dirty Eon paths and use one disposable temporary root for experiment files.
2. Reread the parent AgentRun requirements and the agent-work reference routes. Define the smallest provider-neutral state, event, result, and effect contract without inventing scheduling or provider semantics.
3. Implement the reducer and laws in Bend with no IO or `@unsafe` in the proof-bearing core.
4. Run the positive proof and each deliberate negative mutation. Record exact commands, output, time, peak memory, source hashes, and the claim each result supports.
5. Exercise the supported JavaScript export boundary and one native one-shot invocation. Do not patch Bend or treat generated internal C symbols as an API.
6. Measure boundary overhead and model the runtime/package closure on x86_64 Linux and feasibility on aarch64-darwin. Verify that boundary failure can reject agent actions while leaving existing Orbit Sessions and ordinary Eon workspace behavior untouched.
7. Compare the result against a minimum Rust reducer and no new component. Count all project-owned adapter, schema, build, Nix, test, and operational code, not only Bend source.
8. Record one Go, Defer, or No-Go decision. A Go must name the complete responsibility Bend removes, the exact supported integration mechanism, proof limits, replacement/removal path, and the first separately authorized production slice. Stop for user approval.

## Acceptance criteria

- The issue contains an exact, reproducible proof record for every required law and at least the six named negative mutations.
- Bend is the only transition-policy implementation in the experiment; any Rust or JavaScript is a transport/test adapter and contains no reconstructed lifecycle decisions.
- The result demonstrates a supported integration boundary or records the exact missing Bend capability. Generated private C internals and a compiler fork do not count as supported integration.
- The comparison records complete owned LOC and toolchain/runtime closure for Bend, adapters, packaging, tests, and the smallest credible Rust alternative.
- Failure observation demonstrates that Bend unavailability or malformed output cannot launch, stop, accept, or relabel work and cannot terminate existing Sessions.
- The conclusion distinguishes proof of the pure reducer from unproved compiler, runtime, adapter, transport, persistence, and effect behavior.
- No production source, dependency, manifest, contract, profile, running supervisor, or live Session changes.
- The user receives the Go, Defer, or No-Go evidence before any production Bead is created.

## Verification

- `BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun <exact-bend>/bend2/main.ts <experiment>/PROOF.bend` exits 0 and prints `All terms check.`
- Each named mutated candidate exits nonzero at its intended law rather than at an unrelated parse or type error.
- The JavaScript export and native one-shot boundary produce byte-for-byte deterministic results for the same bounded trace corpus.
- A killed, missing, timed-out, or malformed boundary produces no effect intents and leaves the previous state usable in the harness.
- `git -C /home/lucca/pjs/eon/eon diff --check` exits 0; product changes remain exactly the pre-existing user-owned dirty paths plus Beads planning state.
- `br show <this-id> --json`, `br dep list <this-id> --json`, and `br sync --flush-only` confirm the decision record, parent relationship, and exported planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the pure reducer or a required proof needs `@unsafe`, foreign code, IO, floating-point reasoning, or unchecked termination.
- Stop if Rust or JavaScript must reproduce transition policy, state invariants, or provider semantics to use the result.
- Stop if production use requires patching Bend, depending on generated private C symbols, or adding a second handwritten Eon schema.
- Stop if Bend failure cannot be isolated from existing Sessions and ordinary workspace operation.
- Stop if the experiment changes an EON contract, production code, Nix composition, active profile, or running supervisor.
- Stop if evidence implies autonomous scheduling, provider compatibility, durable-work completion, or UI scope not explicitly chosen by the user.

## Maintenance notes

This is the only Bead created for the Bend AgentRun idea. Do not create speculative implementation children. The existing workspace reducer is the runner-up candidate, but it remains rejected for the first adoption because it is already proved, effect-coupled, and latency-sensitive. Component validation is rejected as insufficient payoff; EONW, Orbit, and Venus are rejected because byte/OS/F32/native boundaries dominate the proofable core.

- Zeron: the state authority is independent of views; actions are explicit and effect outcomes remain host-owned; pending/unknown remains visible.

- EONW, Orbit, or Venus ownership: byte, OS, F32, and native boundaries dominate their responsibilities.
- Generated C internals or a Bend fork: unsupported integration surface.
- Provider-specific lifecycle meanings, autonomous scheduling, durable persistence, and UI scope: no user decision authorizes them.

Minimum code shape:
- Separate execution, provider-semantic, attention, and explicit outcome fields.
- Opaque identity wrappers for work, run, attempt, provider session, Orbit session, and process.
- Monotonic event sequence admission for bounded replay protection.
- At most one effect intent and one bounded rejection reason.
- Rust/JS may only transport values, serialize results, enforce timeout/fail-closed behavior, and execute already-authorized effects; they may not reconstruct policy.

Cheapest falsifiers: one Bend proof module, six law-specific mutations, identical fixed-corpus output through the documented JS import path and native whole-program path, and a fail-closed adapter harness.

comments.text:
## Decision: DEFER

Do not put Bend in Eon production at Bend 2.0.5. Reconsider only when Bend ships a supported, versioned native embedding target for pure definitions with generated typed C/Rust bindings on x86_64 Linux and aarch64 macOS. That capability must remove both the Bun sidecar and a second handwritten transport schema; generated private C symbols, foreign IO, or a compiler fork do not qualify.

The pure AgentRun transition kernel remains the right responsibility to test if that capability appears. The experiment validated that the boundary is coherent and proof-friendly; it did not validate a supportable way for Rust Eon to own and call it.

### Contract and ownership tested

Input: current provider-neutral AgentRun state plus one sequenced user action or source-labeled provider/process observation.

Result: either an applied next state, one bounded effect intent, and one bounded view; or a rejection carrying no state and no effect. The caller retains its prior state on rejection.

Bend alone owns execution/semantic/attention/outcome transitions, six distinct identity roles, freshness admission, terminality, replay admission, effect authorization, and projection. Adapters only transport and validate values, enforce timeouts, and execute returned effects. Beads, Orbit, Venus, provider adapters, persistence, and operating-system effects remain outside.

The model deliberately does not add scheduling, provider-specific completion, an at-most-one-active-attempt product rule, persistence, or UI policy.

### Reference and source identities

- Eon `edge`: `3103a00a904c347472899549ce611da765a71650`.
- Eon `AGENTS.md` blob: `dd472623face19ed56042be93148305dd6826f5e`.
- Bend 2.0.5: commit `38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7`.
- Bend release archive SHA-256: `4db70e77ce1b1027f1d0e15dee025921fa794a9b415add4350ec7c64acf2775b`.
- Bend license: Apache-2.0; license SHA-256 `0beb288abd3d067e231f3fbe7df1f8ee37344061fc67f22018150a19e4b26c35`.
- Exact primary-reference content hashes and adopted/rejected mechanisms are in the preceding Reference gate comment.

### Proof result

Environment: Linux 7.1.5 x86_64; Intel Core i5-13450HX, 16 logical CPUs; Bun 1.3.13; Ubuntu clang 18.1.3; rustc 1.96.0.

Exact command:

```text
BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun /tmp/orb-bend-1re.TQSeSK/release/bend2/main.ts <experiment>/PROOF.bend
```

Result: exit 0, `All terms check.`, wall 0.12 s, peak RSS 124756 KiB.

Law coverage:

1. `distinct_identities_survive_start`, plus wrong-attempt/provider/process rejection.
2. `process_exit_is_not_success` and `weak_signal_is_not_success` over terminal detach, output growth, silence, and provider-session end.
3. `stale_evidence_is_rejected` and `uncertain_evidence_is_rejected`.
4. `replay_is_rejected` and `focus_replay_cannot_repeat_effect`.
5. `terminal_attempt_cannot_resume` and `fresh_retry_starts`.
6. Exact launch, notification, acceptance, stop, and focus laws, plus invalid acceptance and wrong-sequence rejection. Source inspection confirms those are the only five effect-constructor sites.
7. `effect_output_is_bounded` is universal over `Decision`; state, evidence, reason, view, and effect are finite products/enums with no retained collection. The only counter is one `Nat`; Bend documents a runtime abort beyond `2^48-1`, so this proof does not establish runtime behavior at that compiler limit.
8. `rejection_retains_prior_state` is universal over state and reason; `Denied` has no replacement-state or effect field.

Positive cases cover start, working activity, needs input, review handoff, explicit acceptance, explicit rejection, explicit failure, abort, fresh retry, and unresolved process exit.

Model/law/proof source hashes:

- `model.bend` (759 lines): `5ed4c1a5f17083125ce98b2b9d1a036b695bc8428d1e2b62474c436fdc413ffa`
- `LAWS.bend` (97 lines): `dad52855d0137de5482f9e068e2b777b7774839357b2d2b289945eae3f14c709`
- `PROOF.bend` (99 lines): `de6e03841622d3fb32592913bd08ba8a2a58144f1982de31549953edc6d5c807`

No proof-bearing Bend file contains `@unsafe`, foreign imports, IO, or floating point.

### Mutation result

`run-mutations.ts` SHA-256: `5e85744cc81dbf077ac1bfcdef6ed0e937d7ae380d4f6d1089d09f18edb76dac`.

All six type-correct mutations exited 1 at the intended law rather than parsing, typing, or an unrelated law:

| Mutation | Intended failing law |
| --- | --- |
| Identity confusion | `distinct_identities_survive_start` |
| Stale evidence promotion | `stale_evidence_is_rejected` |
| Process exit as success | `process_exit_is_not_success` |
| Duplicate focus effect on replay | `focus_replay_cannot_repeat_effect` |
| Terminal attempt revival | `terminal_attempt_cannot_resume` |
| Unauthorized acceptance effect | `acceptance_without_review_is_rejected` |

Combined mutation run: wall 0.73 s, peak RSS 127744 KiB. The retained `final.log` in the proof archive contains every exact diagnostic.

### Integration and failure evidence

The documented JavaScript loader and native whole-program output produced byte-for-byte identical output for the same 12-case corpus. Two runs of each surface were also byte-identical.

Fixed workload measurements on the environment above:

- Pure JS-export transition: 10 rounds x 200000 calls; 351.35 ns minimum, 359.44 ns median, 426.81 ns p95/max.
- JS loader cold process: 20 samples; 134.72 ms minimum, 140.08 ms median, 145.20 ms p95, 145.25 ms maximum.
- Native fixed-corpus process: 20 samples; 0.66 ms minimum, 0.76 ms median, 1.11 ms p95, 1.86 ms maximum.
- Native build: 6.69 s, 165000 KiB peak RSS.
- Minimum Rust alternative: five 2,000,000-transition runs observed 14.85–16.21 ns/transition; final rustc build 0.19 s and 113180 KiB peak RSS.

The native Bend artifact was a 64656-byte x86_64 ELF depending on libc and libm. `nm -g --defined-only` exposed `main` but no supported callable transition symbol. Passing a dynamic input argument exited 1 with `bend: unknown option dynamic-input`. Therefore the fast native number applies only to a closed, compile-time corpus; using it for real transitions would require foreign IO, private generated symbols, source generation plus a 6.69 s rebuild, or a Bend change. All are rejected.

The supported JS path works dynamically but requires the 101818016-byte Bun executable, a 136 MiB Nix runtime closure, Bend source/compiler loading, and plain-object constructor knowledge on both sides. The experiment needed handwritten input and output shapes. A Rust product would therefore need a Bun service/subprocess plus a second schema and lifecycle/packaging work. A long-lived service could amortize 140 ms startup but would create exactly the new component, protocol, and operations surface excluded by this decision slice; it would not remove the duplicate schema.

The fail-closed harness exercised a valid response and then missing loader, killed process, 100 ms timeout, and malformed output. Every failure retained the exact prior-state object, exposed zero effects, and left an independently running sentinel process alive. The three pre-existing Eon processes remained the same PIDs before and after (`5765`, `1746157`, `2181496`); no live supervisor or Session was stopped or restarted.

### LOC and closure comparison

Complete disposable experiment LOC:

- Bend policy model: 759.
- Bend laws and proofs: 196.
- Bend native wrapper: 5.
- JS transport, mutation, failure, and measurement code: 208.
- Reproduction runner: 24.
- Total Bend path investigation: 1192.
- Minimum complete Rust reducer plus self-check/benchmark: 189, standard library only.

The Bend 2.0.5 release subset used by the experiment was 73 files, 477107 bytes (720 KiB allocated). The JS runtime adds the 136 MiB Bun closure. Native runtime closure is small, but there is no supported dynamic native boundary. Production Nix/service/protocol LOC is zero because it was not authorized or implemented; that makes the current JS path incomplete rather than cheap. Rust uses Eon's accepted language/toolchain and adds no product runtime, protocol, component, package, or schema.

Current nixpkgs evaluation exposes Bun 1.3.13 for aarch64-darwin, and Bend source contains Apple compile branches. This establishes plausibility only. No Apple Silicon build or behavior proof ran, so macOS feasibility remains unproved and no Eon platform claim changes.

### Proof boundary and rejected alternatives

The proof covers equations in the pure Bend source. It does not prove the Bend parser, checker, compiler, generated JS/C runtime, JavaScript adapter, JSON transport, persistence, effect executor, provider interpretation, Bun, clang, Nix packaging, or platform behavior. Bend documents a young unaudited compiler and a runtime abort beyond `2^48-1` for `Nat`; those remain trusted/runtime concerns.

Rejected now:

- No-adapter native embedding: no supported ABI exists.
- Generated C internals: private and only `main` is public in the probe.
- Native foreign IO: leaves the proof-bearing core and adds host code in both JS and C.
- JavaScript sidecar: fails net-complexity, duplicate-schema, component, and runtime-closure gates.
- Long-lived service: startup may improve, but ownership and protocol costs remain and scope does not authorize it.
- Existing Rust plus Bend duplicate reducer: violates one-owner policy.
- Bend rewrite of the accepted Eon workspace reducer: greater coupling and less proof payoff.

The proof value is real, but at this responsibility size the 759-line affine Bend model and 196-line proof surface do not remove enough Rust/product responsibility to justify the current integration cost. Ponytail's minimum-sufficient bias materially favors the 189-line existing-toolchain Rust owner until Bend can remove an entire runtime boundary rather than add one.

### Reproduction

After reconstructing the attached proof archive and the exact Bend 2.0.5 release tree:

```text
bash <experiment>/run-all.sh <bend-release>/bend2/main.ts
```

The final unchanged-candidate run exited 0. It includes proof, all mutations, JS/native byte comparison and repeatability, performance samples, failure containment, native dynamic-input rejection, and the Rust comparison.

Phase: decision implemented and mechanically verified. This is not Eon runtime dogfood, platform acceptance, or promotion. No EON contract, production source, dependency, manifest, Nix profile, supervisor, or live Session changed. No implementation Bead was created. Parent `eon-pxn` remains deferred.

title: Decide whether Eon should offer declarative source/preview/action pickers
description:
## Question
Should Eon offer user-declared pickers, each defined by a source, a preview and an action? This is the core idea of Television "channels" (https://github.com/alexpasmantier/television, MIT; inspected main 4257bf10, 2026-10-15). A channel is one TOML file: `[source]` commands produce entries, `[preview]` renders the selected entry, and `[actions]` run templated commands (`{}` = selection) in execute or fork mode, plus keybindings and UI options. tv ships 103 community channels (files, git, docker, k8s, zoxide, tmux/sesh sessions, shell histories).

Origin: Nova rejected adopting Television (`yazelix-evaluate-channels-television-45q5-tor`, 2026-10-17) because Nova's menu is a curated allowlist and its history, completion and directory pickers already have owners. Declarative pickers were the one idea Nova lacked; the maintainer asked to track it for Eon.

## Contract (proposed, unapproved)
A user declares a picker in Eon product configuration (source, optional preview, action) and opens it on a workspace surface. Selecting an entry runs the declared action in the intended workspace/tab/pane context; Escape dismisses it without leaking keystrokes into a terminal. Failed sources, previews and actions are reported honestly. This is a decision bead: it does not authorize a contract, configuration schema or implementation.

## Decide
1. User problem: name two or three concrete pickers the maintainer would use daily that no existing owner covers (for example Orbit sessions, git branches, agent sessions). Without a named problem, reject.
2. Shape, cheapest first:
   - (a) No Eon code: run a host `tv` (or fzf) in an existing configured popup (Eon Runtime `managed_environment.rs` popups).
   - (b) Package `tv` as an optional tool and ship a few Eon-specific channels.
   - (c) Native Venus picker surface with a declarative Eon configuration schema.
3. Ownership: for (c), Eon owns the configuration schema and defaults, Venus owns presentation, search, keyboard/focus and accessibility, and Eon Runtime owns action dispatch and validation. Actions must not become a second command-semantics owner or a way around confirmations.
4. Relation to `eon-command-runner-uctp`: that bead's runner is explicitly not an arbitrary shell runner or plugin system. Decide whether pickers stay separate, or whether a later runner slice could host picker entries, without widening uctp's first slice.

## Reference gate
Before choosing (b) or (c): read Eon, Venus and Runtime instructions, contracts and `docs/REFERENCES.md`; inspect Television's channel spec (`docs/reference/03-channel-spec.md`) and one more comparable implementation (fzf/skim with a preview command, or a native launcher such as Raycast/Walker scripts). Record inspected revisions, kept constraints, rejected approaches and the cheapest falsifying check. For (b), apply the dependency gate (tv is in nixpkgs as `television` 0.15.9; a single main maintainer).

## Acceptance
- Record the named user problems, or a reject because none exist.
- Record the chosen shape (a, b, c or reject) with reasons and the rejected alternatives.
- For any adopt: propose the contract and its owners, and get user approval before a separate implementation bead and any `EON-C`/`VEN-C` contract are created.

## Scope boundary
Research and decision only. No new configuration fields, packages, Venus surfaces, protocol changes or contracts from this bead. Not a plugin system and not a replacement for the command runner or the Shortcuts viewer. Portability: neutral unless (c) adds platform-specific UI.

title: Qualify and publish the Nix-only Linux public alpha
description:
## Why

Eon has a strong accepted internal Linux alpha, but no single issue owns the transition to a public, credential-free, honestly scoped release. The release must accept the core user workflow on one exact graph and preserve explicit limits; it must not wait for macOS or direct bundles.

Contract: an unauthenticated x86_64 Linux user on native Wayland installs the Nix release candidate, starts useful work, discovers shortcuts, closes the native window while Sessions continue, reconnects, exercises tab and pane directories and runtime generations, diagnoses exact versions, and can stop the intended generation without hidden data loss. Unsupported targets and unproved recovery remain explicit.

## Evidence

- Baseline `18f1874`: `README.md:13-27` describes the current Nix-only x86_64 Linux native Wayland alpha and its unsupported platform/lifecycle boundaries.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:519-521`, `883-885`, `1046-1048`, and `1129-1131` leave EON-C8 workspace, EON-C11 generations, EON-C15 same-boot recovery, and EON-C17 tab directory at Candidate despite useful implementation proof.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md:492-494` leaves combined Linux and Apple Silicon platform contract EON-C7 Planned; a Linux release must state its proved half without implying macOS support.
- `docs/DISTRIBUTION.md:203-215` records the Nix alpha acceptance surfaces.
- `docs/DISTRIBUTION.md:47-59` correctly reserves direct distribution for later sustained dogfood and maintenance readiness.
- `eon-prove-full-eon-apple-silicon-macos-t8o` owns the separate Apple Silicon proof.

Impact: CRITICAL release confidence and product clarity. Effort: L. Risk: MED because acceptance may expose child or lifecycle defects. Confidence: HIGH.

## Prerequisites

- `eon-simplify-new-user-docs-2ah` provides the concise, accurate public entry path.
- `eon-credential-free-nix-alpha-9mh` provides the exact credential-free source graph.
- Use exact accepted Orbit and Venus revisions. Warn and stop if manifest pins are stale.

## Scope

In scope:
- One immutable Nix-source public-alpha candidate for x86_64 Linux on native Wayland.
- Exact installed qualification of EON-C8, EON-C11, EON-C15, and EON-C17; promote each only from current-candidate evidence accepted on the release revision, otherwise narrow the release claim or route a concrete defect.
- Precise Linux treatment of EON-C7 without claiming Apple Silicon, X11, Xwayland, other architectures, or non-systemd proof.
- Clean-user installation, first use, detach/reconnect, generation selection, workspace directories, shortcuts/help, diagnostics, explicit stop, failure reporting, known limitations, and release identity.
- A public issue-report path and one clean observation outside the development account or machine state.

Out of scope:
- Apple Silicon qualification, direct bundles, Home Manager, signing/notarization, auto-update, background service management, machine-restart persistence, live handoff, new features, agent semantics, or support for additional platforms.
- Treating compilation, documentation, or prior proof on another revision as release acceptance.

## Implementation Notes

1. Freeze one exact Eon, Orbit, Venus, manifest, lock, and Nix candidate. Compare child pins with their latest accepted revisions before any build.
2. Run the smallest complete installed workflow from a clean unauthenticated user context on native Wayland. Exercise the actual candidate rather than development binaries.
3. Reconcile EON-C8, EON-C11, EON-C15, and EON-C17 against the observations. Promote only accepted exact behavior; split defects only when concrete and release-relevant.
4. Keep the support matrix narrow. Full Apple Silicon work continues independently and does not block this Linux alpha.
5. Present the complete candidate evidence and known limitations to the user. Stop until the user explicitly approves public release/tag/announcement.
6. Publish one immutable source tag or equivalent canonical Nix reference; do not invent release automation for a single alpha.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --locked` exits 0 on the exact candidate.
- `nix flake check path:.` exits 0 for every declared Rust, manifest, package, and Nix check.
- `cargo run --locked -p eon-manifest -- components/eon-alpha-v3.json` exits 0 and matches `eon versions` from the installed candidate.
- In a clean unauthenticated native-Wayland user environment, install the immutable Nix candidate and dogfood first launch, F1 help, tab and pane work, directory selection, close/detach, `eon attach`, `eon generations`, failure diagnostics, and explicit `eon stop` without development checkout state or credentials.
- `rg -n "Status: (Candidate|Planned)|EON-C(7|8|11|15|17)" docs/CONTRACTS.md` shows every remaining non-Proven status is intentional and consistent with the public support claim.
- README support, install, first-use, limitations, issue-reporting, release identity, and LOC scorecard match the accepted artifact; `git diff --check` exits 0.

## Stop Conditions

- Stop before a public tag, release, or announcement without fresh explicit user approval of the exact candidate and limitations.
- Stop if a child pin is not an exact accepted revision, an input still needs credentials, or the installed artifact differs from the recorded graph.
- Stop if a candidate core contract cannot be accepted or honestly excluded from the advertised workflow; record the exact defect rather than paper-promoting it.
- Stop if publication requires direct-distribution machinery, a second graph, or widening the platform promise.

## Maintenance Notes

This is the Linux public-alpha gate. It intentionally does not block on Apple Silicon macOS. Sustained public Nix dogfood after acceptance becomes evidence for `eon-p93`, the separate direct-distribution graduation decision.

title: Qualify the Nix-free Linux install
description:
## Contract

A user without Nix can obtain the selected x86_64 Linux native-Wayland candidate, install it through the manual or installer path, perform the documented useful Eon workflow, preserve active work across upgrades and remove the owned installation safely. Nix and direct delivery consume the same canonical component graph. This issue owns the Go/No-Go recommendation for publishing the Nix-free install.

## Disposition

Deferred on 2026-10-11, resumed by Lucca on 2026-10-16. Under `eon-versioning-beta-bfyf` every
0.x release is beta, so this qualifies the Nix-free Linux install as a 0.x delivery milestone, not
a beta stage. No release, promotion, new feature or support expansion is authorized here.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

The user approved planning this sequence on 2026-10-07: lifecycle/delivery repairs, accepted Nix reliability, eon-p93 distribution graduation, eon-ohh direct Linux bundle and small installer, then wider beta. eon-ohh was accepted on 2026-10-11; its prerequisite chain includes accepted reliability and the graduation decision. That completed dependency does not override the current user-directed deferral. Read EON-C1 through C7 and the active workspace/lifecycle contracts, docs/DISTRIBUTION.md, actual install/upgrade/remove documentation and exact repair, reliability and bundle proofs. Select and record one immutable candidate, its graph, exact accepted child revisions, archive/installer identities and verification metadata.

## Acceptance

- On a clean non-Nix native-Wayland machine/user environment, manual extraction and the verified installer both deliver the exact graph without relying on a host Nix installation/store, development checkout state, local credentials or Nix services. Record the declared host prerequisites and supported environment.
- First launch, help, managed tools, tabs/panes and independent windows, representative configuration/child errors, detach/reopen, exact intended Stop and the separately documented EonTerm command path have current candidate proof. Reuse valid runtime proof and add only the distinct outermost delivery/onboarding observation needed.
- Direct upgrade and rollback preserve the original live work, keep retained generations usable under their accepted contracts and select the intended graph for new launches. Removal affects owned installation/integration only and preserves user configuration/data. Any payload still required by a live retained generation remains available or removal is staged; no silent active-work termination.
- Artifact verification, partial-install/upgrade failure and recovery behave as documented. Direct and supported Nix diagnostics report the same graph; Nix remains supported without making deferred Home Manager work a prerequisite.
- Record an explicit Go/No-Go, exact evidence and honest hardware/compositor/accessibility/provider/recovery limitations. Go requires accepted runtime and delivery proof with no unresolved installation/core-use or active-work-loss blocker. Material candidate changes invalidate the affected earlier proof.

## Scope boundary

This is qualification only. Public tags, release publication, announcements, channel promotion and any expansion of advertised support remain explicit user decisions on the concrete candidate. No auto-updater, new runtime feature, Home Manager, macOS, additional Linux architecture, X11/Xwayland or extra package format. This issue is planned and unclaimed.

Accepted p93/manual-bundle/installer/ohh development work remains closed and unpublished. Preserve qualification acceptance criteria for future use, but select a fresh exact candidate and revalidate material changes when resumed. No beta-readiness claim, release, promotion, new feature or support expansion is authorized.
Reopened by the user on 2026-10-16; the 2026-10-11 deferral disposition above is superseded.
