title: Expose phased bounded read-only terminal observation for Eon agents
description:
Contract routing:
- Requires a new user-approved observer contract and explicit ORB-C3 change before implementation; this planning epic reserves no permanent ORB-C ID.
- Requires an Eon-owned authorization and session-selection contract before product exposure.
- The minimum visible-state observer consumes already accepted live presentation and lifecycle authority. It does not require retained-history search or semantic command regions.
- Later enrichment may consume exact accepted history and semantic-region contracts without changing the minimum proof into a durable transcript.
- Planning changes no contract index or runtime behavior.

Why:
Agents need bounded authoritative terminal context without hijacking the interactive client, scraping pixels or turning Venus frames into a log. Orbit already owns the live screen, title, CWD, active screen, revision and session lifecycle. The previous all-or-nothing plan delayed even minimum observation behind advanced history and semantic work.

Phases:
1. Minimum observer: explicitly authorized local read-only queries for session and process lifecycle, current visible text projection, title, CWD, active screen and exact revision. Text is explicitly lossy.
2. Enrichment: bounded history and last authoritative semantic command or output only after their owner contracts are accepted.

Out of scope:
Synthetic input, mutating actions, process control, provider-status inference, durable transcripts, arbitrary shell execution, remote or MCP exposure, automatic secret redaction, raw PTY or ORBF access, multiple interactive clients and bypassing the owner loop.
design:
1. The user activated this epic for planning on 2026-08-19. Before any implementation child is claimed, select observation as the single frontier and approve the observer contract, scoped ORB-C3 change, Eon policy contract, and exact cross-repository update order.
2. At activation split this epic into an Eon authorization/security decision, minimum Orbit observer owner, Eon capability consumer, adversarial acceptance, and later enriched observer children. The enriched child alone depends on accepted history and semantic regions.
3. Required reference evidence for the minimum phase: exact accepted Orbit contracts; exact current Herdr socket/read and agent-observation mechanisms; VS Code Agent Host; one local agent-terminal observer such as Wave or Open Terminal; FrankenTerm lifecycle/security boundaries; and relevant local Unix credential APIs. References are not dependencies by implication.
4. Define a distinct observer role and handshake. It never claims the one interactive attachment, sends input or resize, receives raw terminal bytes or obtains process-control authority.
5. Orbit owns the bounded projection and attaches session identity, revision, projection kind, source and lossy labeling. It exposes semantic or history values only from later accepted owner contracts.
6. Eon owns user consent, AgentRun and session selection, capability issuance, expiry and revocation. Orbit enforces the chosen local capability at its boundary.
7. Bound observers, queries, rows, bytes, response time, retained storage, cancellation and rate. Observer pressure cannot delay PTY mutation, presentation or cleanup.
8. Prove denial, expiry, revocation and pressure before product integration. Prefer the existing local transport/codec and standard library; any new auth, serialization, async or capability dependency requires the crate gate.
9. Keep Eon mutating actions in astra-db8.9. MCP may later adapt an accepted capability surface but is not part of either observer phase.

Stop if authorization has no single owner, minimum observation weakens interactive semantics, sensitive content can be read without explicit capability, pressure affects the owner loop, or the design requires a durable log, remote server or generic plugin framework.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Planning activation is recorded. Before implementation, the user selects observation as the single frontier after the closed `orb-bi4.7` decision and completed initial `eon-pxn` workspace slice; the observer contract, scoped ORB-C3 change, Eon policy contract, and update order are approved and indexed first.
2. The minimum phase does not depend on history or semantic-region implementation. One interactive Venus client remains the only input-capable attachment.
3. Authorized minimum queries return bounded session identity, process or session lifecycle, title, CWD, active screen, exact revision and explicitly lossy current visible text.
4. Observers cannot send terminal input, resize, lifecycle or process-control actions and cannot receive raw PTY bytes, ORBF frames or hidden terminal internals.
5. Unauthorized, expired, revoked, malformed, oversized, stale and cancelled queries fail deterministically without revealing terminal content.
6. Observer count, outstanding work, rows, bytes, memory, time and rate are bounded; slow observers cannot disturb PTY processing, Venus or cleanup.
7. Deterministic checks cover concurrent interactive and observer access, authorization, expiry, revocation, revision consistency, disconnect, pressure, child exit and Orbit shutdown.
8. A separate Eon proof demonstrates explicit user-controlled AgentRun and session authorization against the exact Orbit revision.
9. Later enriched observation adds bounded history or semantic command/output only after their exact accepted contracts and cannot alter the minimum API into a transcript or guessed provider-state model.
10. Read-only observation remains separate from Eon mutating actions, provider integrations, MCP, plugins, remote transport and redaction claims.
11. Closure records security model, compatibility, dependency footprint, portability, LOC, exact proofs, pressure measurements and excluded control or remote scope.
notes:
Priority P1 among future Orbit directions because agents are strategically central to Eon. The minimum observer no longer depends on orb-3gf. Later semantic enrichment remains conceptually gated by orb-3gf and history but does not block the first useful read-only slice.

Rejected alternatives: screen capture or OCR as authority, handing agents Venus frames, an always-on transcript database, unpermissioned local reads, synthetic keystrokes, output scraping as provider status, general remote or MCP exposure and claims of automatic secret redaction.

Planning estimate remains large for the complete epic because authorization, sensitive data and pressure are high risk. Splitting minimum and enriched phases prevents those risks from forcing advanced semantics into the first slice.

No child Beads are created until this frontier is explicitly activated.

Agent-driven terminal-testing comparison evidence — 2026-08-13:
- Eon decision `eon-pxn.7` owns whether Eon ships any testing component. This Orbit epic remains a bounded read-only observer and does not gain input, pixels, tape semantics, or another interactive-client role.
- qwertty `829539399b4dcfd95f85758a285f5200f1bc711c` is comparison-only evidence for app-side terminal ownership, semantic events, capability evidence, and policy gates. It is not a proposed Orbit dependency.

Reject their PTY and terminal-emulator ownership inside Eon because Orbit already owns both.
- Any exclusive headless input-capable client, new concurrent client role, image path, or harness remains separately user-approved contract and implementation scope.

Readiness reconciliation (2026-08-21): this epic remains a deferred planning container. The Venus lifecycle remediation frontier is complete; activate only when the user selects bounded observation as the next frontier, approves its authorization contract, and creates one non-epic first slice.
2026-10-15 (prime-beads): `astra-db8.9` in Design step 9 is a pre-consolidation ID. Agent terminal input is now planned in `eon-agent-terminal-control-n8ic`, which depends on this epic for observer identity, authorization and the Eon policy contract.

title: Provide permanent SSH terminal access to Eon sessions
description:
## Outcome

Let a user reach a live Eon session from any ordinary SSH terminal, including a phone, without installing an Eon-specific mobile app. The user connects to a host through its existing SSH service, invokes a stable Eon command, selects or names a live session through Eon-owned identities, attaches one terminal projection, detaches, and later reconnects to the same Orbit-owned process and terminal state.

This is a permanent recovery and universal-access surface, not disposable scaffolding for native mobile.

## Contract routing

- This deferred epic is a planning container. It changes no ORB-C, EON-C, or VEN-C contract, reserves no contract ID, and authorizes no code, dependency, package, listener, compatibility promise, or public release.
- At activation, first compare consumption of the exact accepted local Orbit contracts with the smallest explicit contract addition. Approve and index any new user-visible Orbit or Eon behavior before creating implementation children.
- Preserve Orbit as the sole PTY, terminal-state, viewport, selection, copy-text, effect, and terminal-query authority. Preserve Eon as workspace/session identity, selection policy, command, composition, and distribution owner.
- Preserve the accepted one-active-client rule. SSH access does not authorize multiplayer, observation beside Venus, session stealing, or a compatibility window.

## Boundary

The intended minimal flow is:

phone or terminal SSH client -> host sshd -> Eon terminal client on that host -> local Orbit socket -> Orbit PTY and terminal authority

The host SSH implementation owns network authentication, encryption, keys, reachability, and SSH failure semantics. Eon and Orbit do not open a remote listener or invent an authentication protocol for this slice.

The terminal client consumes the canonical Orbit protocol and may produce an explicitly lossy ANSI/terminal projection. It never parses raw PTY bytes, instantiates a second terminal emulator, answers terminal queries, or reconstructs hidden terminal state. It sends semantic input and resize requests back to Orbit.

The Eon client may decode the controlling terminal's input and capabilities and retain only ephemeral draw state. That outer-terminal adapter is not an emulator for the Orbit-owned child terminal. It must enter a known presentation state and restore raw mode, cursor visibility, mouse/focus/paste modes, and any alternate-screen choice on every normal, error, signal, or connection-loss exit.

## Deliberate limits

- No native touch UI, mobile notifications, native clipboard integration, browser client, remote workspace provisioning, file synchronization, port exposure, relay, multiplayer, or Orbit restart persistence.
- No second Eon topology owner or terminal layout engine. Reuse Eon's accepted workspace/session identities and actions; start with explicit session selection rather than inventing a full terminal workspace shell.
- Rich graphics and native effects are capability-gated. A terminal projection must state what it cannot faithfully represent and cannot claim ORB-C6 rich-presentation fidelity.
- SSH access and native mobile are independent product surfaces. Neither blocks nor replaces the other.
- The first slice targets the accepted full-Eon workspace/session owner. It does not redefine EonTerm, replace Venus inside EonTerm, or promise remote EonTerm product behavior.

## Success Criteria

- An ordinary desktop or phone SSH client can reach one selected live Eon session through the host's existing sshd and later reconnect to the same Orbit-owned process.
- The permanent fallback adds no remote Orbit listener, bespoke authentication, second terminal authority, multiplayer, or hidden fidelity claim.
- The accepted slice remains small enough to ship and maintain independently of native mobile.
design:
## Activation shape

Do not implement this epic directly. When the user activates it, create repository-owned children in this order:

1. Contract and reference decision: define the exact Eon command, target identity, TTY requirement, attach/detach result, Busy behavior, capability report, and failure taxonomy. Required evidence includes current EON-C8/EON-C10 workspace ownership and actions; current ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 and canonical protocol proofs; official OpenSSH client/server, PTY-allocation, authentication, and connection-loss behavior; exact current Herdr mobile-over-SSH workflow; Qwertty raw-mode restoration, query correlation, and typed-input mechanisms; the current Orbit diagnostic client as validation-only evidence; and exact zmx SSH behavior for comparison. Mosh is conditional only if measured reconnect or lossy-link behavior requires state-synchronization evidence. Reject broader multiplexer, raw-tail, multiplayer, remote-workspace, and session-management scope.
2. Orbit boundary check: prove whether the existing canonical local protocol is sufficient for a terminal projection. Any protocol or owner change is a separate Orbit child and precedes consumers.
3. Eon terminal-client implementation: consume exact accepted Orbit contracts, use Eon-owned workspace/session identities and existing actions, and render one bounded terminal projection with explicit capabilities.
4. Eon package/command integration: expose the stable command through the existing Eon composition graph without installing or configuring sshd.
5. Acceptance: dogfood from at least one desktop SSH terminal and one phone SSH terminal through detach, reconnect, resize, network loss, Busy rejection, session exit, and cleanup.

## Smallest-first rule

Prefer the host's existing SSH service and the existing local Orbit socket. Do not add an SSH library, daemon, remote Orbit listener, relay, terminal UI framework, or new network protocol unless an independently proved contract gap requires it and the applicable dependency/security gate passes. Do not promote Orbit's stdin-line diagnostic client into a product client by default; it is a validation consumer and does not own interactive terminal presentation.

Use the existing Eon CLI for deterministic list/select behavior before building compact terminal navigation. Add responsive terminal chrome only if dogfood proves command-level selection insufficient.

## Security and failure ownership

- sshd authenticates the remote user and establishes the host account boundary.
- Eon authorizes which of that account's workspaces/sessions may be selected.
- Orbit enforces attachment negotiation, one-client exclusion, bounds, semantic input, and PTY/session lifecycle.
- The Eon terminal adapter owns only the outer controlling TTY's capability discovery, bounded split-sequence input decoding, ephemeral draw state, resize observation, and unconditional terminal-mode cleanup. It never becomes child-terminal authority.
- Define interruption, SSH loss, client crash, stale endpoint, Busy, incompatible protocol, terminal exit, host shutdown, and abandoned client cleanup without killing the Orbit session on mere client loss.

Portability disposition is neutral above the host SSH and existing local-platform seams. Each activated child must record its own exact Linux/macOS proof limits.
acceptance_criteria:

title: Prove a macOS-credible platform seam
description: Before the structured-presentation proof, preserve the accepted Linux-first scope while proving that PTY, process, signal, polling, socket-path, permission, and platform-specific EOF behavior do not shape Orbit core ownership or cross-repository contracts. This is a portability-seam audit and the smallest justified isolation work, not a macOS implementation or support promise.
design:
Start from the accepted Linux candidate and preserve ORB-C1, ORB-C2, ORB-C3, and ORB-C5 behavior. Inventory every OS-dependent operation before choosing code shape: PTY creation and controlling-terminal setup, child process groups and termination, nonblocking reads and final-output EOF semantics, polling, file-descriptor flags, resize ioctls, signals, user identity, runtime directories, Unix-socket permissions, and stale-socket cleanup. Inspect the exact libc Linux and Apple target definitions plus recorded official Darwin or macOS documentation. Keep terminal authority, semantic input, diagnostic or presentation messages, revision semantics, and future durable state outside the platform boundary. Prefer one small concrete platform seam; do not build a generic backend framework or trait hierarchy for a second implementation that does not exist. Do not implement or claim macOS build, runtime, CI, packaging, or support. If isolation requires a new dependency, material ownership change, or surprising LOC increase, pass the Crate gate and stop for user choice before implementation.

If the inventory shows that the current concrete functions already isolate these semantics, an evidence-only closure with no production refactor is preferable to moving code merely to create a platform module.
acceptance_criteria:
1. An Execution baseline and pre-implementation Reference gate route ORB-C1, ORB-C2, ORB-C3, and ORB-C5 as preserved or hardened; the Bead creates no macOS behavior contract.
2. The audit maps every current Linux-specific PTY, process, signal, poll, file-descriptor, socket-path, permission, and EOF or error assumption to its owner, core leakage risk, and credible Darwin or macOS replacement shape.
3. Terminal authority, semantic input, client messages, presentation framing and revisions, and future durable state contain no Linux-only value or semantic assumption.
4. OS-specific mechanics remain behind one narrow concrete seam with the smallest justified code shape. No generic portability framework, speculative trait hierarchy, second backend, compatibility layer, or unrelated module split is introduced.
5. Existing Linux unit and subprocess contract checks remain green and prove unchanged ORB-C1, ORB-C2, ORB-C3, and ORB-C5 behavior after any isolation work.
6. The result records an evidence-backed macOS implementation estimate, remaining blockers, and one portability disposition: neutral, isolated platform dependency, or macOS blocker. It does not claim a macOS build or supported platform.
7. Any dependency or feature change passes the Crate gate before manifest edits and updates docs/CRATES.md with Linux and macOS consequences. Using the existing direct libc shape is also recorded explicitly.
8. A material blocker that would shape the core, cross-repository protocol, durable format, ownership model, or require significant LOC stops for explicit user choice.
9. CHANGELOG.md receives no entry for architecture-only isolation. Any unexpectedly changed accepted user- or consumer-visible behavior is recorded under Unreleased with affected contract IDs and proof revision.
10. Closure evidence records exact sources, ownership and code shape, rejected alternatives, checks, owned LOC, dependency footprint, portability disposition, limitations, and verification commands.
11. If production, test, or manifest changes touch a proved contract owner or implementation surface, closure reruns the indexed canonical checks and advances ORB-C1, ORB-C2, ORB-C3, and ORB-C5 to the exact accepted proof-bearing commit, or downgrades each affected contract with its gap. An inventory-only result explicitly retains the existing proof revision and does not claim that audit consumption refreshed it.
notes: Accepted proof revision 2b1a8e3ba4a256c3bdb1018c6dc48a8b089193e0. One concrete src/platform.rs owner around direct libc 0.2.189 encapsulates PTY creation and normalized I/O closure, controlling-terminal and process-group lifecycle, resize and descriptor flags, raw polling and neutral readiness conversion, signals, socket paths, permissions, stale cleanup, and socket identity. src/main.rs retains terminal authority, semantic input, protocol, and processing order without libc or poll-descriptor concepts. Rejected for this proof: generic traits or backends, a second implementation, portable-pty, nix or rustix replacement, Ghostty application or thread architecture, dependency changes, macOS implementation or CI, and protocol changes. Canonical checks passed on the proof revision: cargo fmt --check; cargo check --locked; cargo test --locked (13); cargo clippy --locked --all-targets -- -D warnings; git diff --check. Owned Rust is 1,554 lines, +68 from the pre-bead baseline: main 579, platform 336, tests 639. Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock are unchanged. A post-candidate pty-process 0.5.3 scratch build passed the same checks and reduced owned Rust by 44 lines while adding pty-process, rustix, and linux-raw-sys to the normal Linux graph; it remains a credible separate user-approved crate decision, not part of this proof. Portability disposition: isolated platform dependency. A future user-authorized macOS slice is estimated at 0.5 to 1 day and must remove the Linux crate cfg, settle Apple libc compile details, and prove Darwin PTY, process, signal, poll, socket, and cleanup behavior. No macOS behavior is claimed.

title: Decide whether Orbit needs its custom governance compiler
description:
## Contract routing

This is a planning-only repository-governance decision. It changes no ORB product contract, runtime behavior, dependency graph, CI workflow, or repository file. Any chosen implementation requires a separately authorized implementation Bead.

Consumer: Orbit maintainers and agents relying on machine-checked repository planning and proof metadata.

Trigger: compare the custom `orbit-governance` compiler with the current capabilities and actual use of `br`, Starcompass, Cargo checks, and review.

Result: record one evidence-backed decision—retain, shrink, replace, or delete—with one owner for every invariant that remains required and no silent loss of a governance safeguard.

Important failures: do not equate non-runtime code with no value; do not delete validation merely because another tool has a similar name; do not retain duplicate validation without identifying the unique invariant it protects.

## Why

`tools/governance/src/main.rs` is 765 Rust lines plus a dedicated package and two direct dependencies. It parses contract Markdown, Beads JSONL, and crate-decision tables, then enforces Orbit-specific planning and proof conventions in CI. Much of that may overlap `br`, Starcompass, Cargo, or human review, but the overlap has not been mapped invariant by invariant.

Impact: MED. Investigation effort: S. Decision risk: MED. Confidence in excess-cost hypothesis: HIGH.

## Evidence

- `tools/governance/src/main.rs:1-559`: owned parsers and checks for contract tables, Beads records, closure evidence, dependency decisions, and portability markers.
- `tools/governance/src/main.rs:603-765`: fixture machinery and tests for the custom checker.
- `tools/governance/Cargo.toml:8-10`: dedicated `serde` and `serde_json` dependencies.
- `Cargo.toml:7-9`: the governance package is a workspace member.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml:69-79`: CI compiles/tests the workspace, runs `orbit-governance`, and separately runs Starcompass.
- `README.md:271-305`: the repository documents the custom governance command and its claimed boundary.

## Prerequisites and reference gate

- Use exact current Orbit, `br`, and pinned Starcompass revisions; record them in this Bead.
- Read every check in `tools/governance/src/main.rs`, the governing AGENTS.md planning/proof/dependency rules, `br capabilities` and relevant `br robot-docs`, and the pinned Starcompass consumer-check behavior.
- For each enforced invariant, record whether `br`, Starcompass, Cargo, a cheap native check, or no automation already owns it. Demonstrate coverage from actual commands or source; do not infer it from tool names.
- Inspect CI frequency and, if cheap and reproducible, compare the isolated governance package's compile/test time and dependency graph with a baseline that omits it.

## Scope

In scope:
- `tools/governance/**`, its workspace membership and lockfile-only dependency cost.
- Its invocation and path filters in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.
- The repository metadata and invariant classes it reads.
- Existing `br`, Starcompass, Cargo, and review mechanisms that could own the same invariants.

Out of scope:
- Editing or deleting implementation, tests, docs, CI, Cargo files, or Beads other than recording this decision.
- Weakening product tests, trust-boundary validation, dependency review, proof integrity, or imported-protocol verification.
- Replacing the checker with a new custom framework or generalized policy engine.
- Changing ORB contracts or runtime behavior.

## Decision method

1. Build a complete table of every current `orbit-governance` failure condition, its reason, frequency/relevance, and present alternative owner.
2. Classify each check as uniquely valuable, duplicated, obsolete, or better enforced at a different existing boundary.
3. Compare four complete shapes: retain unchanged; shrink to unique Orbit invariants; replace entirely with existing tools/native checks; delete and rely on existing workflow.
4. Estimate resulting owned LOC, direct/transitive dependencies, CI work, documentation burden, false positives, and lost guarantees.
5. Select the first sufficient shape. Record meaningful rejected alternatives and the condition that would reverse the decision.
6. If change is selected, describe the smallest implementation slice and exact checks, but create no implementation Bead without separate user authorization.

## Acceptance

- Every current custom check is accounted for; no required invariant disappears implicitly.
- The record distinguishes product-contract proof from repository-process preference.
- The chosen decision names one owner and one cheapest falsifying check for every retained invariant.
- The decision includes measured or source-backed LOC, dependency, and CI consequences.
- Retain is acceptable only if unique value justifies the custom parser/compiler lifecycle.
- Shrink/delete is acceptable only if remaining owners demonstrably cover the required safeguards or the user explicitly retires them.
- The Bead records exact evidence, rejected alternatives, reversal conditions, and whether a later implementation Bead is warranted.

## Verification

- `cargo run --locked --quiet -p orbit-governance -- .` should establish the current checker baseline.
- `cargo tree --locked -p orbit-governance` should record its exact dependency surface.
- `br capabilities` and the relevant `br robot-docs` output should identify actual tracker-owned checks.
- The pinned Starcompass `check-consumer` command should establish only its exact imported-protocol coverage.
- `git diff --check` should exit 0; implementation files must remain unchanged.
- `br lint <this-id>` should report no issue for this Bead.
- `br sync --flush-only` should persist only authorized planning state.

## Stop conditions

- Stop if the exact checker or its governed schemas change during the investigation; record the new snapshot and restart the mapping.
- Stop if evaluating an alternative requires editing implementation or CI.
- Stop if a required safeguard has no surviving owner; report it rather than assuming manual review.
- Stop if the decision would change an ORB product contract or trust boundary.

## Maintenance notes

Prefer deletion only after the invariant table proves it safe. A smaller second custom checker is not a win unless it owns a concrete Orbit-only invariant that existing tools cannot enforce.

title: Replace mandatory cgroup shutdown with PTY lifecycle cleanup
description:
## Contract routing

Change ORB-C12. Preserve non-destructive detach in ORB-C1 and the owner-routed management authorization, identity, lease, and tombstone ordering in ORB-C13.

## Contract

- Consumer: Orbit launchers and users starting or stopping a Session.
- Trigger: PTY startup, accepted SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP, or an authorized management Stop.
- Result: startup needs only the selected Linux PTY/process APIs. If the direct child has already exited, Orbit reaps it without signaling a recyclable numeric identity. Otherwise Stop sends SIGHUP to the live initial PTY process group and current terminal foreground group and gives the child a bounded grace period. If the direct child remains unreaped, Orbit sends SIGKILL to its still-stable initial group and the then-current terminal foreground group. If the child exits during grace, Orbit sends no later signal to the cached foreground-group number. Orbit reaps the direct child before success.
- Important failures: Orbit returns non-success when its direct child cannot be reaped by the deadline. Deliberately detached jobs, non-foreground groups outside the initial group, and SIGHUP-ignoring foreground jobs whose shell exits during grace may survive. Orbit does not scan procfs, infer descendants, or claim whole-tree cleanup. Orbit must not signal a numeric process or group identity after it can refer to an unrelated target.

## Reference gate

Inspected the exact current shutdown owner/tests, pre-containment Orbit, POSIX.1-2024 terminal/process-group semantics and rationale, Linux kill/tcgetpgrp/pid allocation, Linux PTY TIOCSIG, Linux pidfd signaling, and zmx bounded terminal cleanup.

Adopted:

- remove cgroup creation, membership, verification, killing, CI delegation, and Eon Sessions documentation;
- retain the existing direct child, initial PTY group, terminal foreground group, 500 ms grace, two-second reap bound, and no-dependency platform seam;
- HUP the live initial and foreground groups, but perform forced group escalation only while the direct child remains unreaped;
- send no delayed SIGKILL to a cached foreground-group number after the direct child exits;
- keep client disconnect non-destructive and management authorization/tombstone ordering unchanged;
- state honestly which detached or HUP-ignoring jobs may survive.

The user selected this weaker safe cleanup on 2026-08-24. It preserves the existing Linux kernel boundary and removes the delayed cached-PGID reuse path after Orbit reaps the child.

Rejected: optional cgroups, procfs/SID tree scans, subreaping as discovery, service-manager APIs, namespaces, helper daemons, new crates, a Linux 6.9 minimum for PIDFD_SIGNAL_PROCESS_GROUP, and knowingly retaining the cached-PGID race.

## Scope

Orbit Linux PTY lifecycle owner, focused lifecycle proof, current Orbit contracts/docs, CI, and LOC scorecard. Eon consumer pinning and removal of the Eon cgroup launch gate are a separate owner-first run after an accepted Orbit revision.

No protocol, dependency, optional backend, process scan, service-manager integration, namespace, kernel-minimum change, or broader process-ownership promise.

## Acceptance criteria

- Ordinary Linux startup succeeds without a delegated writable cgroup.
- No delayed signal can target a recycled process or process-group identity.
- Focused lifecycle proof covers graceful direct-child HUP, safe forced escalation while the child remains unreaped, a SIGHUP-ignoring foreground survivor after shell exit, a deliberately detached survivor, unrelated-process preservation, and bounded direct-child reaping.
- No production, test, CI, or current Eon Sessions documentation cgroup requirement remains.
- Cargo formatting, check, workspace tests, governance, Starcompass consumer check, Clippy, diff, Beads graph, and LOC checks pass at one unchanged candidate.
- The accepted immutable Orbit revision precedes a separate Eon pin/preflight-removal/dogfood run.

## Stop conditions

Stop for a user decision before adding pidfds or a Linux 6.9 minimum, using procfs/tree discovery, adding a dependency/service-manager API/namespace, changing protocols, or making a broader ownership promise.

Fresh-eyes and simplification correction — 2026-08-24 America/Sao_Paulo

This supersedes the shutdown-ordering details and mechanical proof in candidate comment 718. The contract remains Partially proved and no proof-bearing commit exists.

Confirmed bug:
- The first candidate called Child::try_wait before signaling the child-derived process group. Rust 1.96 std::sys::process::unix records that try_wait reaps and caches the status; after that, the numeric PID can be recycled. A later negative-PID signal was therefore not safe.
- Final owner ordering returns immediately when the child had already exited, so no signal is derived from that recyclable identity. When shutdown begins with a live child, Orbit captures and HUPs the initial and foreground groups while the identity is stable. If the child remains unreaped after the grace deadline, Orbit KILLs the stable initial group and the then-current foreground group. If the child exits during grace, Orbit KILLs only the distinct foreground snapshot captured while the child identity was stable.

Rejected intermediate:
- Keeping the child unreaped for a fixed 500 ms made cooperative Stop take at least 500 ms and increased the lifecycle suite from 2.70 s to 14.47 s.

- The final conditional retains the distinct foreground snapshot only when the shell exits during grace; otherwise it re-reads the current foreground group. It avoids both the child-derived PID-reuse bug and the foreground survivor.

Simplification result:
- Removed the redundant positive-PID SIGKILL wrapper and its forwarding helper. The direct child is the leader and member of the initial PTY process group, so the group signal already owns escalation.
- Kept the two bounded wait loops explicit. A shared helper would change their deadline-check ordering or add parameters solely to preserve it, so it did not clear the isomorphism bar.
- Kept direct group calls rather than adding a collection/helper layer for two targets and two phases.

Reference correction and required decision — 2026-08-24 America/Sao_Paulo

This supersedes the foreground-PGID safety conclusion in comments 717–719; their measured candidate evidence remains valid only for ordinary non-reuse runs.

Confirmed contract gap:
- The corrected candidate avoids signaling an initial group derived from a reaped direct-child PID, but retains the distinct foreground PGID as a bare integer. If that group disappears during the 500 ms grace period, its number can later identify another group before kill(-pgid, SIGKILL).
- POSIX rationale explicitly identifies disappearance/reuse of a terminal foreground group as a race. Linux tcgetpgrp returns only a numeric PGID, kill resolves a negative number at signal time, and kernel free_pid removes an unused number from the allocator even while other struct-pid references may remain.
- The existing unrelated-sibling and 20-run lifecycle proofs do not force PGID reuse and therefore do not establish the no-unrelated-signal contract.

Native alternatives inspected:
- Current Linux PTY TIOCSIG safely dereferences the kernel-owned foreground-group object but accepts only SIGINT, SIGQUIT, and SIGTSTP, so it cannot provide SIGHUP/SIGKILL escalation.
- PIDFD_SIGNAL_PROCESS_GROUP provides race-free process-group signaling only from Linux 6.9 and requires a validated live process-group-leader pidfd. Adopting it changes the minimum kernel/capability boundary and needs focused acquisition/failure proof.
- Removing the delayed cached-foreground SIGKILL is smaller and portable across the existing Linux boundary, but an HUP-ignoring foreground job may survive after the direct shell exits.

Per the Bead's original stop condition, no source edit or widened proof was made. Required user choice: accept the weaker safe cleanup, approve a Linux 6.9 pidfd group-signaling boundary, or explicitly accept the numeric-PGID race (not recommended).

title: Preserve viewport scroll through synchronized output
description:
## Observable outcome

Consumer: one healthy exact-version Venus attachment using ORB-C8 preview and signed-scroll messages.

Trigger: a relative vertical preview or signed-scroll request arrives after DEC 2026 synchronized output begins and before its complete frame is released.

Result: Orbit retains at most the one unresolved vertical request already permitted by the client contract, continues parsing PTY output and ordered effects, publishes no partial frame, and resolves the request exactly once against current authoritative terminal state after DEC 2026 ends or the existing one-second watchdog releases it. Synchronized output delays scrolling; it does not fail or cancel the gesture.

Important failures: a future revision, malformed distance, output pressure, disconnect, or a second unresolved vertical request remains bounded and explicit. Terminal-owned routing is re-evaluated at release. No accepted request mutates twice or crosses to a later attachment.

## Prerequisites

ORB-C4 complete synchronized presentation, ORB-C7 bounded output admission, and ORB-C8 authoritative relative scrolling are already proved. Exact active product pins are Orbit a65e199e16e97330175e314cacf791fa00f53069 and Venus 7f325a31d0052d84a1a09ff065c0e9103563c0e8.

## Scope boundary

In scope: the smallest Orbit-owned pending lifecycle for ORB-C8 PreviewVertical and ScrollVertical, one Codex-shaped split DEC 2026 regression, current contract/reference/docs, exact consumer adoption, profile refresh, and installed Codex dogfood.

Out of scope: a new wire message or version, Venus retry policy, client-owned scrollback, raw physical-wheel protocol changes, PTY flow control, disabling synchronized output, frame pacing, selection behavior, dependencies, and platform expansion.
design:
## Reference gate and decision

Question: how can a split-process terminal preserve one user scroll intent without exposing a partially synchronized repaint or transferring terminal authority to Venus?

Inspected local baseline: clean Eon Sessions edge 651a0fcebccc981525fee291fd70562b5fa00bb9; accepted runtime source a65e199e16e97330175e314cacf791fa00f53069; ORB-C4, ORB-C7, ORB-C8; runtime PTY-before-client poll order; Presentation synchronized deadline and release; both ORB-C8 interaction handlers; bounded attachment output; exact active Venus 7f325a31d0052d84a1a09ff065c0e9103563c0e8 reset behavior.

Primary producer: OpenAI Codex 0d226929622ce177b56e35d09cf39dd001721466 uses crossterm SynchronizedUpdate around TUI rendering. Comparable owners: Alacritty ede2ac144da4dec4c075bfa803aacf3b3739bce6 applies scroll directly to its terminal grid; WezTerm 27d55bef144f34a73e23585302838a36ec3aa30e keeps stable row identity while history advances.

Adopt: keep the request in the existing Orbit presentation authority, bounded to one unresolved preview or signed commit, then feed it through the existing ORB-C8 handler after synchronized release. Re-evaluate authoritative routing at release and reuse the existing output admission and one-second watchdog.

Reject: client retry from a Terminal failure because it duplicates transient policy and can loop; a new Deferred wire outcome because no new information must cross the boundary; client history or screen freeze because Orbit remains sole terminal owner; PTY reordering because an already-open synchronized hold still races; PTY pausing or DEC 2026 disabling because each changes process or presentation semantics.

First falsifier: extend the existing real-PTY split DEC 2026 proof with a held signed-scroll request and require silence during the hold followed by one complete released frame and one exact scroll outcome. A focused interaction check covers held preview. No dependency or protocol version changes.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The unchanged baseline fails a deterministic Codex-shaped split DEC 2026 check because Orbit emits a Terminal failure for the held ORB-C8 request.
2. PreviewVertical and ScrollVertical received during synchronized output produce no immediate response or mutation, occupy at most one bounded pending slot, and do not block PTY parsing, terminal replies, ordered effects, semantic key input, or synchronized watchdog release.
3. Normal DEC 2026 end and the one-second watchdog each release the request exactly once against current authoritative routing. The response contains only a complete authoritative frame or preview and preserves ORB-C8 signed-distance, revision, edge, selection, and pressure rules.
4. Disconnect or client replacement clears pending client-owned intent. A second unresolved request fails explicitly without overwriting the first. Raw physical-wheel behavior and ORBS v10 bytes remain unchanged.
5. Focused red/green checks, affected canonical Rust verification, exact contract/reference/README and LOC checks pass. The exact accepted Orbit revision is adopted by Eon, the active profile resolves to the built artifact, and isolated installed Codex dogfood shows a fling surviving live synchronized output without restarting existing supervisors.

title: Preserve active host selection through compatible PTY output
description:
## Contract change

Consumer: an attached client performing Orbit host selection while the PTY continues producing output.

Trigger: a Begin, Update, or Finish selection gesture is active and Orbit applies ordinary PTY output that libghostty can reconcile with its tracked terminal references.

Result: ORB-C9 preserves the authoritative gesture, click classification, selected cells, and presentation through compatible output so drag, double-click word selection, and triple-click logical-line selection can finish without waiting for output to stop. Orbit remains the sole selection and terminal-state owner.

Important failures: incompatible screen replacement, resize or reflow, attachment loss, explicit cancellation, invalid tracked references, and terminal-mouse routing changes cancel safely. Frozen text after Finish remains immutable.

## Ownership and compatibility

Orbit owns this ORB-C9 behavior change. It is a compatible semantic improvement to existing ORBS v10 selection messages and requires no new wire shape. Venus remains an admission and presentation consumer; its consumer gate is eon-desktop/ven-select-during-live-output-752.

## Reference classification

Required before code: ORB-C9 and its proof, the exact Orbit interaction owner and regression tests, docs/REFERENCES.md libghostty routing, and the selection/gesture API from the pinned libghostty-vt revision. Comparison only: current Venus admission gate, to confirm no client shadow state is required. Rejected scope: new protocol messages, client-owned terminal cells or text, another queue, configurable click timing, dependencies, and platform expansion.

Portability disposition: neutral.
design:
1. Prove the existing failure at the Orbit interaction boundary by inserting PTY output between selection phases.
2. Preserve the active libghostty gesture through ordinary vt_write calls instead of maintaining any Orbit or Venus shadow coordinates.
3. Detect only demonstrated incompatible terminal transitions at the Orbit owner and clear through the existing cancellation helper.
4. Preserve completed-selection frozen text, terminal-mouse routing, revision checks, and attachment cleanup.
5. Adopt the accepted Orbit revision in Venus and Eon in later consumer runs.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A deterministic ORB-C9 regression fails before the fix and proves Begin, compatible PTY output, Update, and Finish produce an authoritative completion instead of rejection.
2. Output between clicks does not reset libghostty double-click word or triple-click logical-line classification.
3. Compatible scrolling output keeps selection anchored to authoritative terminal content; no client or protocol state is added.
4. Demonstrated incompatible screen, geometry, lifecycle, and routing transitions still cancel explicitly; completed frozen text remains stable through later output.
5. The complete locked Rust verification surface passes and ORB-C9 candidate metadata records the exact checks and remaining native Venus acceptance.
6. README LOC is current. No new dependency, protocol version, module, platform surface, or second selection owner is introduced.
notes:
Accepted correction proof: 91999d79546422b49bdbc124166a65859d0bd872 hardens ORB-C9 under unchanged exact-version ORBS v10. A Begin from an already-presented, non-future revision resolves once against current authoritative terminal state, eliminating the PTY-output race before gesture admission. Future authority, current geometry validation, ordered Resize/Selection handling, route pinning, active-gesture rejection, pressure, lifecycle cancellation, terminal-mouse transition, invalid-anchor cleanup, and frozen copy remain unchanged.

Red/green proof: authoritative_selection_accepts_presented_input_and_freezes_copy failed on c64c919 with selection frame revision is stale, then passed with the single not-ahead guard. title: Propagate reverse-screen color changes through libghostty snapshots
description:
## Problem

Fix the DECSCNM regression proven by orb-vt-unicode-baselines-i32 comment 478: after CSI ?5h, the global foreground and background in the authoritative presentation snapshot do not swap, although cell-local SGR inverse works.

Exact root evidence at pinned libghostty-vt 0.2.1 / Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083: the normal Ghostty stream handler marks terminal.flags.dirty.reverse_colors when reverse-screen mode changes, while the embedding StreamTerminal adapter groups reverse_colors with autorepeat and performs no dirty update. Orbit reads RenderState colors and serializes them correctly; Venus consumes those frame colors directly.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch VTTEST 20251205 as the real PTY child of the exact installed Eon composition.
2. Run the focused global reverse-screen DECSCNM case with distinct foreground and background colors.
3. Toggle CSI ?5h and CSI ?5l. The native Venus frame remains at the ordinary global colors instead of swapping and restoring them; the separate cell-local SGR inverse case passes. Comment 478 records the exact composition, environment, scorecard, and hashes.

## Contract Routing

Hardens ORB-C6 and preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C5 and ORB-C7 onward. It changes no ORBF or ORBS field and adds no compatibility promise. The owner is the pinned terminal dependency or its narrow Orbit integration seam, never Venus.

## Scope

Prove the missing RenderState update with one focused regression, select the smallest accepted dependency shape, and rerun the reverse-screen slice through the real composed stack. Do not invert colors after snapshot extraction, add a reverse-screen protocol flag, compensate in Venus, create another terminal-state owner, or claim general DEC or xterm compatibility.

## Acceptance Criteria

The canonical criteria are stored in this Bead acceptance_criteria field.

Before the first edit, claim this Bead, record its execution baseline, and pass the reference gate. First write one focused failing check against the actual libghostty embedding API: set distinct default foreground and background colors, feed CSI ?5h and CSI ?5l, request snapshots, and observe the swapped then restored RenderState colors without reconstructing terminal state in the test.

A crate gate is mandatory before any manifest patch, override, upgrade, replacement, or feature change. After the accepted dependency shape passes local checks, rerun only the DECSCNM VTTEST slice through the exact refreshed Eon composition, plus one ordinary-color and cell-local inverse guard. Portability disposition: neutral terminal-mode semantics with Linux proof; no macOS claim.

title: Prove no-survivor Orbit shutdown on macOS
description:
## Outcome and contract routing

Extend the accepted ORB-C12 explicit no-survivor Session shutdown contract to Apple Silicon macOS after its Linux owner proof and the ordinary Darwin Orbit runtime are accepted. This changes no protocol and creates no weaker macOS-specific shutdown promise.

- Consumer: Eon or EonTerm stopping one Orbit Session on `aarch64-darwin`.
- Trigger: the accepted Orbit shutdown path receives SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP.
- Result: graceful cleanup runs first, then every Orbit-owned descendant is gone and the owned containment is verifiably empty before success; unrelated processes remain untouched.
- Important failures: if macOS cannot establish and verify equivalent per-Session descendant containment, shutdown fails honestly and macOS remains blocked for ORB-C12 consumers. PID/name scans, process-tree snapshots, and broad user-session termination are never authority.

## Ownership and decision gate

Orbit keeps one platform-neutral shutdown state machine and one ORB-C12 contract. Only containment establishment, membership, signaling, reaping, empty verification, and cleanup may differ in the platform owner. Linux cgroup v2 is a mechanism, not the cross-platform contract.

Required before code: exact accepted `orb-prove-no-survivor-session-shutdown-btg` proof; exact `orb-prove-orbit-apple-silicon-macos-w4j` proof; current Apple process, job-control, launchd/service, signal, wait/reap, audit/inspection, and sandbox/entitlement sources; and credible no-new-dependency and native-provider shapes. Pass the crate/tool gate and stop for user approval before adding a helper, service, entitlement, or runtime dependency.

Rejected: weakening ORB-C12 on macOS, keeping a second shutdown state machine, assuming process groups contain descendants that call `setsid`, polling an eventually consistent process list as authority, requiring root, killing unrelated user work, or claiming compile-only proof.

## Acceptance

1. Exact accepted ORB-C12 and ORB-C13 proofs are prerequisites and are recorded before implementation.
2. A real Darwin regression creates initial, foreground, resistant distinct-group, and `setsid` descendants plus an unrelated sibling. Accepted shutdown succeeds within its bound only after every owned descendant is gone, direct children are reaped, owned containment is verified empty, and the sibling remains alive.
3. Graceful exit avoids escalation; resistant descendants exercise bounded escalation. Containment unavailable, permission or identity mismatch, escape, stuck cleanup, and empty-verification failure are explicit non-success.
4. The platform-neutral shutdown state machine, deadlines, exit truth, ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 behavior, and canonical protocols remain shared with Linux.
5. Native macOS and Linux canonical checks pass at exact revisions. Closure records the selected native mechanism, rejected candidates, dependency/entitlement cost, environment, bounds, limitations, and Eon/EonTerm handoff.
6. `x86_64-darwin`, packaging, signing, notarization, restart persistence, and launchd-managed background-service support remain outside this proof unless separately selected.

Stop if no unprivileged native mechanism can satisfy ORB-C12 exactly; record the macOS blocker and return for a product decision rather than weakening shutdown.
close_reason: Superseded by ORB-C14. The accepted ORB-C12 contract deliberately owns bounded PTY process-group shutdown and direct-child reaping while permitting deliberately detached survivors; the user did not choose a stronger macOS-only guarantee.

title: Prove containment-scoped explicit Orbit Session shutdown
description:
## Contract routing

Create the user-approved containment-scoped ORB-C12 explicit Session shutdown contract while preserving ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 and canonical ORBF v1 and ORBS v4.

Consumer: a local user explicitly stopping Orbit directly or through Eon/EonTerm.

Trigger: Orbit receives an accepted SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP after launching one PTY Session.

Result: accepted shutdown succeeds only after the direct PTY child is reaped and every process still in the exact Orbit-owned Linux Session containment is gone. If the direct child remains unreaped, Orbit sends SIGHUP only to that child by positive PID and gives the exact containment 500 ms to empty. Orbit never targets a numeric process group. It then escalates through cgroup.kill when members remain, requires cgroup.events populated=0, and removes the exact containment.

Ownership boundary: the direct PTY child remains signal/reap-owned. Current cgroup membership owns the rest of the Session lifecycle scope. Distinct job-control groups, setsid descendants, daemon-style forks, concurrent forks, nohup, and disown remain owned while contained. Launch or migration into an external lifecycle manager transfers forced-cleanup ownership. Orbit does not explicitly signal a handed-off process through a retained process-group relationship, but ordinary kernel terminal hangup may still signal it while it remains in the PTY foreground group; full signal isolation requires terminal-session detachment. The containment is not a hostile-code sandbox and does not promise ancestry-wide escape resistance against deliberate same-user cgroup manipulation.

Client disconnection remains the separate non-destructive ORB-C1 path.

Important failures: containment establishment fails before PTY exec. Identity, escalation, reaping, empty verification, or exact cleanup failure is bounded non-success. Orbit does not use PID, process-name, PGID, SID, or broad process-tree scans as non-child membership authority and does not signal processes outside its current containment except its still-owned direct child.

## Required references

- Current AGENTS.md, complete Bead and comments, ORB-C1 and adjacent lifecycle contracts, docs/REFERENCES.md PTY/session-lifetime route, docs/RATIONALE.md, docs/CRATES.md, platform and owner-loop code, and lifecycle tests.
- POSIX.1-2024 terminal, signal, nohup, process-group, and setsid semantics.
- Linux cgroup v2 membership, migration, cgroup.kill, cgroup.events, and delegation semantics at the recorded kernel revision.
- GNU Bash disown, GNU Coreutils nohup, systemd v255 unit ownership and KillMode=control-group, and representative tmux, Zellij, and Kitty detach/stop behavior.
- Process Triage staged action and verification plus recorded FrankenTerm, zmx, shpool, and abduco comparisons.

Rejected scope: negative process-group signaling; PGID/SID or process-tree scans; per-member graceful enumeration; freeze/pidfd machinery; privileged helper; user/cgroup or PID namespace; system-owned service; new binary; daemon; dependency; systemd runtime integration; Eon-owned PTY cleanup; remote or restart persistence; hostile-code sandboxing; or a macOS support claim.

## Smallest implementation

Use the existing owner loop, libc dependency, and platform.rs seam. Create one private per-Session cgroup before exec while Orbit remains outside. Move the PTY child into it in pre_exec. Send one positive-PID SIGHUP only to an unreaped direct child, preserve one fixed 500 ms containment interval, then use cgroup.kill only for remaining members, reap the direct child, require populated=0, and remove the exact verified cgroup.

Add no helper, namespace, service, crate, runtime, protocol, compatibility surface, process enumeration, or fallback that silently weakens stop semantics.

Portability: isolated platform dependency. Linux cgroup v2 is the proof target. macOS remains unsupported until an independently proved lifecycle-scope replacement exists; it does not need escape-resistant sandbox semantics.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A real-PTY regression creates initial, foreground, HUP/TERM-ignoring distinct-background, setsid, and concurrent-fork members plus an unrelated process outside the containment.
2. Accepted stop succeeds within the bound only after the direct child is reaped, every contained process is gone, cgroup.events reports populated=0, and the exact containment is removed; the unrelated process remains alive.
3. One real-PTY ownership-boundary check moves a same-initial-process-group descendant into a separate exact test-owned cgroup, places a different contained process group in the foreground, proves Orbit does not explicitly group-signal the handed-off process, proves Orbit stop empties its own scope without killing the handed-off process, and removes the external scope exactly during test cleanup.
4. An unreaped direct child receives positive-PID SIGHUP and the exact containment gets 500 ms to empty; resistant contained members take bounded cgroup.kill escalation. Orbit never targets a numeric process group, including after the direct child is reaped.
5. Containment unavailable, identity or permission mismatch, stale ownership, stuck cleanup, and empty-verification failure are explicit non-success; PTY exec never occurs without containment.
6. ORB-C1 detach/reattach, terminal authority, attachment, input, presentation, clipboard, and protocol behavior remain unchanged.
7. ORB-C12 remains Partially proved until an immutable accepted proof commit refreshes the canonical checks; ORB-C1 through ORB-C11 and ORBF v1 / ORBS v4 are classified and verified as preserved.
8. Focused lifecycle checks, canonical locked Rust/governance/Clippy checks, exact process observations, diff/LOC checks, and Linux environment details pass. No macOS or hostile-code containment claim is made.
notes:
Accepted result: ORB-C12 is explicit Linux Session lifecycle cleanup by exact current cgroup membership. Client disconnection remains the non-destructive ORB-C1 path. Orbit sends SIGHUP only to an unreaped direct child by positive PID, gives the containment 500 ms to empty, then uses cgroup.kill for remaining members, requires populated 0, reaps the child, revalidates identity, and removes only the exact private cgroup. Migration or launch into another lifecycle scope transfers forced-cleanup ownership; the boundary is not a hostile-code sandbox, and controlling-terminal hangup semantics remain until terminal-session detachment.

Ownership and code shape: src/platform.rs owns Linux cgroup files, identity, membership, and signaling mechanics; src/main.rs owns shutdown ordering and exit truth. The standard library and accepted libc 0.2.189 pre_exec seam are sufficient. No helper, namespace, service, binary, process scan, protocol, compatibility surface, manifest, lockfile, or runtime dependency was added.

The unit was removed. systemd 255 also documents ProtectControlGroups= as unavailable to per-user services. A system-manager transient service was unavailable without interactive authorization and would require a separately approved system policy/helper and a larger PTY/FD ownership integration.
- Accepted kernel mechanism: current Linux cgroup-v2 documentation defines cgroup-namespace delegation with nsdelegate as a migration boundary. In a disposable private child cgroup, unshare --user --map-current-user --cgroup made that child the namespace root. Direct migration to the known sibling cosmic-launcher.scope and nsenter back into the parent cgroup namespace were both rejected; the probe exited, cgroup.events reached populated=0, and the exact child cgroup was removed.

Unmapped root also makes setuid-root behavior unavailable. That silently changes ordinary shell, device, desktop-session, and sudo behavior and is not an acceptable Orbit terminal contract.
- Rejected PID namespace as primary owner: Linux guarantees that namespace members are killed when its PID 1 exits, but unprivileged creation has the same user-namespace compatibility loss and requires a new PID-1 supervisor/reaper plus proc semantics. It is larger than the membership boundary already proved by cgroup namespaces.
- Smallest credible strict shape: a separately installed, root-owned, capability-bearing launcher performs only unshare(CLONE_NEWCGROUP) after Orbit has placed it in the exact private cgroup, then immediately execs the requested command as the original UID, GID, and supplementary groups. The command receives no file capabilities from an ordinary executable, while nsdelegate keeps its descendants below the private cgroup namespace root. Orbit remains outside, retains cgroup.kill, populated=0 verification, exact identity/removal, and owner-loop exit truth.
- Security/packaging consequence: CLONE_NEWCGROUP requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the owning user namespace; capabilities(7) explicitly classifies CAP_SYS_ADMIN as overloaded. The launcher therefore creates a new privileged executable and installation policy, even if its privileged lifetime is one syscall. It must receive a separate security and packaging gate, have fixed behavior rather than configuration or a general supervisor, validate the expected cgroup/mount context, avoid privileged path or environment interpretation, and prove capabilities are absent after exec. Nix/system installation and cross-repository ownership remain unresolved.
- Adversary limit: this shape blocks an unprivileged descendant acting with the Session user authority. Privileged root execution or collusion with an already external same-user process is not proved contained and must be made explicit in the final contract proof.
- Recommendation: authorize a fresh gate for the minimal cgroup-namespace launcher; reject user systemd, an unprivileged user namespace, and a PID-namespace supervisor. Do not promote the current cgroup-only candidate or close ORB-C12 until the privileged launcher and packaging path are approved and proved.

title: Prove ORB-C14 on Apple Silicon macOS
description:
Outcome: prove the accepted ORB-C14 Apple Silicon macOS contract without weakening ORB-C1 through ORB-C13 or the accepted Linux implementation.

## Execution shape

This is a planning container, not an implementation unit. Execute these beads in order:

1. `orb-prove-orbit-apple-silicon-macos-w4j.1` — native PTY, process, attachment, filesystem, and lifecycle behavior for ORB-C1 through ORB-C12.
2. `orb-prove-orbit-apple-silicon-macos-w4j.2` — native management identity and authority for ORB-C13, then final ORB-C14 proof.

The split follows the two independent failure domains already present in `src/platform.rs`: PTY/process lifecycle and the fail-closed management trust boundary. Both reuse the same production crate and one bounded hosted Apple Silicon CI job. Their explicit IDs provide the umbrella link; no parent-child dependency is used because `bv` treats a deferred parent as blocking while `br ready` does not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Both execution beads are accepted on exact revisions and closed.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` records ORB-C14 as Proven with the exact Apple Silicon macOS environment, outermost observations, component revision, and retained proof artifact when needed.
- The unchanged candidate passes the complete Linux Rust suite and the accepted Linux ORB-C1 through ORB-C13 behavior remains supported.
- The final proof stays within the Nix-first Eon program and the R$100 monthly hosted-macOS ceiling; it does not claim Venus, Eon composition, direct distribution, x86_64 macOS, or Nova support.

## Scope

Apple Silicon macOS Orbit proof only. Do not claim or implement this epic directly; claim the first ready execution bead.

title: Run Orbit PTY Sessions on Apple Silicon macOS
description:
Outcome: Orbit can run and attach to real PTY Sessions on Apple Silicon macOS without activating the management launch path. This is the first executable slice of ORB-C14.

## Contract routing and ownership

- Consumer and trigger: a local native macOS user starts the same Orbit server/client crate used on Linux, without `--management-v1`, and drives a real PTY Session.
- Result: ORB-C1 through ORB-C12 retain their accepted semantics on `aarch64-darwin` for spawn, attach, input, resize, detach/reconnect, bounded flow control, EOF, permissions, and shutdown.
- Owner: Orbit `src/platform.rs` owns the Darwin PTY, process-group, signal, polling, descriptor, EOF, listener, and runtime-filesystem mechanisms. Existing runtime and protocol owners remain unchanged.
- Boundary: this bead does not prove ORB-C13 management authority, peer credentials, management records, process-start identity, Eon composition, Venus behavior, Nix packaging, or direct distribution. Compile-only accommodation for the later management slice is not proof.

## Reference gate

Revalidate the official Apple/Darwin and Rust/libc sources routed by `orb-pmp` against the current source revision before choosing each native mechanism. Prefer existing libc and standard-library support; any new dependency requires the repository crate gate. Record adopted and rejected mechanisms in this bead before implementation.

## Acceptance Criteria

- On hosted Apple Silicon macOS, the production Orbit binary and client build and exercise a real native PTY through spawn, attach, input, resize, detach/reconnect, EOF, and bounded shutdown observations covering the platform-sensitive parts of ORB-C1 through ORB-C12.
- The native check proves owner-only runtime-directory and attachment-socket permissions plus the accepted ORB-C12 survivor boundary without relying on Linux `/proc`, `SO_PEERCRED`, cgroups, systemd, or Wayland.
- The unchanged candidate passes the complete Linux Rust suite so the accepted Linux contract is not weakened.
- One bounded, secret-free Apple Silicon GitHub Actions job provides the hosted proof: explicit timeout, least permissions, concurrency cancellation, fork-safe behavior, no retained artifact unless failure diagnosis requires it, and paid overage disabled under the R$100 monthly ceiling.
- ORB-C14 remains partial after this bead: no native ORB-C13 or downstream platform-support claim is made.

## Scope

Minimum native runtime slice only. Stop and return to planning if correct PTY/session behavior requires a new runtime dependency, privileged helper, launchd ownership, entitlement, protocol change, or weakening any Linux/security contract.

title: Prove Orbit management authority on Apple Silicon macOS
description:
Outcome: Orbit management launch, replacement, and stop preserve ORB-C13 authority on Apple Silicon macOS, completing the native proof required for ORB-C14.

## Contract routing and ownership

- Prerequisite: `orb-prove-orbit-apple-silicon-macos-w4j.1` has accepted the native PTY/session slice on the exact candidate.
- Consumer and trigger: the same local macOS user invokes `--management-v1` launch, replacement, and stop against native Orbit runtime state.
- Result: authorized requests succeed and stale, foreign, substituted, or ambiguous endpoint/process identities fail closed with the accepted ORB-C13 outcomes.
- Owner: Orbit `src/platform.rs` owns native peer identity, process-start identity, endpoint identity, and safe filesystem primitives; `src/management.rs` remains the sole management policy owner.
- Boundary: this bead does not change the management wire protocol, trust model, Session protocol, Eon composition, Venus behavior, Nix packaging, or direct distribution.

## Reference gate

Before implementation, inspect current official Apple/Darwin sources for local-socket peer credentials, process identity and lifetime, Unix-domain endpoint identity, and filesystem race resistance. Compare them with the accepted Linux mechanisms and record the adopted mechanism, rejected candidates, and cheapest falsifier. Do not substitute UID-only or pathname-only checks for the existing identity contract.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Hosted Apple Silicon macOS proof exercises management launch, same-owner replacement, idempotent stop, `Busy`, wrong-owner/peer rejection where representable without privilege, stale process identity, endpoint substitution, record substitution, and the accepted detach boundary.
- Native identity and cleanup checks fail closed on missing, stale, mismatched, or raced evidence and preserve owner-only runtime/socket/record permissions.
- The proof extends the single bounded Apple Silicon CI job created by the prerequisite; it does not add a second hosted macOS workflow or require secrets, privileged runners, launchd, or entitlements.
- The unchanged candidate passes the complete Linux Rust suite and the native PTY/session observations from the prerequisite.
- `docs/CONTRACTS.md` records the exact accepted revision, Apple Silicon macOS environment, hosted command/observation, and artifact for ORB-C14; only then may the Venus macOS frontier activate.

## Scope

Native ORB-C13 trust boundary and final ORB-C14 evidence only. Stop and return to planning if macOS cannot supply identity evidence strong enough for the existing fail-closed contract or if a new dependency, helper service, protocol change, or weakened security invariant would be required.
notes:
Accepted result

Orbit management v1 preserves ORB-C13 on Apple Silicon macOS and completes the native Orbit boundary for ORB-C14. The shared management policy, protocol, owner loop, filesystem identity, Ready locking, replacement, permission, lifecycle, and tombstone paths are unchanged. src/platform.rs alone supplies Darwin peer identity with libc getpeereid and opaque process-start identity with libc proc_pidinfo(PROC_PIDTBSDINFO), exact-size/PID validation, bounded microseconds, checked arithmetic, and nonzero validation. Linux SO_PEERCRED and procfs start ticks remain unchanged.

Rejected shapes: UID-only or pathname-only authority; PID without start identity; LOCAL_PEERPID alone; private PROC_PIDUNIQIDENTIFIERINFO; sysctl or process scans; copied ABI values; a second management owner; protocol/schema changes; new dependency, helper, entitlement, launchd integration, workflow, or relaxed permission, identity, or timeout behavior.

Accepted proof: source 0233f4d34b294a50c5bc7f373859cf4ec04d2414 passed GitHub Actions run 34654742795. Apple job 103444570636 ran on GitHub-hosted `macos-15-arm64` runner, macOS 15.7.9 (24G830), Rust/Cargo 1.98.1, Zig 0.15.2; all-target check, 32 Orbit tests with 2 ignored, and 15 lifecycle tests passed in 2m06s. The lifecycle proves live proc_pidinfo identity, stale process-start rejection, launcher loss, one-winner/Busy replacement, status, continued presentation, Stop, natural/explicit tombstones, record/endpoint substitution, exact permissions, and cleanup. Linux job 103444570391 passed the complete canonical format/check/test/governance/Starcompass/strict-Clippy route at the same source in 4m20s: 33 Orbit tests with 2 ignored and 18 lifecycle tests.

A first native failure was a test-generated management socket at Darwin sun_path length, not a runtime-policy defect. The final fixture uses a shorter private test directory label; diagnostic stage labels remain. The fresh-eyes pass replaced the existing wrong-logical-ID negative with stale process-start rejection because the accepted Linux proof already covers logical identity mismatch and this bead owns Darwin identity. Later code simplification passes found no remaining implementation defect; a proof-record pass corrected the unobserved Apple M1 model to the exact `macos-15-arm64` runner label.

Contracts and policy: ORB-C12 and ORB-C13 proofs refresh to the exact source, and ORB-C14 is Proven at the native Orbit boundary. Venus, Eon, Nix packaging, signing, direct distribution, x86_64-darwin, remote transport, restart persistence, and same-UID sandboxing remain outside this result. The deferred umbrella planning bead is ready for a later planning-only closure; it is not modified here.

Dependency and size: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, workflow, protocols, and wire values are unchanged. Net product Rust is +5 lines: 14,468 product Rust, 15,235 total owned Rust, and 15,988 total owned implementation source.

Verification: cargo fmt --all --check; focused Linux management lifecycle tests; cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets --target aarch64-apple-darwin; cargo clippy --locked --workspace --all-targets --target aarch64-apple-darwin -- -D warnings; hosted run 34654742795; orbit-governance; source-independent and manifest-pinned source-backed Starcompass checks; br lint; LOC and contradiction scans; git diff --check.

title: Provide bounded retained-history search
description:
Contract routing:
- Requires the accepted pre-graduation Orbit history contract and a separate user-approved search contract before implementation.
- Preserves ORB-C1 through ORB-C7 and the accepted history, selection, and copy contracts.
- Orbit owns complete retained-history matching; Venus owns query interaction, result presentation, and ephemeral navigation.

Why:
Search is useful but is not required to prove native history, scrolling, selection, and copy. Keeping it separate prevents an optional indexing and query surface from delaying the minimum usable Eon dogfood path.

Scope:
- Provide bounded literal search over Orbit-retained history through the smallest authoritative libghostty-owned surface.
- Before choosing an algorithm, inspect the exact then-current published safe Rust API, public C API, and underlying Ghostty search implementation. Compare direct public reuse, a small upstream binding addition, a bounded Orbit-owned scan, and no search.
- Define explicit query-byte, direction, case, result-anchor, continuation, cancellation, pruning, epoch-change, pressure, and incomplete-result semantics.
- Add a separately owned Venus consumer that navigates exact authoritative result anchors.

Out of scope:
- Regex, fuzzy or semantic search, indexing service, durable transcript, command database, shell-history integration, cross-session search, agent API, remote search, client-side scanning of unfetched pages, copied Ghostty search code, a private libghostty adapter, or a fork.

Implementation gate:
The user activated search for contract-first planning on 2026-08-19 after the accepted history baseline and completed initial `eon-pxn` workspace slice. Before implementation, select search as the single frontier and split the reference/ownership decision, Orbit owner, Venus consumer, and acceptance work into independently provable children.

At activation, use a sufficient public libghostty search API if one exists. Otherwise determine whether a small upstream binding addition removes the complete terminal-search responsibility while preserving bounded synchronous owner-loop work. Implement an Orbit-owned bounded literal scan only after the public and upstream routes are reproducibly unavailable or insufficient. Stop for user choice before a fork, private adapter, substantial wrapper, second terminal parser, or independent history index.
design:
Current discovery evidence, not a future Reference gate: crates.io libghostty-vt and libghostty-vt-sys 0.2.1 pin Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083. The safe Rust crate exposes no terminal search module or method, and the pinned public C headers expose no search API. The underlying Ghostty terminal/search.zig exports internal Active, PageList, Screen, and Viewport search implementations and states that its search thread is unavailable in libghostty because of the xev dependency. This disproves direct public reuse at 0.2.1 but does not preselect an Orbit scan for a later version.

At activation, rerun the Reference gate against exact current identities. Prefer an existing dependency surface that removes terminal matching, Unicode, wrapping, reflow, and retained-history traversal as one responsibility. A proposed upstream addition must prove a small supported synchronous API; it must not import the unavailable search thread or its event-loop dependency by accident. If that route fails, the local fallback scans only authoritative Orbit/libghostty-retained state, performs bounded work per owner-loop turn, and adds no duplicate transcript or index by default.

Orbit owns query execution, continuation, cancellation, and authoritative anchors. Venus owns native query editing, result display, and ephemeral navigation. Any new crate, feature, fork, wrapper, or persistent index requires its own approved gate. If no shape can provide stable bounded result anchors across the accepted history lifecycle, retain no search rather than inventing a second history owner.
acceptance_criteria:
1. The user approves and indexes the search contract before implementation with exact owner, consumer, bounds, cancellation, and failure behavior.
2. Before choosing code shape, the Reference gate inspects exact then-current libghostty safe Rust and C APIs plus underlying Ghostty search machinery, and records direct public reuse, a small upstream binding addition, a bounded local scan, and no search as accepted or rejected with reproducible reasons.
3. A sufficient public libghostty API is reused. If it is absent, a small supported upstream binding addition is evaluated before local matching. Orbit-owned scanning is allowed only after those routes are unavailable or fail the accepted bounds, ownership, portability, or maintenance requirements; no private adapter, fork, copied search engine, second parser, or independent history index is introduced implicitly.
4. Literal matching is correct across Unicode, wrapping, resize and reflow, pruning, alternate-screen policy, detach, reconnect, epoch changes, and session exit.
5. Query length, retained rows scanned, work per turn, result count, continuation state, queued bytes, and cancellation latency are explicitly bounded.
6. Search cannot block PTY processing, live presentation, history interaction, semantic input, effects, or cleanup.
7. Venus receives exact authoritative result anchors and never reconstructs or searches unfetched terminal history.
8. Closure records exact Orbit and Venus proofs, libghostty and Ghostty identities, upstream outcome where attempted, compatibility order, dependency footprint, portability, LOC, performance evidence, and rejected regex, indexing, transcript, agent, private-adapter, and fork scope.

Priority:
P2 and deferred until search is selected as the sole frontier. This Bead preserves the approved search outcome without making it a pre-graduation requirement or an active implementation frontier.
notes:
Pinned discovery on 2026-08-07: libghostty-vt 0.2.1 has no public safe Rust terminal-search API; its pinned public C headers also expose none. Ghostty a887df42c56f6de86c0fe6da9c4eeca37931e083 contains internal terminal search implementations for active state, page lists, screens, and viewports, while terminal/search.zig excludes the xev-backed search thread from libghostty. Recheck all of this at activation because the binding is evolving.

The preferred ownership order is public dependency API, then a small accepted upstream exposure, then a bounded local literal scan, then no search. This order prevents Orbit from duplicating terminal semantics merely because the currently pinned wrapper lacks an API.

No dependency, binding change, upstream proposal, local scan, contract, protocol revision, or implementation is authorized by this planning correction.

Readiness reconciliation (2026-08-19): Search remains an approved outcome for later contract-first planning, but it has no approved search contract or owner-specific children and is not the active frontier.
